text: This group is traditionally listed as six, with some variations between lists. A typical version would include the two “jewels of the middle way,” Arya Nagarjuna (c. 200AD) and his heart disciple, Master Aryadeva (c. 250AD); the two “jewels of higher knowledge,” Arya Asanga and his half-brother, Master Vasubandhu (c. 350AD); and the two “jewels of accurate perception,” Masters Dignaga (c. 440AD) and Dharmakirti (c. 650AD). This way of listing the six is from the Great Dictionary (B16, R00002); see the entry under rGyan drug in any of the various editions.

text: “Lama of the Golden Isle” is a reference to Suvarna Dvipa Guru, whose personal name was Dharmakirti, not to be confused with the later master of logic and perceptual theory by the same name. He lived on the island of Sumatra c. 1000AD; a presentation about his life, and that of his contemporaries, may be found in the preface to the Diamond Cutter Classics publication Deathless Nectar for Helping Others: Notes to a Teaching on the “Crown of Knives” (bibliography entry E2 below). Vidya Kokila, an Indian master of the Middle Way school, is also dated to about 1000AD. It seems that his name should be correctly spelled in Tibetan as Rig-pa'i khu-byug, rather than Rigs-pa'i khu-byug.

The point is that—when monastics or us modern people sit, especially together, and read Je Rinpoche's text out loud—these particular lines are not (as for Je Tsongkapa) a statement of what we have accomplished, but of what we hope to accomplish. Still, on an advanced level, seeing ourselves as him and reciting his words as he would himself itself represents a traditional, powerful practice of the steps of the path.

text: These are covered in many of the more detailed presentations of the steps of the path. The Path of Bliss, for example, composed by His Holiness the First Panchen Lama, Lobsang Chukyi Gyeltsen (1565-1662), briefly describes the “cause” here as beginning with a prior practice of completely pure morality, accompanied by practices such as the perfection of giving, and then also immaculate prayers or intentions. As for essential nature, a fully functional human being is simply statistically extremely rare, among all the possible forms of life. Finally, the occurrence of a healthy, human body & mind can be compared to the metaphor of a star shining in broad daylight: impossible almost by definition. source: A Song of My Spiritual Life (tr. Chang w/ GMR, 2025)
text: We find a detailed explanation of these four, of course, in Pabongka Rinpoche's Gift of Liberation (see the section starting at f. 111b, B12, S00004). (1) The “power of the basis” involves the practice of going for refuge, in actions such as re-committing ourselves to our daily meditation practice, or daily reading of scripture. (2) The “power of destruction” refers to feeling strong regret for our mistaken actions, and of course involves a strong understanding of all the bad things those karmas will inevitably bring us. (3) The “power of restraint” is described as the most powerful of the powers, and refers to making a commitment to avoid repeating our mistake. In a case where the mistaken behavior is especially chronic or easy to commit, we might want to set a doable time limit for not repeating the action: for example, not engaging in useless talk for the next 24 hours. (4) The “power of the antidote” refers to particularly effective opposite actions, such as (with useless talk) seeking out conversations with our fellow Dharma students about the topic of emptiness.

Many versions of the root text (such as our own, here) spell this word here with a homonym: brtan-pa. This word would indicate that our feelings of disgust and exhaustion with our current life situation should be very strong, or firm.

source: A Song of My Spiritual Life (tr. Chang w/ GMR, 2025)
text: These begin with three actions that we commit physically: (1) taking life, (2) stealing others' things, and (3) sexual misconduct—here, primarily referring to adultery with another person's committed partner. Next are four bad deeds of speech: (4) lying; (5) splitting up other people with things that we say; (6) harsh types of speech; and (7) idle talk. Then finally are the three mental misdeeds of (8) being unhappy when something good happens to someone else; (9) being happy when something bad happens to them; and (10) wrong views such as the belief that the laws of karma are mistaken, or that there is no ultimate refuge.

source: A Song of My Spiritual Life (tr. Chang w/ GMR, 2025)
text: Traditional Sanskrit, and Tibetan, poetics features vivid, made-up words as sort of riddles, to represent different objects and beings in the world. Here “palm walker” (in Sanskrit, bhujaṅga) refers to a snake, since it slides on its flat belly. And then “skyglider” (in Tibetan, nam-mkha' lding) connotes the garuda, a powerful mythical eagle much like the western phoenix, and which delights in carrying off snakes and eating them in mid-air. Your translators have observed this in person with the American eagle and rattlesnake, in the Arizona desert.

source: A Song of My Spiritual Life (tr. Chang w/ GMR, 2025)
text: These three are the following. First we have the “armor-like” effort that we see here, where we are iron-plated in our determination to help all other beings. Then there is “joyful effort in the accumulation of goodness,” which is a joy in undertaking all the practices of the Dharma. And then finally we have “joyful effort in accomplishing the needs of others,” which includes for example the different traditional methods for attracting and serving our own disciples. For a great description, see as usual that of the great Pabongka Rinpoche and Trijang Rinpoche in A Gift of Liberation, starting from f. 344a (B12, S00004).

text: It appears that the standard Tibetan spelling of the term that we have translated as “individual understandings” here is so-sor rtog-pa; the English translation is supported by the most common Sanskrit original, which is pratyavekṣa. And this is how we find the spelling in our root text. But we also frequently see Tibetan writers using so-sor rtogs-pa, as we do here in the commentary, which would tend more to mean “individual realizations,” or a more direct sort of perception. It seems that what is meant here is more the understanding.

This first one is found in Je Tsongkapa's famous praise of the Buddha for teaching dependence from the point of view of emptiness (f. 15b, B9, S05275-15).

text: As is traditional, the verse is filled with classical poeticisms that date back to ancient India. The friend of the night-blooming jasmine is the moon, whose rays coax its petals open. Moon & sun are both seen as moving across the sky mounted on a grand chariot drawn by massive mythical horses, called “racers.” The “road of the gods” is a reference to the sky.

source: A Song of My Spiritual Life (tr. Chang w/ GMR, 2025)
lemma: Sustain the life of everlasting joy
text: This entire verse is a reference to an ancient Indian myth known as Samudra Manthana: the churning of an ocean of milk by the gods—using the central mountain of the world as a churning stick—to produce the nectar of immortality.

text: The historical Buddha was the leader of his clan, known as the Shakyas. Thus for example the way he is called Shakyamuni: Lord of the Shakyas.

source: The Other Side of Emptiness (tr. Chang w/ GMR, 2026)
text: “Appearance” here refers to the way in which the things we see in the world are actually composites of luminous images emerging from karmic seeds within our own mind; this is in fact why they are referred to as “dependent events,” as they rely on those seeds, planted when we were good or bad to other people. “Emptiness” then is the fact that there is nothing in the universe which does not come about in this same manner.

source: The Other Side of Emptiness (tr. Chang w/ GMR, 2026)

text: It's a tradition in these opening verses to add many allusions and poetic images. The “Land of Snows” is, of course, Tibet; also referred to here as “the northern lands.”

source: The Other Side of Emptiness (tr. Chang w/ GMR, 2026)
text: This phrase is part of the original title of Je Tsongkapa's praise of Lord Buddha for teaching dependent events, and significantly is also part of the title of Je Rinpoche's very famous work on interpreting the Buddha: The Essence of Eloquence: A Classical Commentary on the Topic of Distinguishing the Figurative from the Literal, in Lord Buddha's Teachings. The name of our Buddha's father translates as “Pure Repast.”

text: This was a catch-all term for non-Buddhist schools in ancient India, many of which believed that one could achieve salvation by sitting on a special platform slightly submerged in the Ganges River. Several typical “teachers” of these groups are named here. Those who would like further detail here can refer to the Diamond Cutter Classics publication Great Ideas of the East: A Survey of 101 Enlightening Belief Systems from Ancient Asia (%%E1).

source: The Other Side of Emptiness (tr. Chang w/ GMR, 2026)
text: We very frequently see—and most classically in the Treasure House of Higher Knowledge by Master Vasubandhu (c. 350AD) (see f. 5a, %%S1, TD04089)—the dichotomy of ethical behavior into that instigated by our own conscience, and that inspired by a concern for how others will view us. The former, in Tibetan, is called ngo-tsa (technical spelling the same); while the latter is trel-yu (spelled khrel-yod).

source: The Other Side of Emptiness (tr. Chang w/ GMR, 2026)
text: A ritual among certain non-Buddhists of ancient India, where a person sits between a number of large fires, tortured by the heat as some kind of personal purification. It basically represents any kind of practice where we purposely damage our body or mind, with the idea that it benefits us in some way spiritually.

source: The Other Side of Emptiness (tr. Chang w/ GMR, 2026)
text: Our world—and in fact the universe composed of all such worlds—is said in Buddhism to be divided into three discrete realms. We live in the desire realm, distinguished by our desire for food and sex. Beyond our level is the form realm, populated by beings of exquisite bodies and possessions who typically drop to the hells after they die, as their fine karma is exhausted. And then there is the formless realm, inhabited by suffering beings of a very subtle existence almost beyond the physical.

source: The Other Side of Emptiness (tr. Chang w/ GMR, 2026)
text: The “countless” here can also refer to a specific number from ancient times; say, ten to the sixtieth power of eons (a decillion).

text: Je Tsongkapa himself, in his Highway for Bodhisattvas, describes these five as words which are (1) deep, like the thunder roar of a dragon; (2) sweet and melodius, like a beautiful song; (3) heart-stealing, pleasing; (4) perfectly logical, in their clarity; and (5) worthy of our attention, since they contain no contradiction.

source: The Other Side of Emptiness (tr. Chang w/ GMR, 2026)
text: In ancient times in Asia, the light of the sun was perceived as hot enough to ripen crops; while the light of the moon was cool enough to reduce heat or pain.

source: The Other Side of Emptiness (tr. Chang w/ GMR, 2026)
text: The “moon” here is chandra in the Sanskrit, and thus represents Master Chandrakirti, who clarified the meaning of Arya Nagarjuna's works in works like Entering the Middle Way and A Clarification of the Verses, where “clarification” utilizes the same native word as our “light” here. Both of these classics shed light on The Root Text on Wisdom, by Arya Nagarjuna, itself that garden of night-blooming jasmine, releasing its scent only when struck by the light from this waxing disk of the moon.

source: The Other Side of Emptiness (tr. Chang w/ GMR, 2026)
text: Remember that “only this” (de kho-na) is also a code word for emptiness: the flip side of the dependence coin.

source: The Other Side of Emptiness (tr. Chang w/ GMR, 2026)
text: Lord Buddha was originally a member of the royalty in a people of India known as the Shakyas.

source: The Other Side of Emptiness (tr. Chang w/ GMR, 2026)
text: “Moon announced” is the literal meaning of the name of the great emptiness teacher Master Chandrakirti. A “young” moon is the crescent moon; and the great Hindu god of creation & destruction—Shiva—holds one at the crown of his head. Here we are picturing Je Tsongkapa, “Lobsang” Drakpa, with this same power.

source: The Other Side of Emptiness (tr. Chang w/ GMR, 2026)
text: The thousand-petalled chakra—pictured as a lotus—in the body is located in the head, connected with the intellect. The “older brother” here is Gyalwa Gendun Gyatso, His Holiness the Second Dalai Lama, senior continuation of the First, a disciple of Je Tsongkapa. The Second's name literally means “ocean of aspiration for goodness,” and he “released” the meaning of Je Rinpoche's eulogy in a work entitled The Ultimate Point of Entry. This and the resulting lineage has allowed us lucky “bees” (bhramara in Sanskrit) to enjoy this deathless nectar.

source: The Other Side of Emptiness (tr. Chang w/ GMR, 2026)
text: It is said that there are eight great dragon leaders spread throughout the seas of our planet; and so they have come to represent the number 8. Really perfect water—like the kind you'd want to have if you were offering water bowls on your altar—is said to have 8 different qualities: the water is (1) cool to the touch; (2) it is delicious to taste; (3) it is soft; (4) it is crystal-clear; (5) it does no harm to the throat; (6) it does no harm to the stomach; (7) it is free of any noxious smell, and (8) it is light.

source: The Other Side of Emptiness (tr. Chang w/ GMR, 2026)
text: A reference to Sarasvati, the traditional Indian goddess of song and poetics. The entire verse is a reference to another ancient Indian belief that the world was created when the gods churned the milk of a timeless sea. The “King of Camphor” is a reference to the moon, again used as a crown to represent high intelligence.

source: The Other Side of Emptiness (tr. Chang w/ GMR, 2026)
text: This is a sometimes-seen name which seems to relate to Lady Sarasvati (at times the consort of Gentle Voice, or Manjushri, the Buddha of Wisdom), as a reference to her lyrical skills; it is sometimes used for His Holiness the Second Dalai Lama, Gendun Gyatso (1507-1554), who has also written a commentary—entitled A Matchless Point of Entry—to Je Tsongkapa's classic on dependence. Chok-Hla Wuser (1429-1500) was an eminent scholar from Ratu Monastery who is best known for his work on the collected topics of logic; a very rare copy has been published by the Asian Classics Input Project. He is referenced in a minor writing of His Holiness Gendun Gyatso.

source: The Other Side of Emptiness (tr. Chang w/ GMR, 2026)

text: Gyaltsab Je here bows to his own immediate teacher, Je Tsongkapa Lobsang Drakpa (1357-1419). The name “Gyaltsab Je” in fact means “Lord Regent,” indicating our author's position as the direct successor of Tsongkapa in the lineage. The fact that Gyaltsab Je is continuing his own teacher's commentarial tradition to Nagarjuna's work is reflected by the lecture notes we have included at the conclusion of the present volume; they were taken by Gyaltsab Je himself when Je Tsongkapa taught the same text, and were preserved for the next six centuries.

source: The Sixty Verses of Nagarjuna (tr. Lashaw w/ GMR, 2023)
text: That is, Master Nagarjuna. Perhaps his most famed writings are the “Collection of Six Works on Reasoning”; but it's important to remember that most of the “reasoning” mentioned in these contexts refers to proving the fact of emptiness.

source: The Sixty Verses of Nagarjuna (tr. Lashaw w/ GMR, 2023)
text: We are using “realized one” as a translation of the Sanskrit word arya, which refers to anyone who has experienced the direct realization of emptiness: one of the most crucial steps for later achieving nirvana and Buddhahood. Only a handful of realized ones are classically recognized in scripture, and Master Nagarjuna is perhaps the most prominent. Thus he is often referred to simply as “The Arya,” which is why we will be capitalizing “Realized One” when it refers to him.

source: The Sixty Verses of Nagarjuna (tr. Lashaw w/ GMR, 2023)
text: A reference to Buddhist practitioners who do not accept the Mahayana, or Greater Way—which is characterized by an advanced understanding of emptiness and a desire to reach enlightenment to assist all living beings.

source: The Sixty Verses of Nagarjuna (tr. Lashaw w/ GMR, 2023)
text: The Sanskrit version of Arya Nagarjuna's text is incomplete; but we will insert fragments such as this which we find available. We will first present the full technical transcription of the line with traditional diacritical marks; and then give the closest normal English pronunciation, broken out into separate words as far as possible, for those who are not Sanskrit scholars but who may want to read the Sanskrit out loud, or even memorize specific portions. Our primary source for these fragments is Yuktiṣaṣṭikākārikā, Editions of the Sanskrit, Tibetan and Chinese Versions, with Commentary and a Modern Chinese Translation (see bibliography entry C1).

The “collection of merit” produces the physical forms of a Buddha; and the “collection of wisdom” creates their mental component: their omniscience. The most famous reference to these two is in fact the final, sixtieth and final verse within the current text of Nagarjuna.

text: The two works listed here, along with the Sixty Verses itself, represent three of Arya Nagarjuna's famed “Six Books on Reasoning.” The other three are Wisdom; Crushing Mistaken Arguments into Powder; and The String of Precious Jewels.

source: The Sixty Verses of Nagarjuna (tr. Lashaw w/ GMR, 2023)
text: See ff. 2a-2b (S8, TD03864) of Master Chandrakirti's Commentary to the Sixty Verses on Reasoning. Here, Master Chandrakirti explains that Seventy Verses on Emptiness and Putting an End to All Argument are extensions of The Middle Way (another name for Nagarjuna's Root Text on Wisdom)—and that, since they don't stand on their own, they don't have their own offerings of praise. He shows that Seventy Verses on Emptiness is a refutation of an idea put forth in The Middle Way, which starts with the lines: “Anything that grows, stays, or perishes is like an illusion, a dream, like a city of phantoms.” Putting an End to All Argument is a refutation of an idea in the work that begins with: “The nature of all things is that they lack causes. They are not things in & of themselves, nor by any means are they something else.”

text: A group of three ancient Buddhist schools who hold that what things do is inherently part of them: producing heat, for example, would be a quality which belongs to fire inherently, and does not come from the person experiencing the heat. These three schools are the Detailist; the Sutrist; and the Mind Only. See for example Pabongka Rinpoche's commentary to The Three Principal Paths (f. 36a, B42, S00034).

text: All these points need a little background. The “path of a realized being” refers to the direct perception of ultimate reality being discussed here; Gyaltsab Je is proving that it must be a product of conditions, implying a subject state of mind and objects contributing to it. Each of the eight components of this path, moreover, are as well products: right view, right thought, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration (for a nice treatment, see Je Tsongkapa's seminal work, Illumination of the True Thought, f. 61a [B38, S05408]).

This only means, of course, that there is no philosophical position which is not coming from the seeds we have planted in the past, through our good or bad actions towards others; it does not at all mean that we should never take philosophical positions, or that they don't exist.

text: This is a reference to the total of twelve links in the chain reaction of cause-and-effect dependence, as illustrated in the traditional painting of the Wheel of Life. Again, for a very detailed presentation refer to the Diamond Cutter Classics volume entitled Stopping the Circle of Sadness: The Buddhist Teaching of the Wheel of Life (E5). The twelve, in their classic order, are (1) misunderstanding; (2) fresh karma; (3) consciousness; (4) name & form; (5) the doors of sense; (6) contact; (7) feeling; (8) initial desire; (9) advanced desire; (10) ripe karma; (11) birth; and (12) aging & death.

text: This refers to a concept where all objects of perception are divided into three types: obvious ones; abstruse ones; and highly abstruse ones. Roughly, the red color of an apple would be an example of the first. A fire deep within a faraway mountain pass would be an example of the second, since it is “hidden”—in the sense that we can perceive it only through inference or deduction, based on the black color of smoke resulting from it which we can see directly. The subtle workings of the laws of karma are a traditional example of a highly abstruse object.

See for example ff. 71a-71b of the fourth volume of the overview of the perfection of wisdom by Sera Jetsun Chukyi Gyeltsen (1469-1546) (B58, S06814-4).

text: Gyaltsab Je is being sarcastic, as he was wont to do. The crucial Tibetan term here is gakja (technical spelling dgag-bya), or “what is put a stop to.” There are two forms of the gakja, and they are completely different. One is a reference to the impossible thing that emptiness is empty of; that is, anything which could exist without coming from our mental seeds (and which therefore could never exist in the first place). The other is a reference to all those (unfortunately certainly existing) negativities within ourselves that we seek to stop, by following the spiritual path. For a detailed explanation, see for example f. 60a of Kedrup Tenpa Dargye's Overview of the Middle Way (B10, S00021).

Choney Lama is playing with ones, twos, and threes, some of which need some explaining.  The three “countless” eons actually do have a count: three trillion trillion trillion trillion trillion—which is the traditional period it takes to reach enlightenment after we have achieved bodhichitta, the wish for enlightenment (itself a high accomplishment).  See for example Biographies of the Lamas of the Steps of the Path, by Yongdzin Yeshe Gyeltsen (1713-1793), Vol. 1, f. 10a (%B2, S05985); and Master Vasubandhu’s own commentary to his Treasure House, at ff. 157b-158b of Vol. 1 (%S2, TD04090).

lemma: The “two collections” are those of merit and wisdom
text: vast masses of good deeds which produce, respectively, the physical and mental bodies of a Buddha.  These bodies are also counted as “three”: the paradise body, or form of an Enlightened Being within their own heaven; the emanation body, the form that a Buddha takes to appear on different worlds to help different people; and the reality body, consisting of the omniscient mind of a Buddha, and their ultimate reality. The “three turnings of the wheel” are the three distinct periods during which Lord Buddha taught, in his lifetime.  They are named from their main subject matter: the Wheel of the Four Truths (during which he taught that things have some nature of their own); the Wheel of Nothingness (during which he taught that nothing has any nature of its own); and the Wheel of Fine Distinctions (during which he qualified his former positions on a self-nature).  See for example the fine presentation by Sera Jetsun Chukyi Gyeltsen (1469-1546) in the first volume of his dialectic analysis of the Jewel of Realizations (%B3, S06815-1, ff. 38b-39a). The “three tracks” are three approaches for attaining nirvana and Buddhahood: that of the listeners, who can listen to the highest track, and repeat it to others, but not follow it themselves; the self-made buddhas, who are not full Buddhas but attain nirvana without following a teacher in this life (although they have had countless teachers in their past lives); and the bodhisattvas of the supreme track, who act out of a desire to reach enlightenment for all living beings.  For respective explanations see the classic Great Book on the Steps of the Teaching by Geshe Drolungpa (c. 1100ad), f. 374b, Volume 2 (%B4, S00070-2); the commentary to Master Asanga’s Compendium of Higher Knowledge by Gyaltsab Je (1364-1432) (f. 194a, %B5, S05435); and the classic definition of bodhichitta in Lord Maitreya’s Jewel of Realizations (f. 2b, %S3, TD03786). The “three ways” are the lower way, where a person works for their own enlightenment only; the higher way which is open, where a person works towards the ability to achieve the good of all beings for as many eons as it takes; and the higher way which is secret—also called the Diamond Way, which requires only one lifetime.

lemma: The “three realms” are the three divisions of the universe
text: the desire realm, where people are primarily motivated by a desire for food and sex; the form realm, where beings are distinguished by an exquisite bodily form; and the formless realm, where beings have a nearly purely mental body, with no physical form.  See for example the commentary to the Treasure House by Gyalwa Gendun Drup (1391-1474), ff. 74a-74b (%B6, S05525). The “three worlds” here refer to the area below the earth; upon the earth; and above the earth.  For one reference see f. 183b of the commentary to Entering the Middle Way by the great Mongol sage Kalka Ngawang Pelden (b. 1806) (%B7, S00981).  The “three doors” are the three ways of expressing ourselves: through our actions; words; and thoughts.

A particularly popular concept with the Sutrist School of ancient India, where unchanging mental images are reflected in external concrete objects: for example, the perfect concept of a water pitcher, and the water pitcher on the table right now.  See for example the entire section starting at f. 118a of Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate, by Ngawang Tashi (1678-1738) (%B8, S00217).  “Gentle Voice” refers to the enlightened embodiment of wisdom, Manjushri.

“Steadfast Wheel” (Skt: Sthira Chakra) is an epithet of Manjushri, the divine tutor of Tsongkapa, with whom he is identified.  “Holder of the White Lotus” is another name for the divine embodiment of compassion, Loving Eyes (Skt: Avalokiteshvara, Tib: Chenresik), with whom the Dalai Lamas are traditionally identified; Ngawang Lobsang Gyatso (1617-1682) was the “Great Fifth” of this line.  Jamyang Shepa Ngawang Tsundru (1648-1721) is a distinguished precursor from the Gomang College of Drepung Monastery—and all are lineage teachers of Choney Lama.

In the customary pledge to compose his text, Choney Lama refers to the ancient Indian tradition of going to the source of gemstones—the ocean—for a wishing jewel (Skt: chintamani).  This magic stone will grant all your wishes if on the full moon you wash it in perfumed water; set it atop the finial of a victory banner; and present offerings before it.  A good scriptural source for this process is to be found in the commentary to the famous Eight Verses on Developing the Good Heart composed by Geshe Chekawa Yeshe Dorje (1101-1175) (p. 207, %B9, S00380).

In our translation here, the root text will be indicated in bold text, along with the chapter and line numbers in square braces.  Where Choney Lama has woven the words of Master Vasubandhu’s root text into his commentary, these words will be italicized.
Choney Lama here utilizes the classical form of a logical argument, to give his text a debate-ground flavor.  He will be doing this throughout the text.

The translators of the Treasure House from Sanskrit to Tibetan, incidentally, are listed in the native catalog to the Derge edition of the Tengyur as the Indian sage Jinamitra and the Tibetan master translator and editor, Peltsek Rakshita; both from the 8th century.  See ff. 448a-448b of this wonderful index (%B10, ACIP TD04569).
That is, obstacles to attaining nirvana (the permanent ending of negative emotions), and obstacles to attaining full enlightenment.

lemma: The decree of the kings of old
text: This decree is described as follows by His Holiness the First Panchen Lama, Lobsang Chukyi Gyeltsen (1570-1662): “The kings, royal ministers, and sages of old decreed that at the beginning of a work belonging to the scriptural section on vowed morality, the translator should bow down to omniscience; and at the beginning of a work belonging to the section on higher knowledge, to glorious Gentle Voice; and at the beginning of a work belonging to the section on the classics, to the Buddhas and bodhisattvas.”  See f. 9a of his “Explication of the First Chapter,” Part of "The Ocean of Fine Explanation, which Clarifies the Essence of the Essence of the ‘Ornament of Realizations,' a Classical Commentary of Advices on the Perfection of Wisdom," (entry %B11, ACIP S05942).

lemma: Enemy destroyer on the listener track
text: Meaning a person who has permanently rid themselves of the enemy of negative emotions, and thus reached nirvana; but who is still at the point where they can only listen to the teachings about reaching total enlightenment for the sake of all beings, and not yet practice these teachings in their own life. Why do you say that?  In sections of Choney Lama’s text which are written in debate format, we will supply in italics lines such as this one, where they are assumed in the traditional process of formal argument—although not necessarily written down in the text itself.

A technical term from the abhidharma (Tib: ‘dun-pa la ‘dod-chags) spelled in different variations, and little explained in the Tibetan tradition.  Our translation is based on Master Sanghabhadra’s commentary to the Treasure House (%S5, TD04091, f. 205b), where this is said to prevent one from moving beyond the desire realm; and on Master Yashomitra (%S4, TD04092, Vol. 1, f. 289b), where the translation would be more like “wanting, then desiring,” since he here defines “wanting” as happening before we obtain something desirable; and “desiring” as a feeling about something we have already obtained.  Yashomitra earlier on states that “As for what is not involved with negative thoughts, we say that they eliminate the desire of wanting—which is an expression that denotes severing the tie of the negative thoughts that focus on a particular object” (%S4, TD04092, Vol. 1, f. 72b).   Master Vasubandhu often uses similar language in his commentary to the Sutra on Dependence (%S6, TD03995).
See f. 26b of the first volume of Vasubandhu’s autocommentary to the Treasure House (%S2, TD04090).

lemma: All existing things of the twelve doors of sense
text: Another way of saying all existing things in the universe, since these twelve include all six inner organs of sense (eye; ear; nose; tongue; body—as the sensor of tangibles; and thought, counted along with the separate consciousnesses they engender) and all six “outer” objects (visible objects, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and all things as the object of the thought).  These twelve are a primary topic of the first chapter of the Treasure House.

These points will be discussed in the sixth chapter below, with lines 221-230 devoted to those who degenerate.  Please note that we will be referencing Master Vasubandhu’s root text internally by English line number (which corresponds closely to the Tibetan line number) rather than by Sanskrit or Tibetan verse number, as this is more precise in the present translation, and more useful for the reader.  The Sanskrit verse or shloka can normally be obtained by dividing by 4; thus, a reader interested in referencing the Sanskrit could check for this reference around the 57th verse of Chapter 6; and this is in fact the correct verse.

A word of advice to our readers.  Many of the teachings of the abhidharma, such as those here, may at first sight seem dry and pedantic; but they have survived for thousands of years because they force us to think more deeply about deep spiritual truths.  So just relax, surrender to the difficulty, and find an application to your real life: this is the goal.  Here, for example, do you think there is any good quality that you are actually capable of, yet have not bothered to manifest in your day-to-day life?  And isn’t that preferable to not possessing that quality in the first place, because you are incapable of it?

A type of meditation where we nearly shut down the mind—not always a desirable goal.  It will be discussed in Chapter 2; at lines 170-176 and 190-194.    Another word of advice to our reader: It’s a conundrum of these ancient commentaries that they present arguments which utilize concepts which we haven’t reached yet.  Get used to it, it’s a nice ah-ha moment later, when you do get to the section that was used to prove something earlier.

Mentioned immediately following; a nice, detailed presentation of the four is found in the treatment of this same portion of Master Vasubandhu’s root text by Gyalwa Gendun Drup; see the section starting at f. 4a of his commentary to the Treasure House (%B6, S05525).

lemma: Five unstained parts of a Buddha
text: The idea of a “stain,” and things which are free of this impurity, is central to the teachings on higher knowledge, and will be covered in detail soon below; as will the five parts of a person.
Buddhism charts five different stages in our spiritual development, each one known as a “path.”  These will be discussed in Chapter 6, “The Path and the Practitioner”

lemma: Conducive to a part of freedom
text: This is a phrase used to describe the first of the five paths, or stages in our spiritual development.  This first path is called the “path of accumulation” because, as the great sage Sera Jetsun Chukyi Gyeltsen (1469-1546) notes, “this is the first of the paths on which we are accumulating good karma to freedom” (see f. 60b of %B12, S06814-4).

bhāgīya, Tib: cha-mthun] to freedom [Skt: mokṣa, Tib: thar-pa] because, as the same author notes, “Freedom we describe as the truth of the end of pain, where we have gotten rid of the obstacles to nirvana.  A part [cha] of this freedom is the truth of the end of pain where we have gotten rid of obstacles to nirvana which are learned, [as opposed to inborn].  And this path represents a point in our spiritual life which is conducive [rjes-su mthun-pa] to achieving that part” (see f. 16a, %B13, S06826).
See f. 9b of his wonderful commentary to the Treasure House (%S7, TD04093-1).

lemma: Only by showing us the truth
text: Choney Lama is referring to the verse as it appears for example in Je Tsongkapa’s Entry Point for Amazing Miracles (see ff. 4b-5a, %B14, S00953).  Since it is well known to his readers, Choney Lama quotes only the first and last lines; we have supplied here the two intervening lines, which are: ,'gro-ba'i sdug-bsngal phyag gis mi sel la, / ,nyid kyi rtogs-pa gzhan la 'pho min te,.  Although the idea that the Buddha cannot for example wash away our mistakes with water is repeated a number of times in the ancient Indian scriptures, the source for the verse as it stands today seems to be the one, with minor differences, found in a famed work entitled A Compendium of Advices Granted for Specific Purposes (see f. 72b, %S10, TD04099).

A reference to self-made Buddhas of the “rhinoceros” type, from the famed Jewel of Realizations, by Lord Maitreya and Arya Asanga; they are so named because, like a rhinoceros, they prefer to carry out their practice alone, away from crowds of other people (see f. 5a of %S3, TD03786).  For a nice description of the rhino see Sera Jetsun at f. 30b of %B12, S06814-5.
See f. 95b of the autocommentary, at %S5, TD04091.
See ff. 94a-94b of A Praise of That Which is Beyond All Praise, at %S8, TD01138).

See f. 9b of the second volume of Master Purnavardhana’s commentary, at %S@, TD04061.  The next two lines of the Tibetan, incidentally, are ,de bzhin de bzhin gshegs byung yang, / ,bsam pa yongs smin kho na sbyong,—meaning: Those Gone Thus May make their appearance, But only those fully ripe Will be purified. For an extended presentation of this metaphor in an original sutra, see ff. 87b-89a of the Cloud of Jewels (%S9, KL00231).
From Lord Maitreya’s famed Jewel of Realizations (f. 11b, %S3, TD03786), and often quoted in the centuries since.

This concept will be discussed in Chapter 4, which is devoted to a presentation of karma.  Suffice here to say that, at certain levels of meditation and realization, we are no longer capable of certain negative deeds; and the negative deeds in question relate primarily to those which are physical, carried out either in our actions or words.  A “realized being,” as we will see, is someone who has had a direct perception of the way in which nothing is itself—what we most often call “emptiness” in other schools.
See f. 12b of the root text (%S1, TD04089).

The full statement reads, “The unstained form of self-control can be possessed by those born into the desire realm.  It is had even with those born into the formless realm; excepted are those at the exceptional concentration stage, and those born as beings without conception.”  An important condition is then added: “With those in the formless, it is had as held, but not as manifest” (f. 191b of the first part, %S2, TD04090).

lemma: Had by beings who are realized
text: At f. 11b of the root text (%S1, TD04089).

How something can be in the form realm, and not be taken in by the level of the form realm, is a fine distinction we’ll encounter a number of times in the coming masterwork.  For now, think of a deep state of meditation where we are sitting here in the desire realm, but our mind would be counted on the level of the form realm.
See f. 19b of the root text (%S1, TD04089).

See ff. 7b-8a of the commentary to the Treasure House by Master Yashomitra (%S4, Vol. 1, TD04092).  The colophon at the end of the second volume calls him rgyal-po’i sras, which would mean son of the king (prince), rather than the common rgyal-ba’i sras: son of the Victors, meaning bodhisattva.  Both expressions are abbreviated as rgyal-sras, and need to be distinguished here.  His commentary is sometimes simply referred to as the “Book of the Prince” (rGyal-sras-ma).

lemma: Actually the word of the Buddha
text: The “us” that Choney Lama is talking about—as we’ll see below—is a reference to the expression “us followers of the Sutrist School” found in the commentary of Master Yashomitra and seemingly referring to Master Vasubandhu himself.  The Tibetan particle lo in the root text here (corresponding to kila in the original Sanskrit) though is to indicate that the author of our root text (Vasubandhu) disapproves in some way of the position expressed in the verse.  We will observe this device repeatedly throughout the rest of his text, written as it was as a third-party summary of a school with which he had actually come to disagree.

As indicated, these lines are a versed summary of lists found elsewhere.  Two such sources are Master Yashomitra (see f. 9a, Volume 1, %S4, TD04092) and Master Purnavardhana (ff. 15a-15b, %S7, TD04093).  The Mongol sage Chujey Ngawang Pelden (b. 1806) remarks on how the followers of the Sutrist School question if the seven were even realized beings (f. 64b, %B15, S00987).  A possible source for the versed summary is the version found in the commentary to Master Vasubandhu by His Holiness the First Dalai Lama, Gendun Drup (1391-1474); see ff. 8b-9a, %B6, S05525.  It seems that, of these seven works, only a section of Maudgalyayana survives in the Tengyur; see for example f. 448 of the native catalog to the Derge edition of the Tengyur (%B10, TD04569).

lemma: Us followers of the Sutrist School
text: See f. 9a of Master Yashomitra’s commentary (%S4, TD04092).

We haven’t located any specific statement of this kind in the works of this master available in the Tengyur; but he does indeed employ the second option twice in covering this very section of his disciple Vasubandhu’s work—where Vasubandhu himself uses the first.  See ff. 96a-96b of his commentary to the Treasure House (%S5, TD04091).  The spelling of this teacher’s name in our text, by the way, is a common corruption, perhaps a result of the initial prenasal, where the correct ‘Dus-bzang becomes ‘Dun-bzang; or perhaps instead because the “old-school” Tibetan translation for the Sanskrit sangha includes ‘dun rather than ‘dus.
A statement by Kedrup Je, Gelek Pel Sangpo (1385-1438), an illustrious disciple of Je Tsongkapa.  See f. 44b of his treatment of the three types of vows (%B16, S05488).

It’s good to proceed into the following section with at least a rough idea of what these two refer to.  “Focus” here refers to the growth of a negative emotion or “stain” like anger because we are focusing on, or looking at, someone who makes us angry.  “Mental link” means that our general awareness, and other parts of our mind, are “stained” by anger that is linked up with them inside our thoughts.  More detail to come throughout the text.
See f. 1b of the root text (%S1, TD04089).
See f. 3b of the root text (%S1, TD04089).
See ff. 16a-16b of the root text (%S1, TD04089).
See ff. 1b-2a of the root text (%S1, TD04089).

lemma: By force of an uninterrupted path
text: As we will learn later on, this refers to the core part of the direct experience of ultimate reality; Je Tsongkapa’s illustrious disciple Gyaltsab Je, Darma Rinchen (1364-1432) explains the word “uninterrupted” here as meaning that “after this point we will no longer be interrupted by major spiritual blockages, whether manifest or potential.”  See f. 158a of his commentary on the Compendium of Higher Knowledge (%B5, S05435).

That is, involving elements of the other three truths as well.  An entire section on this and nearly every other point here is coming later on in the text; as mentioned above, it is customary to “tease” the reader with them without completely explaining them, here near the start of a commentary on higher knowledge.  Don’t get frustrated!

Choney Lama seems to be referring to a concept like that of a “hold” (Tib: thob-pa), which will come later: this is said to be a substance or force which keeps a termination “attached” to us in the way that a cinch keeps a saddle attached to a horse.

The first group mentioned consists of members of the Detailist School of ancient Indian Buddhism who followed a sage named Vatsiputra; they are famous for certain misconceptions, such as the belief in an indescribable self.  The famed Jamyang Shepay Dorje (1648-1721) states that they believed that only nirvana was an uncaused entity; and therefore empty space would not be (see f. 28b of the first volume of his massive commentary to the Treasure House, %B17, S19100).  The second group (Detailers, or Vaisheshika; not to be confused with Detailists, or Vaibhashika) are one of the eleven traditional “eternalist” schools of ancient Hinduism.  Their unique idea of space as “substance” is described by Choney Lama himself in his Brief Essence of All the Schools of Philosophy, which is included in the present Diamond Cutter Classics Translation Series (see ff. 7b-8a, %B18, S25008).

It is said that five different types of terminations were classically presented by Lord Buddha.  Two are the ones covered in the root text here: the one which occurs from individual analysis, and the one which doesn’t.  The third, called “impermanence termination,” is where the continued existence of a thing is ended by its impermanence. The fourth is “deep-meditation termination,” where certain undesirable mental states, and the negative actions they inspire, are prevented by our being in deep meditation.  The fifth is “concentration terminations for certain births,” which refers to the parts to a person—the being—that we will never be, in a certain coming life, if we maintain certain levels of deep concentration and thus avoid specific negative thoughts and deeds. The presentation of the five together is complicated, and debated at length by the few authors who have tackled it.  We have relied heavily on the presentation by Jamyang Shepay Dorje in the first chapter of his extensive commentary on higher knowledge; see f. 30b of the first volume (%B17, S19100).  Also helpful was the treatment by Kedrup Tenpa Dargye (1493-1568) in his work devoted to the form and formless realms (see ff. 20b-21a, %B19, S00017).  An important clarification was gleaned from the 8th volume of the deep-digging commentary on higher knowledge by Gyalwang Lobsang Trinley Namgyel (f. 10a, %B20, S00044).

We’re starting here with some typical arguments for a beginning student of higher knowledge.  This one hinges on an old problem.  The first chapter of the Treasure House divides things up either into 5 heaps; 12 doors of sense; or 18 categories.  The first of the heaps is called the “heap of form,” referring to the physical parts of our being.  The first category is called the “category of form,” but the word “form” in that case doesn’t mean “anything physical,” but rather “anything we can see”—that is, colors and shapes; the only physical things we can point out to another person.  The same word can simply refer to the body. The word for “form” in both cases, in the original languages, is unfortunately the same: gzugs in Tibetan, and rūpa in the Sanskrit; which leads to much confusion and many good debates.  Readers might be interested to know that the Sanskrit here corresponds to an old Indo-European root /kwrep, which means body or form, and is found in English cognates such as corpse, corps and corporate.  See p. 46 of Watkins’ American Heritage Dictionary of Indo-European Roots (%E1).
See f. 3a of the root text (%S1, TD04089).

The subject of “communicating” and “non-communicating” form is soon to be treated; again, the present reference is just a teaser.  Simply put, a traditional explanation of the two is that—when we kneel to take a vow, for example—the form our body assumes communicates to an observer that we are probably feeling some virtuous intent inside.  While we take the vow, a “cosmic photograph” is taken of that good deed, and the vow imparts a kind of aura around us.  It’s physical, but not visible to a normal observer, and thus does not communicate our intentions.  Again, more coming on this subject too.

Since, as we’ll learn below, this type of form belongs rather to “category of things”; see for example Gyalwa Gendun Drup, His Holiness the First Dalai Lama, at f. 20b of his Light on Path to Freedom, in explanation of the Treasure House (%B6, S05525).
Referring to the fact that, as we will learn later, instances of consciousness do serve as the eventual object of another of our consciousnesses.
This is a common, sort of artificial way to begin a debate with a general fact.

lemma: Equanimity in how we apply ourselves
text: The word in the ancient texts here—upekṣa in the Sanskrit, or btang-snyoms in the Tibetan—has three distinct connotations, and so qualifiers such as the “in how we apply ourselves” (Tib: ‘du-byed) are added to distinguish them.  The first refers to not overdoing it in our meditation, study, and so on—maintaining a proper balance.  The other two are “experiential” equanimity, meaning neutral feelings, between pain and pleasure; and “limitless” equanimity, which in general refers to an equal desire to see all living beings freed from pain and guided to happiness.  A good treatment of the three appears in Chujey Ngawang Pelden’s Overview of the Perfection of Wisdom (see f. 106b of Volume 1, %B21, S00982).

Four mental functions are called “variable” because they could swing towards being a virtuous state of mind or they could swing towards being non-virtuous.  The first is sleep, which is simply described as the uncontrollable withdrawal of the sense powers from their outer objects.  The second is regret, which is variable because—if we regret a good deed—that’s a bad deed; and—if we regret a bad deed—that’s a good deed.  The third and fourth are noting and examining, which are simply two modes of the mind where we are roughly noticing an object, and then delving deeper into it; these again could be good or bad.  For a nice presentation, see ff. 4b-5a of the treatment of mind and mental functions by Lama Quicksilver, Ngulchu Dharma Bhadra (1772-1851) (%B22, S06354). Deathless Nectar For Helping Others: Notes to a Teaching On the “Crown of Knives”
The text has been input from a book typeset on computer, but which records as well the original folio numbers; hence, we include both for the benefit of researchers.

The person who took the lecture notes presented here, Gyalwang Lobsang Trinley Namgyal (c. 1800), is referring to his teacher, the lama who granted the lecture, Trichen Tenpa Rabgye (1759-1815).  The “Holder of the Diamond,” or Vajradhara, is the form that Lord Buddha assumed to grant the high secret teachings of Buddhism.
It is a custom in Tibetan text that the writer (in this case, the monk who took notes of the teaching) starts with a humble introduction of himself.
It is a vow in the secret teachings not to use your Teacher’s name lightly.

Referring to the great lamas. The word “lama” in a monastic setting refers, nowadays, primarily to the reincarnated teachers.  The monastery’s name, “Ganden Samten Ling,” literally means “The Heaven Meditation Center”: a Buddhist institute of learning where you can go into a deep heaven-like meditation.  The Tibetan word for “monastery” here, bzhi-sde, is literally an ancient expression for an abbey with a required core group of four monks.  It could also simply be a misspelling of gzhi-sde, meaning a specific location.

A “lineage blessing” is where a lama gives a public recitation of the root text to the assembly, apart from the formal explanation, simply as a deep blessing.  This particular teaching went on for eleven sessions, most likely each of them requiring most of a day.  The Tibetan word for “a teaching for developing the good heart” is lojong, a genre of instruction which became popular in Tibet almost exactly a thousand years ago. This genre emphasizes developing (jong) the mind (lo); in this case, “mind” has the specific meaning of bodhichitta, or the Wish to become enlightened, in order to be of help to all living beings.  The common rendering of lojong into English as “mind training” then is an undertranslation.  For a good explanation of the term see for example f. 410a, Volume 2, of the famed Life Stories of the Teachers of the Steps to Enlightenment by the master tutor Yeshe Gyeltsen, who was also Trichen Tenpa Rabgye’s own lama (%B6, ACIP digital text S05985).

For the original, see f. 1b of his famous Guide to the Bodhisattva’s Life (%S4, ACIP digital text TD03871).  The remainder of the verse reads: For if you cannot manage / To do some good in the here and now, / How will you ever be blessed again / With such an opportunity?
A purposely loaded expression, for this is the term used in the secret teachings for enlightenment itself.

Referring to Purbuchok Ngawang Jampa (1682-1762), who took his geshe degree at Sera Monastery and became the tutor of His Holiness the 8th Dalai Lama in 1761; he is best known for his textbook on Buddhist logic and perceptual theory.

lemma: Precious tutor and Holder of the Diamond
text: Referring to Trichen Tenpa Rabgye’s own lama, Yongdzin Yeshe Gyaltsen (1717-1793) from Tsechok Ling monastery.  He also served as a mentor to the same Dalai Lama, and is best known for his exhaustive history of the teachers through whom the teachings on the steps to the path to enlightenment (lam-rim) have been passed down.
A province on the border between Tibet and Nepal.

In this instance, the name seems to connote a college of a monastery.  Jampa Munlam’s dates are unknown, but obviously overlap with Trichen Tenpa Rabgye’s; he is said to have served as the 32nd abbot of Sera Jey Monastery, where our speaker also studied.
A monastic way of saying, “between semesters.”
This is an alternate name of Purbuchok Ngawang Jampa, just mentioned.

Trichen Ngawang Chokden (1677-1751) was associated closely with Gyumey Tantric College and served as the 54th holder of the Throne of Tsongkapa, one of the highest monastic positions in Tibet.  His Holiness the 7th Dalai Lama, Kelsang Gyatso, was a renowned writer especially on topics in the secret teachings, and lived 1708-1754.

Traditionally explained in this way: People of lesser capacity seek only to save themselves from falling to a lower rebirth (as a hellbeing, craving spirit, or animal) after they die.  Those of medium capacity are developed enough to want to escape, by themselves, from all forms of rebirth in the cycle of suffering.  Those of higher capacity seek to achieve enlightenment so that they can gain the capacity to lead every living being out of their pain.

The title of our text has sometimes been translated into English with names like “Wheel of Sharp Weapons”; but we are drawing our translation, “Crown of Knives,” from a specific reference in the ancient sutras to a circular device like a bicycle wheel that floats like a modern drone in the air, and has knife-like blades swirling around on the inside, something like the rotor blade on a helicopter but facing inward from the hub. The context of the crown’s appearance in scripture is very moving, and so we have included a translation here of the entire story in which it appears (see Appendix A).  This is from a work called All the Kinds of Karma (Sanskrit: Karma Vibhanga, see ff. 465a-469b of bibliography entry %S3, KL00338-2), which in fact will itself appear as one of the volumes translated for our Diamond Cutter Wisdom Series.  A Sanskrit version is still extant, and from it we learn that the wheel has a unique Sanskrit name, asidharam chakra, meaning “the wheel fitted with knife blades” (see p. 54 of Levi’s edition below, same reference numbers).  In Tibetan this is ral-gri ‘khor-lo in the sutra and mtson-cha ‘khor-lo in modern times, both referring to a wheel of swords or other blades.

In English we have the expression of “go for the jugular,” because the jugular vein in the neck is a vulnerable point which, if pierced even slightly, will cause a person to quickly bleed to death.  The corresponding Sanskrit here is to “strike at the death point,” or marmahata—where marma means death (related English words are mortal or murder); and hata comes from the verbal root /han, meaning to strike (related word ahinsa, or “non-violence”; and even the English gun).

Lord Buddha, for example in the famous Lotus Sutra, prohibited his followers from taking the life of a human or an animal, for any purpose.  The example here is simply drawn from the everyday life of much of the world’s population, which so far still murders animals for food or other purposes.

Sakya is a district in south central Tibet known for the unique pale (kya) color of the soil (sa) there.  It’s the area where one of the four great lineages of Tibetan Buddhism was born, and thus the tradition is also called “Sakya” (not to be confused with Shakya, which is the clan in ancient India to which Lord Buddha belonged). The Sakyas have a strong heritage of explaining the concept of spiritual “killing points,” with considerable more detail for example on the third master here.  And so we have added an appendix to the current text of a translation of one of their traditional explanations, by the great sage of the secret teachings, Tsarchen Losel Gyatso (1502-1566).  Please see Appendix B below.
Remember that this teaching is being delivered in Tibet around 1800; there were very few such devices in the country at that time, all imported from India or China.

Buddhism, by tradition, charts our spiritual progress through five different stages of understanding, each one called a “path.”  We attain the very first path—known as the “path of accumulation”—when through something like a personal tragedy we gain a great sadness about the pain of this life.  See for example f. 55a of part 4 of Choney Lama’s analysis of the Jewel of Realizations (%B7, S00195).
Basically, the direct perception of emptiness achieved through having enough karmic seeds to experience spiritual bliss—a topic of the secret teachings.
The notation for folio 4b is missing from our input; it picks up again at f. 5a. {$$$Seiji check scan}

lemma: Seek from their hands a boon
text: There’s an elaborate pun in the Tibetan of these lines: the Tibetan expression for “prostration” is chak-tsel, where chak means “a boon in the hands,” and tsel means to aspire to, or to seek.
Again, one of the four Buddhist traditions of Tibet: the Nyingma School.  These four traditions should not be confused with the four great schools of ancient India.

The six traditional preliminaries to be followed before starting a meditation session are (1) preparing our meditation space; (2) putting forth offerings; (3) taking our meditation posture and preparing our heart; (4) looking upon the “Garden of Karma,” meaning the lamas and other holy beings of the lineage; (5) amassing good seeds and purifying ourselves of bad seeds, in order to have a successful meditation session; and (6) asking the high beings for help in our practice.  The Path of Bliss is an awesome, detailed presentation of the steps of the path to enlightenment composed by His Holiness the First Panchen Lama, Lobsang Chukyi Gyeltsen (1565-1662, see %B5, S05944).  It starts right out on the first page with how to conduct a meditation session.
The notation for folio 5b is missing from our input; it picks up again at f. 6a. {$$$Seiji check scan}

“Mind training” (Tib: blo-sbyong) is an alternative translation relevant to the current context but often misused to describe the spiritual genre to which this teaching belongs.  For that, in the current work we are using the translation “developing a good heart.”

lemma: Notes to a lecture on the “Path to Bliss”
text: The collected works of Trichen Tenpa Rabgye include just such a work, entitled The Daymaker, a Record which Opens the Fresh Blooms of the Lotus Flowers of Disciples Blessed with Good Karma (%B14, S06233).

A reference to the ethical life as described by Master Chandrakirti in his masterpiece, Entering the Middle Way (see f. 202b, %S5, TD03861).  Students in a Tsongkapian monastery are normally required to memorize the entire work at a young age, and would have been immediately familiar with the full verse.  This reads as follows: Other than an ethical way of life, There is no cause That can bring normal beings, And those born of the holy words, And those who have confirmed Themselves in their enlightenment, And the sons and daughters of the Victors The achievement of definite good And the higher realms of life. II.25-28

Three different categories of vows are recognized in the Buddhist tradition.  The first, foundational vows are pledges not to harm other beings, and are known as “vows of individual liberation”; the name is traditionally explained as meaning that those who keep their vows pure achieve liberation, whereas those who do not do not—it’s an individual thing.  The second category is the bodhisattva vows, where we pledge ourselves to certain commitments which stress serving others, in order to eventually become an enlightened being who can serve all beings simultaneously.  The third category is the various pledges of the secret way, which if honored will lead us to this same goal within a single lifetime.  A thorough, masterful presentation of all three is found in The String of Shining Jewels, by Geshe Tsewang Samdrup (fl. 1835), a tutor of His Holiness the 10th Dalai Lama (%B15, S00201).

This refers to five internal and five external fortunes.  Pabongka Rinpoche, in his Gift of Liberation, lists these as follows.  The internal ones are (1) you are born as a human; (2) you are born in a place where Buddhism has already spread; (3) you have a fully able body; (4) you have not committed any of the five root downfalls; and (5) you have faith in the teachings.  The five root downfalls consist of (a) killing your father; (b) killing your mother; (c) killing an arhat; (d) causing a split in the community; and (e) drawing the blood of a Buddha, with evil intent. The five external fortunes are that (1) a Buddha has appeared in this world; (2) they have granted teachings; (3) these teachings are still available; (4) people are still following the teachings; and (5) people have mercy—meaning that there are still people who support these teachings, materially.  See f. 156b of the Gift (%B8, S00004), where Pabongka Rinpoche cites Master Asanga’s Levels of the Listeners as his source for the ten.  Refer to f. 4a of the latter work (%S@, TD04036) for this original reference. The Lama in the present teaching has interpreted this last fortune as the fact that we have a teacher who has love for others, and teaches them.

lemma: Love of the heart for others
text: Again, the ultimate source here is f. 4a of Levels of the Listeners, which is written in prose.  Our speaker here is quoting a common versed version of the same, which it seems may have begun with Je Tsongkapa; see for example f. 53a of his magnificent Great Book on the Steps of the Path (%B16, S05392).

The full verses are found at f. 9a of Master Shantideva’s classic (%S4, TD03871): Now finally I have gained a life Which is extremely hard to find, And can bring me limitless benefit. Now supposedly I do possess a mind, And if—having gained a life like this— I turn around and let it lead me Down to the depths of the hells, It’s as though a spell were cast on me; As though I had no mind at all. I would not even be aware Of how confused I really was; Who can ever say what things Lie there, down deep inside us?

The lines are found on f. 10a of Shatideva’s same work (%S4, TD03871).  A relevant verse which immediately precedes them reads: You can burn me at the stake, Or chop off my head—no problem. But I will never submit, In any way at all, To the enemy of negative thoughts.

It is traditional for a lama to make opening remarks as an introduction to the main topic of the day’s teaching; and the person recording the teaching in notes breaks out of them like this in order to segue to the main subject of the talk itself.

This a translation of the Tibetan word “Kadampa,” which was the name of one of the earliest groups of Buddhists in Tibet, about a thousand years ago.  The title is traditionally explained as meaning “those for whom every instruction (ka) of their teacher strikes them as advice (dampa) intended for them personally.”  See for example p. 2 of Konchok Tenpay Drunme’s Amazing Machine of Words of Eloquence (%B17, S00960).

These three sets are described nicely by Keutsang Lobsang Jamyang Monlam (b. 1689) in his lecture notes to A Brief Presentation of the Steps of the Path.  We have provided the entire explanation, for interested readers, in Appendix C below.  You might want to turn to that now, and then return to this point in the text.

The practices listed here are known, collectively, as the Ten Ultimate Riches.  They are covered nicely by Kyabje Pabongka Rinpoche in his commentary to Je Tsongkapa’s Three Principal Paths; for the interested reader, we have translated the entire section in Appendix D below.

This list is traditionally laid out as follows.  First come the three negative deeds we commit in our actions: taking the life of any living being; stealing; and sexual misconduct, especially where we hurt two other people’s committed relationship.  Next are four negative deeds committed in speech: lying; talking in ways that split up other people; harsh words; and meaningless talk.  Finally come three negative karmas committed in thought: feeling unhappy when others get something good; feeling pleased when something bad happens to them; and mistaken viewpoints concerning spiritual truths.

How do we know when we’ve developed real renunciation?  We can always turn, for inspiration, to the story of the two boys that belonged to the sister of Ananda, a close disciple of the Buddha.  They refused to learn and practice the path, and so the sister turned them over to another famed disciple, Maudgalyayana.  He took the boys on a visit to the realms of hell, and they achieved renunciation automatically.  The full account can be found in The Foundation of Vowed Morality, spoken by the Buddha himself (see f. 120a of Part 1, %S8, KL00001).  For interested readers, we have translated this whole section in Appendix E.

That is, the protection afforded by the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.  In the deeper presentations, all three of these as protection are related directly to the understanding of emptiness.  The “core body” of the Buddha Jewel is their emptiness.  The true Jewel of the Dharma, or teaching, is the direct perception of emptiness.  And the Jewel Sangha, the Community, consists of all persons in the universe who have already undergone the direct experience of emptiness.  See the masterful presentation of Kedrup Tenpa Dargye (1493-1568), the principal textbook author for the great Sera Mey Tibetan Monastery, beginning at f. 41b in Part 2 of his Dialectic Analysis of the Perfection of Wisdom (%B18, S00001-2).
See f. 6a of his Song for Opening Pure Hearts (%B@, S05951M).  The word “faith” here has been filled in, presumably by our speaker.

The high, secret teachings of Buddhism are divided into four different groups.  These range from the practices of a group which stresses outside appearance and activities (the lowest); up to a group which teaches that all our efforts should be done on the inside, without outer manifestation (the highest).  “Profound” refers here to the true nature of reality, emptiness; while “clear” refers to the physical appearance of an angelic being.

This is a reference to the twelve traditional guidelines for a person who has made the refuge commitment.  These are: (1) Not seeking refuge in worldly objects and deities, once you have taken refuge in the Buddha. (2) Not harming any living being, once you have taken refuge in the Dharma. (3) Not associating closely with people who do not believe in the path, once you have taken refuge in the Sangha. (4) Considering any representation of the Buddha, regardless of the quality of its artistry or material, as though it were the Buddha himself or herself, once you have taken refuge in the Buddha. (5) Considering any written material at all, from a single letter on up, as though it were the Dharma itself, once you have taken refuge in the Dharma. (6) Considering even a single scrap of the saffron robe as though it were the Sangha itself, once you have taken refuge in the Sangha. (7) Going for refuge over and over again, by calling to mind the good qualities of the refuge objects. (8) In remembrance of their kindness, offering the first part of any food or drink to the refuge objects. (9) Encouraging others to take refuge. (10) Taking refuge three times each day, and three times each night, by bringing to mind the benefits of doing so. (11) Putting all your trust in the objects of refuge, during any activity you may undertake at all. (12) Not giving up the Three Jewels, even if it should cost you your life, and in every situation from that on down to doing so in jest. For a typical presentation of the twelve, see the section starting at f. 2b of the description of the refuge process by the Changlung Arya Pandita, Ngawang Lobsang Tenpay Gyeltsen (1770-1845) at %B20, S12285.

lemma: Four powers of confession and restraint
text: These four steps for purifying ourselves of bad karmic seeds are (1) the power of the basis, meaning that we review our understanding of the teachings, particularly those that relate to karmic seeds and the emptiness into which they project their results; (2) the power of destruction, where we regret our mistake deeply and consider its expanding repercussions; (3) the power of restraining ourselves in the future, which is by far the most essential of the four; and (4) the power of a balancing action, where we resolve to “balance” the karma by performing specific good deeds related to the same theme.  The presentation of these four by Pabongka Rinpoche in his famous Gift of Liberation is especially good (see the discussion starting on f. 111b, %B8, S00004).

A crucial concept in the teachings on the steps of the path is that the practices of people of the three different capacities build upon each other: we don’t reject the practices for those of lesser or medium capacity when we reach those for those of higher capacity; rather we master those and use them as a foundation.  See for example Pabongka Rinpoche’s discussion of the topic, beginning from f. 166b (%B8, S00004).
See f. 2b of his massive commentary on Je Tsongkapa’s presentation on empowerment into the hidden world of the Secret Collection (%B21, S05826).

The wording derives from the earliest teachings of the Buddha; the versification here is from Master Dharmakirti’s Commentary on Valid Perception (see f. 115b, %S10, TD04210), and would be familiar to all the monk students of philosophy in Trichen Tenpa Rabgye’s audience.
Technically known as the “three extraordinary trainings,” of morality, concentration, and wisdom.
A reference to the three greatest monasteries of the Tsongkapian tradition: Sera, Ganden, and Drepung—all in the environs of the capital city of Tibet, Lhasa.

The first refers to the Wish to become an enlightened being, so that we can serve all living creatures.  The second refers to the direct perception of ultimate reality.  See for example the discussion beginning at f. 16b of the overview of the Wish for enlightenment by Kechok Jinpa Dargye (b. 1558) (%B@, S00466).
Referring to the path of the bodhisattva, who seeks to perfect the six perfections of giving; the ethical life; patience; joyful effort; meditation; and wisdom.

This is a well-known section from A Letter to a Student, written by the Indian master Chandragomi around 650ad.  Here is the entire text of the verse: Even a cow knows enough To feed itself: To lean down and eat A few clumps of grass That it comes across by chance. And they know enough To slurp up mouthfuls of water When they’re dying of thirst, And find some puddle of water. The glory though of the human soul Is that they can think about what others want, And devote themselves to making it happen— This is happiness true, and this is real power. See f. 52a of the text (%S9, TD04183).  Je Tsongkapa comments movingly on the verse in his Middle-Length Book on the Steps of the Path: “I will tell you what is the true happiness of humankind, and its true glory, and true power.  It is the realization that it is right to take upon oneself the burden of helping others achieve what they want.  Focusing on our own wishes is something that even common beasts are capable of.  And so what makes a person great is the willingness to lose themselves, completely, in the service of others” (see f. 86b, %B9, S05393).

An important section in Master Dharmakirti’s classic where the infinity of beings is established may be found in the second chapter, in a discussion of the possibility of omniscience.  See f. 108b of the work (%S@, TD04210), as well as pp. 38-39 of the masterful commentary to the chapter by Geshe Yeshe Wangchuk (%B11, S00023-2).

lemma: Stages as they are generally described
text: The stages are seven, and collectively known as the “seven-step, cause & effect presentation for developing the Wish for enlightenment.”  They are (1) coming to a realization that every living being has been my mother; (2) recalling their kindness; (3) deciding to repay this kindness; (4) feeling a sweet love for my mothers; (5) developing compassion for them; (6) taking personal responsibility for their happiness; and (7) achieving, at last, a genuine Wish to bring them to enlightenment.  The ultimate source for this instruction is said to be The Levels of Practice by Lord Maitreya, with dictation taken by Arya Asanga (see for example the discussion including f. 128b of the section known as Levels of the Bodhisattva, %S11, TD04037).  For a nice summary see f. 3a of the second Keutsang Rinpoche’s Supplication to the Lineage (%B12 S12188).
This second of the two classical methods for developing the Wish for enlightenment comes from Master Shantideva’s famed Guide to the Bodhisattva’s Way of Life.  See f. 20b of the text (%S4, TD03871).

That is, one of the most famous meditation practices of all time, where we visualize taking away the trouble of another person, and then give them all well-being.  A classic source for this practice is The Offering to Lamas by His Holiness the First Panchen Lama, Lobsang Chukyi Gyeltsen (see f. 8b, %B23, S05892).

The spelling of the latter in Tibetan (sdar-ma) is quite rare, and in Tibetan script it looks very much like the spelling for the former (sngar-ma), which is very common.  And so the mistake is understandable.

lemma: Lifetime in the days of degeneration
text: Buddhist tradition says that there have been eras, in the far distant past, when human beings possessed lifetimes of millions of years; but that we have now reached the low point, where the span of life is no more than a hundred years.  The classic reference here is the third chapter of Master Vasubandhu’s famous Treasure House of Higher Knowledge (%S12, TD04089).  The promise of the secret way of Buddhism is that by following it we can achieve full enlightenment, and thus serve every living being constantly, within a single lifetime—even a very short one.

These lines are again from Chandragomi’s Letter to a Student, and in fact come just after the previous verse by the same author.  See f. 52a of the text (%S9, TD04183). The sun was said, in ancient times, to be pulled across the sky by seven great horses.  The full verse reads: See the sun above, Racing on his steeds, Illumining the world; See the earth below, Carrying on her shoulders The weight of humankind, And our entire world; Neither is thinking To get something for themselves; And this is the way as well Of people who possess greatness. They lose themselves In a single song: What can I do, to make others happy? What can I do, to help them?

Sometimes the number is given as sixteen, and sometimes as sixty.  See for example A Ritual for Reaching the Great Secret World of the One Who Empties the Lower Realms, f. 114a (%S13, TD02630); and The Sutra of Sagara, ff. 181a-181b (%S14, KL00153).

Basically a king of the entire world; these lived in very ancient times and drew their power from advanced spacecraft shaped like wheels.  See Chapter 3 of Master Vasubandhu’s Treasure House of Higher Knowledge (%S12, TD04089).  The “bodyguards” of bodhisattvas are protecting forces created by their incredible good karma.

This is a common name for the younger Kusali, a famous Indian master.  The famed Biographies of Teachers in the Lineage of the Steps of the Path says of him that—among all his practices—love and compassion were his focus; and that, by cherishing others, he was able to develop the precious Wish for enlightenment.  The same work describes how one day, when a man nearby was beating a dog with a stick, the Maitreya Yogi cried out and fell to the ground.  Other people watching thought that the dog was actually alright, and the yogi was making a big deal out of nothing.  But then they saw that, because of his intense compassion, he had welts on his back in exactly the same places where the dog had been hit on his.  And then they all became believers in the power of love.  See ff. 112b-113a of the text (%B13, S05985).

In this context, “listener” refers to a person who is unable to practice the path of the bodhisattva.  They listen to the bodhisattva teachings, hear them, and hear them so well that they are even able to convey them to others—but are incapable of putting these teachings into practice themselves.  See for example the explanation of “listener” by the incomparable Je Tsongkapa in his Illumination of the True Thought (f. 4b, %B24, SK05408).

lemma: Five paths of the bodhisattva track
text: We have already described the first of these five—the path of accumulation—above; see footnote %23.  The second is called the “path of preparation,” meaning that we are gaining an intellectual understanding of ultimate reality, and preparing to see it directly.  At the third path—the “path of seeing”—we undergo this matchless, direct experience.  During the fourth path, the “path of habituation,” we use this experience to break down our negative emotions forever.  The fifth path, called “no more learning,” consists of the culmination of these efforts: nirvana and enlightenment.  The classic presentation on the five paths is the sixth chapter of Master Vasubandhu’s Treaure House of Higher Knowledge (%S12, TD04089). These five paths altogether represent a “track,” and there are three possible tracks.  The lowest is that which belongs to disciples of the listener group, described above in footnote %67.  These are practitioners who are primarily focused on their own happiness.  People on the second track—called “self-made buddhas”—share this same focus, but because they have studied with countless teachers in the past, they are able to achieve nirvana in this life without great reliance on others.  (And this lower “nirvana” is here referred to as becoming a “buddha,” but with a lower-case first letter, since this is not real Buddhahood.)  The third track is that followed by bodhisattvas, who are dedicated to reaching enlightenment so that they can have the power to help countless living beings at the same time.
This Lord, of course, is Je Tsongkapa (1357-1419).  We haven’t been able to locate the reference in any of his written works.
For an extensive description of the practice of giving and taking (Tib: gtong-len), see appendix %X of this translation.

The Tibetan here uses the word GTSANG PA’I ‘UL MI to refer to servants.  Specifically this refers to people from the Tsang (Tib: gtzang) region of Tibet.  At the time of the teaching in Tibet, servants were often people coming from Tsang. See pg. 2525 of The Great Dictionary (%B25 ACIP R00002)

We have not been able to find a clear record of these eight, but the fact that they do constitute a powerful method for karmic purification is mentioned in The Sutra of How Maitreya Took his Birth in Heaven.  See f. 475a of %S2, KL00199.

lemma: Profound paths of creation and completion
text: The two famous stages of practice in the highest teachings of Buddhism.  During the first stage, we work to make contact with divine angels; during the second, they instruct us personally, to change our body and mind to become like theirs—eternally enlightened.
A pun here, since the Tibetan for “crucial point” (gnad) is the same as for “killing point.”

lemma: Approximate wisdom, which represents the real one
text: A stage in the practice of the secret teachings where spiritual energy (called prana in Sanskrit; chi in Chinese; and lung in Tibetan) enters the inner channels, especially the central channel.  See for example the treatment by Yangchen Druppay Dorje (1809-1887) in his lovely commentary to the incredible versed summary of the practice of the Diamond Angel by Tsarchen himself—a summary known as A Staircase for the Fortunate, for Ascending to the Heaven of the Angel (see f. 40a, %B3, S19111).
As opposed to the direct experience; a famous dichotomy in the secret teachings—it’s secret!

lemma: Someone wants to kill an animal
text: Of course, this is only an image, and no Buddhist should ever cause an animal’s death.
