A direct perception of emptiness brought on when—during a combined moment of great bliss—the inner winds move smoothly in the central channel (see for example Pabongka Rinpoche Dechen Nyingpo at ff. 22b-23a, %B4, S00333).
See f. 120a of Part 1 of the work (%S8, KL00001). Light on the Path to Freedom An Explanation of the Steps For Developing an Understanding That Nothing is Itself

lemma: I bow down to Gentle Glory
text: Obeisance to Gentle Glory (Manjushri, in Sanskrit) at the beginning of a text indicates that the subject of the work is emptiness.
Refers to King Shuddhodana, the father of Gautama Buddha.
In Sanskrit, Ajita; another name for Lord Maitreya, the future Buddha.
In Sanskrit, Manjughosha; another name for Manjushri.

See the following note about the author of this selection.  It is excerpted from a piece in his miscellaneous works entitled A Lamp which Dispels the Darkness of Mistaken Paths (f. 130a, %B2, S05500-46).  Incidentally, in mentioning “the path which pleases the wise,” Kedrup Je is drawing a reference to a famous verse in The Three Principal Paths, a classic summary of the path by his direct teacher, Je Tsongkapa (see f. 1a, %B8, S05275-85).

Refers to Je Tsongkapa Lobsang Drakpa (1357–1419) and his two closest disciples, Gyaltsab Darma Rinchen (1364–1432) and Kedrup Gelek Pel Sangpo (1385–1438).  They are more commonly known, respectively, by their abbreviated names of Je Tsongkapa, Gyaltsab Je, and Kedrup Je.

That is, remaining thinkers of the Detailist School; and followers of the Sutrist and Mind-Only Schools.  It is helpful from the outset to keep in mind the general structure of the four schools, from lowest to highest: (1) the Detailist School (Sanskrit: Vaibhashika); (2) the Sutrist School (Sautrantika); (3) the Mind-Only School (Chittamatra); and (4) the Middle-Way School (Madhyamika), which is itself divided into (4a) the Independent branch (Svatantrika) and (4b) the Consequence branch (Prasangika).

lemma: In its full and definitive form
text: Quoted with slight differences from Kedrup Je’s classic treatment of the secret teaching of the Wheel of Time (Kalachakra); see f. 5a of Volume 1 (%B1, S05463-1).

For the first, see ff. 70b–71b of Je Tsongkapa’s groundbreaking classic on the art of interpretation (%B9, S05396); for the second, see f. 66a of Kedrup Je’s popular manual for meditating upon emptiness (%B6, S05459).
See f. 210b of Master Chandrakirti’s masterwork (%S1, ACIP TD03861).

See f. 308 of Master Chandrakirti's autocommentary (%S2, ACIP TD03862).  The version available to us includes only the first of the two sentences here, although the intent of the second is clearly implied.

lemma: The two Buddhist schools known as “Objectists”
text: Two references help us understand the views of these two schools.  The first is from Gungtang Konchok Tenpay Drunme (1762–1823), who says, “Two schools—the Detailists and the Sutrists—are referred to as ‘Objectists,’ since when they establish outer objects, their principal focus is on them being physical matter; and because this briefer name is an easy way of referring to them.”  See f. 12b of his explanation of the schools of philosophy (%B3, S00918). The second reference is from the famed textbook writer from Sera Mey Monastery, Kedrup Tenpa Dargye (1493–1568), who states, “The two schools that we call ‘Objectists’ hold the belief that outer objects consist of grosser particles composed of tiny atoms that have no sides” (f. 163b, %B4, S00022).

Meaning an idea or viewpoint not that we are born with, but which we develop as we go through life.  The Sanskrit here is parikalpita, and we see two variants  of the corresponding Tibetan: kun-btags and kun-brtags.  The first more implies “artificial,” while the second implies “result of consideration.”

lemma: Schools of both the lesser and greater ways
text: Of the four great schools of ancient India, the two lower schools—the Detailists and the Sutrists—belong to what is known as the “lesser way.”  The two higher schools—the Mind-Only and the Middle-Way—belong to the “higher way.”  What separates these two is that followers of the higher way (Sanskrit: mahayana) are guided by the bodhisattva ideal (Skt: bodhichitta): the Wish to become an enlightened being so that we can be of service to all beings on all worlds.
See f. 48a of the same work (%B6, S05459).

Lord Buddha’s teaching career is divided into three different periods, each with a different emphasis: the first turning, focusing on the four truths; the second turning, focusing on how nothing has any quality of its own; and the third turning, focusing on fine distinctions in the teaching.  See Kedrup Tenpa Dargye, the famed author of textbooks for the esteemed Sera Mey Monastery, for a definitive presentation (ff. 5a–5b, %B13, S00010).

lemma: Never found with someone not influenced
text: From Je Tsongkapa’s Illumination of True Thought, f. 118a (%B5, ST05408).

Choney Lama has here listed some of the greatest philosophical texts ever written in Tibet, by some of her greatest thinkers, in order to drive his point home.  Here is some detail about the works mentioned; the folio numbers given are the sections where the topic treated here is broached. Distinguishing between the Literal and the Figurative is a reference to Je Tsongkapa’s famed Essence of Eloquence (see discussion on ff. 76a–76b, %B9, S05396).  In Kedrup Je’s Interlude of Emptiness, see f. 73b (%B6, S05459).  The Commentary on Difficult Points is a reference to Gelong Sherab Wangpo’s commentary to Tsongkapa’s Illumination of the True Thought; see ff. 174a–174b (%B10, S00273).  Clearing Away the Darkness is a wonderful textbook on Buddhist logic, again by Kedrup Je; see f. 151b (%B11, S05501).

Buddhism charts a person’s spiritual progress through five different levels of understanding, each one known as a “path.”  During the third and fourth paths—known as the “path of seeing” and the “path of habituation”—we are enjoying direct perceptions of ultimate truth, which serve to free us forever from more and more of our negativities. The “uninterrupted” stage of these paths consists of these direct perceptions, as they battle against the negativities; the “liberation” stage is marked by our permanent freedom from them.  For a description of the former term, see Lama Quicksilver at f. 22b of his notes on the practice of the enlightened being known as “Death Slayer” (%B15, S06415).  For the latter, refer to f. 102a of Kedrup Je’s Interlude on Emptiness (%B6, S05459). The “path of seeing” is so called because this is the point at which we first see ultimate reality directly; and the “path of habituation” is characterized by the amazing progress we make spiritually, because of what we have seen.  See Sera Jetsun’s overview of the Jewel of Realizations, f. 61a of Volume 4, for a nice literal explanation of both (%B14, S06814).

At times, our author will break into classical Buddhist debate format.  In the written version of this format, sections that are easily assumed by a trained reader are sometimes left out.  In our translation, we will supply these sections; and when debate sections refer to the opponent of the author’s viewpoint in a debate, they will be italicized, so our reader knows who’s talking.

lemma: Deny the idea of a separate self
text: See ff. 70b–71a of the work (%B9, S05396).
As previously noted, both works by Kedrup Je.
See f. 75a–75b of the work (%B9, S05396).
From Je Tsongkapa’s Ocean of Reasoning, f. 124b (%B12, S05401).

See f. 117a of Master Dharmakirti’s classic (%S3, TD04210).  The verse can only be understood with a commentary; we have followed the extraordinary explanation by Geshe Yeshe Wangchuk of Sera Mey Monastery (see pp. 193–194, %B17, S00023-2).  The context of the verse is the refutation of the Sankhya idea which says that perceiving that “nature” (Skt: prakriti) and the person (purusha) are distinct is the path to liberation.

Je Tsongkapa appears to be referencing the “witness” consciousness (yid kyi rnam-par shes-pa) and foundation consciousness (kun-gzhi rnam-par shes-pa), which he discusses earlier in the Illumination.  See f. 220b–221a (%B5, ST05408).
From f. 221a of Je Tsongkapa’s classic work on emptiness (%B5, ST05408).
Choney Lama uses the term rNam-rig-pa here, which is another word for followers of the Mind-Only School (Sems-tzam-pa).

In classical Buddhist logic, a syllogism is comprised of three parts: (a) the subject, (b) the quality to be proven about the subject, and (c) the reason why this quality is indeed true of the subject.  One traditional basic syllogism, for example, goes like this: (a) Take sound; (b) it’s a changing thing, (c) because it’s made. The validity of a syllogism is established by determining whether three relationships (tsul in the Tibetan here) hold (sgrub-pa) between these elements: (1) Does the reason (c) apply to the subject (a); that is, in this example, is sound something which is made? (2) Is it true that if something is made (c), then it must be changing (b)? (3) Is it true that if something is not changing (b), it cannot be made (c)? The classic source for this definition of a valid syllogism is the first chapter of Master Dharmakirti’s Commentary on Valid Perception (%S3, TD04210).

This type of proof (called, in Tibetan, ‘brel-zla ma dmigs-pa’i rtags) uses the absence of a necessarily related object to prove that a given object is absent.  For example, if two people always go everywhere together, then if one of them is not present in a particular place, it proves that the other is not there either.

The word that we are translating in this section as “body & mind” is actually “heaps,” which is a reference to the five parts of the person in traditional Buddhist philosophy.  These five are our physical form; feelings; discrimination; other factors; and awareness.  They are called “heaps” because each one is a composite or pile of many parts of its own.  Altogether they are exactly equivalent to the very common English expression “body & mind,” which we feel would be much more accessible to the English-speaking reader.

lemma: The very nature of things demands
text: This expression has, in time, become a synonym for logic itself; Je Tsongkapa’s close student Gyaltsab Je, for example, was considered one of the greatest logicians of all time and is classically referred to as “the lord of logic demanded by the very nature of things” (see for example the famous grace over meals found at f. 17a of Lama Quicksilver’s responses on the practice of the “Thousand Angels of the Heaven of Bliss,” %B18, S06370-15).
Which is to say, if something appears to be different from the body & mind, then it cannot be something which is self-standing and is one and the same as the body & mind.
Which is to say, if something does not exist as an object which is different from the body & mind, then it cannot be something which is self-standing, and which is different from the body & mind.

lemma: Latter part of the reason above
text: This refers to the syllogism in section %78.

lemma: The mind of a normal person
text: The expression “normal person” in this literature refers to a person who has not yet experienced ultimate reality directly.

At section %14, where all the schools from the Independent branch on down were said to assert that “the subtle lack of a self-nature to the person is the emptiness where that person is devoid of being substantial, in the sense of being self-standing.”
For a brief description of the three turnings of the wheel, see note %18.

Choney Lama is here tracing back the lineage of teachings on these topics by the Mind-Only School.  Unraveling the True Thought (a title which we sometimes translate simply as What I Really Meant) is an original sutra by Lord Buddha (from 500bc) which is considered the foundation work of the school (%S5, KD00106).  Arya Asanga (c. 350ad) formally founded the school in works such as his Levels of the Bodhisattva (%S6, TD04037); A Summary of the Greater Way (%S4, TD04048); and A Brief Presentation of “The Levels of Deep Practice” (which is anything but brief; see the two volumes at %S7, TD04038-1 and TD04038-2).  Lord (Je) Tsongkapa (1357-1419) then commented in brief upon the ideas of these works in his Essence of Eloquence (%B9, S05396); and this explanation was expanded upon by his disciple Kedrup Je in his extensive classic, An Interlude on Emptiness (%B6, S05459).
This refers to the Detailist and Sutrist Schools.

lemma: A mental seed which is solid
text: This is an unusual but not infrequent description of a mental seed which has become very entrenched, due to habitual repetition of the action which planted it; as opposed to a planting which was merely incidental.  See for example f. 69a of Geshe Tamdrin Rabten’s treatment of the art of interpretation (%B19, S00192); as well as f. 41a of that by Rabjam Mawa Lobsang Gelek (%B20, S06830).  It is sometimes said that a seed must be “solid” to produce a direct experience, as opposed to a deductive one.  See Changkya Rolpay Dorje’s masterpiece on the schools of philosophy, Part 3, f. 33b (%B21, S00062).  The great Geshe Drolungpa, in his Steps of the Teaching, has a nice comparison of perceptions that do not come from a “solid” seed to the stuff of dreams (Part 2, f. 413b, %B22, S00070).
Classically, the “such as” here refers to additional expressions such as “this is a case where visible form is remaining for a time” and “this is a case where visible form is coming to an end.”
Again, referring to someone who has yet to perceive ultimate reality directly.

Again, a reference to the Detailist and Sutrist Schools; see footnote %13 above.  In conjunction with the comments by Konchok Tenpay Drunme there, it’s helpful as well to note another difference he draws between these two groups and the Mind-Only School.  Here he refers to the way that the Objectists describe the two realities, a standard topic in Buddhist philosophy.  They say that things which can be further deconstructed belong to deceptive reality, whereas things which cannot be so deconstructed—meaning indivisible atoms—are therefore ultimate reality.  He notes finally how the Mind-Only School denies that outer objects are physical matter; and in so doing, focusses mainly on consciousness (see f. 12b, %B3, S00918).

In ancient India, a very warm place, every room would have a water pitcher on the table.  When teachers were teaching these ideas, they would automatically point to something close at hand for an example.  And so the water pitcher is a favorite example—and is often referred to as “something with a rounded belly, a flat bottom, and a tapered neck, which also holds water.”

lemma: The Powerful One, and so on
text: These are different names for a single worldly god that would be familiar to students in the author’s time who were versed in the ancient Indian literature.  “Powerful One” in Sanskrit is “Ishvara”; “Destroyer of a Hundred Cities” is “Shatakratu” (sometimes also called “Indra”); and “One with a Thousand Eyes” is “Sahasraksha.”

A common objection to it sheds light on this concept: If it’s true that there is contact without a medium, then we should be able to see something that is far away just as clearly as if it were close.  See the detailed discussion beginning on f. 103a of Chujey Ngawang Pelden’s word commentary to Entering the Middle Way (%B23, S00981).

lemma: A person who holds that things are coming from their side
text: This is a standard technical expression for a person who hasn’t yet perceived ultimate reality directly.

This is a difficult verse which is glossed exactly in the way described up to here by the great Geshe Yeshe Wangchuk, in his commentary to Master Dharmakirti’s classic.  See f. 131b of the original verses (%S3, TD04210), and p. 300 of the explanation of Chapter 3 (%B17, S00023-3).

See ff. 185a–185b of this famous sutra, spoken by Lord Buddha (%S8, KL00107).  Our readers may enjoy reading the entire context, from the original: ,BDAG MED PA YI MNYAM PA STE, ,BZHI PA RNAL 'BYOR RNAL 'BYOR PA'I, ,LTA BA THAMS CAD RNAM BZLOG PA'I, ,RTOG DANG BRTAG PA SPANGS PA STE, ,DMIGS MED SKYE BA MED PA NI, ,SEMS TZAM DU YANG NGAS BSHAD DO, The fourth way things are all equal Is in the way they are not themselves: The practitioner who puts a stop To all the ways practitioners see things Rids themselves of thoughts, Rids themselves of thinking: They see nothing, nothing starts— For I have declared It is all only mind. ,DNGOS MED DNGOS MIN MA YIN PA, ,DNGOS DANG DNGOS MED RNAM PAR SPANGS, ,DE BZHIN SEMS LAS GROL BA NI, ,SEMS TZAM DU YANG NGAS BSHAD DO, Things were never things, Nor were they ever not; Give up thinking things Are things, and give up Thinking things are not. Free yourself From the mind itself: For I have declared It is all only mind. ,DE BZHIN NYID DANG STONG PA'I MTHA', ,MYA NGAN 'DAS DANG CHOS KYI DBYINGS, ,SNA TSOGS YID KYI LUS RNAMS NI, ,SEMS TZAM DU YANG NGAS BSHAD DO, The end of all things Is the way things are; The end of all things Is emptiness. This is nirvana, the Realm of Is; And all these different bodies Are just your different thoughts— For I have declared It is all only mind. ,RNAM RTOG BAG CHAGS 'BREL PA YI, ,SNA TSOGS SEMS LAS BYUNG BA STE, ,MI RNAMS LA NI PHYI ROL SNANG, ,'JIG RTEN PA YI SEMS TZAM MO, All the kaleidoscope of things Is flowing from your imagination; Linked to the seeds inside, The outside appears to people— But all of it is only the mind Of those who live in this world. ,PHYI ROL SNANG BA YOD MED DE, ,SEMS NI SNA TSOGS RNAMS SU SNANG, ,LUS DANG LONGS SPYOD GNAS 'DRA BAR, ,SEMS TZAM DU YANG NGAS BSHAD DO, It’s not that anything at all Is appearing on the outside: The mind itself is appearing As the kaleidoscope of things. Your body, and everything you possess, And the place you live are all the same: For I have declared It is all only mind.
The discussion by Kedrup Je may be found in his Great Interlude on Emptiness; it begins on f. 150a (%B6, S05459). Kamalashila’s Great Commentary to the Diamond Cutter Sutra

For Master Kamalashila’s commentary, we will be using the Derge edition (see bibliography entry %S2, ACIP digital text TD03817); and for the Diamond Cutter itself we’ll be using the Lhasa edition (bibliography entry %S1, ACIP digital text KL00016).  We have inserted the sections of the original sutra where they are commented upon, and followed Kamalashila’s decisions on divisions to create a standard enumeration of the sutra sections. For the Sanskrit of the sutra, we are using a version compiled from different sources, primarily that of Max Müller (see bibliography entry %S1), to match the commentary and the Tibetan edition.  We would not consider this compilation final until we have compared more of the available editions (we are in the process of inputting them), but it is sufficient for scholars who wish to see the corresponding Sanskrit.  We have not located an original Sanskrit version for Master Kamalashila; nor does there appear to be a Chinese translation available. Please note that we have included here, following the commentary, a complete version of the sutra by itself in four languages: Sanskrit, Chinese, Tibetan, and English.  This way interested readers can follow the sutra’s flow by itself.

The wisdom of all the Buddhas in the form of a divine being.  We have translated names of such beings where these can be considered epithets; for a table of these names in translation and the various source languages, see the appendices. The prostration here is a traditional obeisance by the translators and editors of the commentary from Sanskrit into the Tibetan, and is not a part of the original work.  They are listed in the colophon of the Derge edition of the work as “the Indian masters named Manjushri and Jinamitra; along with the master Tibetan editor and translator Yeshe De” (see f. 267a, %S2, ACIP digital text TD03817).

“Jawbreaker” is of course an English expression for an overly difficult idea that takes its name from a very hard candy that can break your teeth.  We’ve used it here as a translation of the expression “ten pomegranate seeds,” which is meant to convey overly difficult, misleading, abstruse explanation.  See for example the discussion of the term by the great comparative philosopher Changkya Rolpay Dorje (1717-1786) (f. 18a of Vol. 1, %B1, ACIP digital text S00986).
The Sanskrit here includes the alternate traditional title of the work: The Perfection of Wisdom in 300 Lines.

This refers to the unique shape of a twinned diamond crystal, and the ritual instrument that came from it—both the diamond and the instrument are referred to with the Sanskrit word for diamond, which is vajra. Well-formed diamond crystals come in an octahedral shape such as that seen here in the first photograph.  The outline of this shape is where the diamond on playing cards, and the diamond of a baseball field, take their name from. In special cases, two of these crystals will form and meld into each other, creating the twinned shape seen in the second photograph here.  The “grain” of the diamonds, which is much like the grain of a piece of wood, then intertwines as well, creating a structure which is even more impervious than a regular diamond: it cannot be cut by any other naturally occurring substance in the universe. This twinned structure was then imitated in the common ritual instrument, or vajra, seen here in the third picture.  And so for the shape of the diamond he is describing, Master Kamalashila has tellingly taken the classic twinned, impervious crystal as his model: one which can cut anything.
Note that the primary Sanskrit edition we are utilizing gives the obeisance here as: I bow to the Conquering Lady, the Exalted Perfection of Wisdom.

This is the traditional obeisance by the translators of the original sutra from Sanskrit into Tibetan, and is thus not commented on by Master Kamalashila hundreds of years prior.  We have added it here for completeness, to match the current version.  The translators listed in the Lhasa edition are Masters Shilendra Bodhi and Yeshe De.
The Sanskrit original that we are using (Müller) divides the original sutra into 32 sections; these section numbers will be included at the beginning of each section in parantheses.

The other three demons are easily understood; the “divine youth” is actually a reference to anything that would distract us from spiritual practices which stop the Lord of Death.  See for example the explanation by Kedrup Tenpa Dargye (1493-1568) at f. 63b, Vol. 4 of his overview of the Jewel of Realizations (%B2, S00009).

A reference to the 37 high qualities which contribute to our enlightenment.  These come in seven groups; the fourth consists of the five powers of faith; joyful effort; awareness; meditative concentration; and wisdom.  See for example ff. 89a-89b of the explanation of Je Tsongkapa’s Illumination of the True Thought by Gelong Sherab Wangpo (1500-1586) (%B3, S00273).

The verse is found in another text by Master Kamalashila—his commentary to “The Mantra for Entering the State Beyond All Thought” (see f. 126a, %S3, TD04000), as well as in a secret teaching of Heruka from the Kangyur (see ff. 245b-246a, %S4, KL00840).  The latter includes a reference to the destruction of the four demons.

It is essentially a traditional definition of an Enlightened Being that they have completed, to perfection, their own and all others’ goals.  The classic reference to this is the opening lines of the Commentary on Valid Perception by Master Dharmakirti (c. 650) (see f. 94b, %S5, TD04210).

Master Kamalashila is obviously making use of a Sanskrit derivation here; it’s not definitely clear since we haven’t got a copy of the original Sanskrit of his work, but we think we’ve got it right; as with the immediately following.

As we go through the sutra, we will see the word “listener” used to describe those disciples of the Buddha who were not yet following the bodhisattva ideal of working to attain enlightenement to be of service to all beings.  It is traditionally said that they can “listen” to these higher teachings—and even repeat them to others—but are not yet capable of following these themselves.
Buddhist technical terms referring, respectively, to the teachings on emptiness and the teachings on compassion.

This is actually the name of a specific number in Buddhist literature: one to the 60th power, or 1 followed by 60 zeroes, where this number is then multiplied times an eon of nearly countless millions of years.
A traditional list of the possible comportment of a holy being: standing, sitting, sleeping, or walking.

lemma: In the way of matchless beings
text: The quoted line appears at f. 3a of the commentary to the sutra called What I Really Meant written by Master Bodhi Irddhi (a reconstruction of the Tibetan, Byang-chub rdzu-‘phrul) (%S6, TD04358).
Our Tibetan translation of the sutra here has gsol rather than mnab, but they evidently refer to the same thing.
A reference to Brahma, a worldly deity who has been born into a temporary paradise because of extremely deep, but worldly, meditation.

These are traditionally listed as twelve; a nice introduction to them may be found in the classic String of Shining Jewels, written by Geshe Tsewang Samdrup (fl. 1835), a tutor of His Holiness the Tenth Dalai Lama.  Here is a simplified list (see ff. 34a-35b, %B@, S00201): (1) Begging for ones daily food (2) Eating this food only once per day (3) Eating this food only in a single, uninterrupted sitting (4) Wearing only the three religious robes (5) Wearing robes only of inexpensive material (in Tibet, wool). (6) Wearing robes only of used or discarded cloth, dyed the proper color (7) Staying only in cloisters located well away from a population center (8) Making as ones “bedroom” the ground at the base of a tree (9) Living there under the open sky (10) Never sleeping excessively; and, when sitting, always in an unsupported meditation posture (11) Using food, clothing, utensils, and bedding which have been discarded in a charnel ground (12) Making ones mattress only from piles of grass or leaves It should be noted of course that the twelve elements of this extreme lifestyle were something appropriate to adepts in the cultural setting of ancient India; and that their application and modification to modern times should be accomplished only under the guidance of a qualified spiritual teacher.

lemma: The two ways in which nothing is itself
text: A classical distinction of the emptiness of things into the emptiness of people, and the emptiness of “things” in the sense of the parts which make up those people.

lemma: He is as well an arhat
text: The two options here rely upon different readings of the Sanksrit word arhat.  The first reflects the Sanskrit verbal root /arh, which means to be worthy.  The second combines ari, a Sanskrit word for enemy, with the verbal root /han, meaning to strike.  The English word gun, and the Sanskrit for “non-violence,” ahinsa, come from the same root.
A Buddhist technical term for last three of the ten bodhisattva levels—a point at which the bodhisattva is making strong progress in eliminating the obstacles to omniscience.

lemma: A listener or a self-made buddha
text: Referring to tracks lower than that of the bodhisattva.  Listeners have been treated above; self-made buddhas are seeking a personal nirvana and—because they have studied under countless mentors in their past lives—they reach this state in this life due primarily to their own personal effort.
A Buddhist technical term referring to emptiness.

The “path of preparation” is a point in our spiritual progress when we achieve a strong intellectual grasp of emptiness; this provides preparation for the later, direct perception. The other two paths mentioned are not standard terms.  The first most likely refers to a spontaneous perception of emptiness; see for example f. 502b of the second volume of The Great Book on the Steps of the Teaching, the extraordinary model for Je Tsongkapa’s Great Book on the Steps of the Path composed by Geshe Drolungpa Lodru Jungne (c. 1100ad) (%B4, S00070). The latter appears only in the commentary, cited above in footnote 18, to What I Really Meant composed by Master Bodhi Irddhi (%S6, TD04358).  Here it refers to wasting our life by chasing after material things, which we also perceive as “real.” Sunlight on the Path to FreedomA Commentary to the Diamond Cutter Sutra

This is entitled Words to Please Fair-Minded Folks; see bibliography entry B10 (ACIP digital text S25004) below.  We have also relied heavily on the excellent biographical summaries found in The Treasury of Names (pp. 485-490, B1, ACIP S12327) and The Treasure of Knowable Things (pp. 449-451, Vol. 1, B27, ACIP R00003).  These in turn are based largely upon a biography, which we have also referenced, written by a student ten years before the versed piece; this is known as The Play of the Stars (B13, S25005).

lemma: Ngawang Tashi of the Clan of Sey
text: His presentation of the Collected Topics of logic is perhaps the best ever, and has been included in the present Diamond Cutter Classics Translation Series.

lemma: Never again go to a bad place
text: See for example f. 23a of Je Tsongkapa’s famous Illumination of the True Thought (B19, ST05408).
See for example f. 144a, Part 1, of Master Vasubandhu’s autocommentary to his Treasure House of Higher Knowledge (S17, TD04090).

The divine embodiment of all the wisdom of all the Buddhas, also known as Manjushri.  See the appendices for a list of equivalent terms in different languages for the names of divine beings and places.
That is, the mind and the ultimate reality of an enlightened being.

That is, all the things we need and all the things that others need; and only a Buddha has accomplished both.  Perhaps the most famous discussion of this concept is that found in the opening lines of Master Dharmakirti’s Commentary on Valid Perception; see f. 94b of bibliography entry S8, corresponding to ACIP digital text TD04210.  See as well Gyaltsab Je’s renowned explanation of these lines at f. 3b of B12, ACIP S05450.

An epithet of Manjushri (Gentle Voice), the enlightened being who embodies all the wisdom of the Buddhas.  The Sanskrit here is Sthirachakra; it seems to be a reference to the traditional 8-spoked wheel which represents the continued passing on of the teachings of the Buddha; see for example f. 8a of A Ritual, Written in Prose, for Reaching the Angel of the Wheel of Solid Earth, S53, TD03309.  The name has also been used in reference to the flying disk or troop transport of a world emperor (see f. 204a of B2, S12222).
One who has seen emptiness directly, and used this knowledge to eliminate their negative emotions forever—thus reaching nirvana.
That is, Je Tsongkapa (1357-1419), greatest Buddhist master of Tibet, whose ordination name was Lobsang Drakpa.
As noted below, another name by which the Diamond Cutter Sutra is commonly known.

In the version of the Tengyur (canon of ancient Indian Buddhist works in Tibetan translation) as we currently know it, there are two Indian commentaries to the Diamond Cutter: Master Vasubandhu’s Commentary in Seven Topics and Master Kamalashila’s Detailed Commentary.  The former is more of a summary, in 25 folios; and the latter is a full 63 folios (126 pages), very detailed—this may be the point that Choney Lama is making.  See bibliography entries S16 (ACIP digital text TD03816) and S4 (TD03817).

Readers please note we will be adding to the English of the root text the reference numbers to Master Kamalashila’s commentary to the Diamond Cutter; that is, you will be able to see where he divided the text by topic, which may not always be the same place where Choney Lama makes his division.  These will be in square brackets with a “K” letter (e. g. here, [K1]).
That is, the accusative: to the other side.
The Sanskrit here is Shakra, another name for Indra.  The Tibetan literally means “Destroyer (Conqueror) of the Hundred (Cities),” where the “hundred” is simply an expression for “many many.”

It was a custom for scholars translating ancient Buddhist texts from Sanskrit into Tibetan to bow down to specific holy persons or objects, to help the reader identify the subject of the work.  This line is not part of the original sutra but is found in our edition.

Choney Lama assumes that his readers have probably memorized the original sutra and thus does not insert sections of it as he goes.  We instead have inserted these, from the Derge edition of the Tengyur, to aid the modern reader.  Our translation of the sutra is based on this careful rendering by the Tibetan translators of old; at some points the Sanskrit available to us is missing or different, but we have included it in the reference version of Choney Lama’s commentary for comparison by scholars.

The location of this ancient Indian city is about 380 miles (610 kilometers) east by road from the modern capital of New Delhi.  An ancient monastery constructed at the site of the garden has been excavated and makes for a pleasant visit.

In the present context, “listener” refers to disciples of lower capacity who can listen to the higher teachings on the bodhisattva path, and even report their contents to others, but are not drawn to put these into practice themselves.  The “bodhisattva path” is one where the spiritual practitioner seeks enlightenment in order to be of help to all living beings.  See for example Geshe Drolungpa’s great classic, The Great Book on the Steps of the Teaching, f. 374b, Volume 2 (B30, S00070-2).

Choney Lama is following a venerable convention where he weaves the words of the root text into his commentary, which can sometimes make the prose seem a little forced, because it is.  We will indicate these words in italics throughout the translation.

lemma: Six great cities of ancient India
text: The six are listed in the teachings on vowed morality as Shravasti, Vaishali, Varanasi, Champaka, Saketa (also identified with Ayodhya), and Rajagirha.  See f. 84b of Master Vinitadeva’s commentary to The Divisions of Vowed Morality (S19, TD04114).
A common epithet of the Buddha, Bhagavat in Sanskrit.
The famed disciple of Lord Buddha who serves as the protagonist of the Heart Sutra.

lemma: Impossible for a Buddha to suffer hunger or thirst
text: See ff. 233b-234a and 245b-246a of the sutra, which is especially prominent in Mongolian Buddhism (S28, KL00556).

lemma: Knowledge of the store of space
text: Basically, the ability to pluck material needs out of thin air.  A connection with an understanding of emptiness is expressed in the sutra of the bodhisattva of the same name: Knowledge of the Store of Space (S46, KL00148).
See f. 12a of this renowned work of Maitreya and Arya Asanga (S15, TD03786).

lemma: No urge to eat anything at all
text: The account may be found in two different sources: The Sutra of the Ten Qualities (f. 294b of S40, KL00053) and The Section Requested by Bodhisattva named “Highest Wisdom” (ff. 134a-134b of S38, KL00082).
Refer to the section mentioned above at ff. 233b-234a.
Another epithet for an Enlightened Being; in Sanskrit, Tathagata.

lemma: Like a lump of solid gold
text: See ff. 200b-201a of the sutra (S39, KL00047).

A form of address for Subhuti pioneered by Master Vasubandhu in his commentary, and repeated by Master Kamalashila; meant to indicate that this “junior monk” (as the sutra calls him) is not what he seems.  The term for “junior monk” in Tibetan is tse dang ldan-pa (Skt: ayushmat), which literally means “the one who has time”; and so it has itself been mistranslated on occasion as elder.  The word though is traditionally explained in monastic circles as meaning “time to go,” thus connoting junior.
See the discussion beginning at f. 209a of Master Kamalashila’s commentary (S4, TD03817).
The eighteen may be found on f. 210a of Master Kamalashila’s commentary (S4, TD03817).

lemma: Desire realm, form realm, & formless realm
text: The universe, according to the Buddha, is divided into three massive realms.  We live in the “desire realm,” so called because we are born here by attraction to sense objects typified by a desire for food and sex.  There is a higher realm (but still suffering) where beings have accumulated enough good karma to be born into a godlike realm marked by extreme physical beauty.  And above that, for those who have put together still greater good (but still impure) karma, is a realm in which beings live almost totally within the mind.  The third chapter of Master Vasubandhu’s famous Treasure House of Higher Knowledge (Abhidharma Kosha) is a classic source for information on these three (S18, TD04089).

lemma: Levels known as the Great Result and the Peak of Existence
text: The form realm is divided into four levels, the fourth of which contains eight sub-levels; and the third of these is known as the Great Result.  The formless realm is also divided into four levels: Infinite Space, Infinite Consciousness, Pure Nothing, and Peak of Existence.  Note that these levels are a karmic result of deep but content-less meditation: not a place we want to go.  Again, Master Vasubandhu’s third chapter is an important source.

lemma: Two extremes, two obstacles, and the parts of a person
text: The two extremes mentioned here are the “extreme of suffering life” and the “extreme of a lower peace.”  The first is to continue as we are, inevitably suffering and dying.  The second is to reach a lower, personal, nirvana—and to stop there, without going on to full enlightenment, from where we could help all living beings in the universe.  For a brief summary see Choney Lama’s own commentary to the third chapter of Maitreya’s Jewel of Realizations (f. 6a, B4, S00195-3). The two obstacles are obstacles to nirvana (the permanent end of our negative emotions), and obstacles to omniscience (complete Buddhahood).  For a perfect discussion, see the section starting at f. 118b of the dialectic analysis of Middle-Way philosophy by Kedrup Tenpa Dargye (1493-1568) (B24, S00022). The parts of a person are also known by the technical term of “heaps,” or huge collections of parts; these are the Buddhist equivalent of what we would simply call “mind and body.”  The five are our physical form; our feelings; our capacity to discriminate; the parts to ourselves not covered by the other four; and our consciousness.  The first chapter of Master Vasubandhu’s Treasure House is the classic source (S18, TD04089).

As noted, the reality body of an Enlightened Being can be divided into their mind, and their emptiness.  “Essence body” refers to this emptiness, which is more specifically the emptiness of the other three bodies of a Buddha: their body in paradise; their body as shown in places like our Earth; and their mind.  This particular emptiness allows these three bodies a place to manifest.
One place where his story is told is in the second part of The Foundation of Vowed Morality (S48, KL00001-2).
See for example f. 122a of the 3rd volume of the Foundation of Vowed Morality (S48, KL00001-3).

The Wish for enlightenment (which we will frequently refer to simply as “the Wish”) is sometimes divided into the “deceptive” form (Tib: kun-rdzob sems-bskyed) and the “ultimate” form (don-dam sems-bskyed).  The former is the motivation of a bodhisattva, briefly defined as the wish to become enlightened so that we can be of true help to all living beings.  The latter is a “code name” for the direct perception of emptiness.  See the discussion by Kechok Jinpa Dargye (b. 1558), starting at f. 16b of his Overview of the Wish for Enlightenment (B31, S00466).

Buddhism says that the evolution of all spiritual seekers follows a journey along five paths, or states of realization.  The first step is called the “path of accumulation,” and typically begins with a personal tragedy which alerts us to the pain of life.  The second is the “path of preparation,” where we gather information towards the goal of seeing emptiness directly.  Third is the “path of seeing,” where we do see, in deep meditation, this ultimate reality.  Fourth is the “path of habituation,” where we use what we saw to overcome our negative emotions forever.  And fifth is the “path of no more learning”: the place where we have accomplished this goal.  So the bodhisattva referred to by Choney Lama has yet to see emptiness directly.  The five paths have spawned an entire genre of literature on “how to achieve the paths” (Tib: lam thob tsul).  See for example the presentation of the paths and levels by Sera Jetsun Chukyi Gyeltsen (B22, S06826).

lemma: Total enlightenment for the sake of others
text: This most famous brief definition of bodhichitta, the Wish for enlightenment, may be found in Lord Maitreya’s Jewel of Realizations (see f. 2b, S15, TD03786).
A “realized being” (Skt: arya) refers to any person who has experienced the direct perception of emptiness.
A technical term for the non-existent thing that emptiness is empty of.

lemma: Consequence Group of the Middle-Way School
text: The Middle-Way School (Madhyamika) is the highest of four ancient schools of India taught by Lord Buddha.  It is divided into two sections: the Independent section and the Consequence section.  The former is so named because of its belief in the self-efficacy of statements of reason, an idea not accepted by the latter—which does though place great emphasis on the general utility of logical statements where we point out the absurd consequences of an opponent’s position.

lemma: They are all established by concepts
text: The reference is to a sutra named A Presentation of Vowed Morality Requested by Upali; here is the full context of these very famous lines (at f. 243b, S35, KL00068)— The petals of a rainbow Of attractive blooms open wide; Lovely palaces of pure gold Shine in the morning light. And yet there is no one at all That ever made any of them— They are all created by thoughts. The entire world Is a construction of our thoughts; None of the things we hold, None of the things we cannot, Has ever happened at all. It is all a fabrication, Like an illusion, like a mirage.
See f. 133a of Master Chandrakirti’s commentary (S5, TD03865).
See f. 85b of Je Tsongkapa’s landmark work on emptiness (B19, ST05408). How could it ever be anything else?  See ff. 109b-110a of the work (S11, TD04158).
See f. 71a of this sutra (S42, KL00127); the Tibetan for the version we have reads differently, with the same intent: ji-ltar bdag gi ‘du-shes rig, de bzhin kun tu blo yang gtong.

lemma: The prison of six different births
text: See f. 41a of his Commentary on the Wish for Enlightenment (S9, TD01800).

This seems to be a reference to a description, from the 400 Verses of Master Aryadeva, of the “ultimate bodhisattva” as someone who has seen emptiness directly at the first bodhisattva level.  See for example ff. 39a-39b of the famous commentary by Gyaltsab Je (B11, S05428).

We haven’t located the reference with certainty, although it could well be the commentary to the Compendium found in the Tengyur, by Vairochana Rakshita.  See the section beginning on f. 203b (S20, TD03943).
That is, technically the term “person” can also refer to an Enlightened Being, whereas “living being” classically refers to a suffering living being.

text: See f. 202a of Master Chandrakirti’s classic (S6, TD03861).
This term, in context such as the present, refers to someone who has not yet experienced the direct perception of emptiness: the opposite of a “realized being,” or arya.

lemma: The length of time the teachings will remain
text: See the discussion beginning on f. 221a of Master Kamalashila’s commentary (S4, TD03817).
A reference to the country of India, where in ancient times so many people were able to see emptiness directly.

The “Six Jewels” are shining examples for the world (which is sometimes called “the Continent of Jambu,” after the sound of a certain fruit dropping into the waters off its shores) who lived in ancient India: Nagarjuna, Aryadeva, Asanga, Vasubandhu, Dignaga, and Dharmakirti.  The Sakya Pandita, Kunga Gyeltsen (1182-1251), is the most illustrious teacher in the history of the long Sakya lineage of Tibet.  Buton Rinpoche Rinchen Drup (1290-1364) is a glorious Tibetan sage who took primary responsibility for assembling the Kangyur and Tengyur collections of nearly 5,000 important scriptures from ancient India.  The “Three Lords” is a reference to perhaps the greatest explicator of Buddhism in history—the Tibetan master Je Tsongkapa (1357-1419)—and his two closest disciples, Gyaltsab Je (1364-1432) and Kedrup Je (1385-1438).
See f. 222b of Master Kamalashila’s commentary (S4, TD03817). Where could you ever find?  See f. 13a of the work (S10, TD03824).

At f. 329a of the sutra, Lord Buddha speaks of teaching the Dharma as being like a dream; f. 390b also touches on the topic (S46, KL00148).

lemma: A third-order system is a thousand of these
text: See f. 9b of Master Vasubandhu’s cryptic classic (S18, TD04089).

Just one part of a long list of the matchless qualities of an Enlightened Being.  The ten include (1) knowing perfectly what can happen and what cannot, as far as what karmas can create what results; (2) knowing exactly how specific karmas will in fact ripen; (3) knowing the aspirations of every sort of being; (4) knowing the infinite variety of the categories of things; (5) knowing the different capacities of beings; (6) knowing all the different paths that beings can take; (7) knowing all the different kinds of meditation and other spiritual methods; (8) perfect perception of the past circumstances of all living beings, back through beginningless time; (9) knowing precisely where all beings were in their past life; how they died and came here; and where they will be born next; (10) a direct perception of when and where all beings will finally overcome all their negativities.  For a nice treatment see the commentary to Entering the Middle Way by Gomde Namka Gyeltsen (1532-1592), starting from f. 121a (B25, S01001).

lemma: They would be holding to some self-nature
text: See f. 38a of Je Rinpoche’s masterful commentary, commonly known as The Illumination of the True Thought (B19, ST05408).

Known as the “four fruits of the practice of virtue”; they are: entering the stream (our first direct perception of emptiness); returning once (to the desire realm, in a future life, since we still possess negativities that would take us there); never returning again; and defeating the enemy (attaining nirvana, or the permanent end of our negative emotions).

The four fruits are traditionally divided into a causal and a resultant stage: in the first, we are in the act of eliminating the negativities associated with each fruit; by the second, we are finally free of these negativities.  This is covered immediately below.

The full term here literally means “the view of the group of destruction,” and a typical explanation is found in The Precious Vase of Deathless Nectar which Helps Ourselves and Others, by His Holiness the Third Panchen Lama, Pelden Yeshe (1738-1780): The five heaps that make us up are, first of all, something which will be destroyed.  Moreover, viewing ourselves as a “self” is something which depends upon the five of these heaps grouped together.  As such, we call it the “view of the group of destruction”; and its root relies upon nothing other than our misunderstanding (B28, S12230, f. 6a). The view itself will also inevitably be destroyed, and so there is a tradition of explaining the word “destruction” in its name this way.  See for example f. 229b of the first part of Master Vasubandhu’s autocommentary to the Treasure House (S17, TD04090).

This is a reference to a set of nine different negative emotions that we feel when we focus upon objects of desire located in the desire realm.  The nine are organized into three groups of three, beginning with the grossest version of the grosser emotions; through the three degrees of medium versions; and proceeding up to the most subtle version of the subtle emotions—these last being the most difficult to rid ourselves of.  For a detailed treatment see for example the essay on the form and formless realms by Kedrup Tenpa Dargye (1493-1568) (B23, S00016).
As we’ve mentioned previous, this refers to the highest of the levels of the formless realm, and thus implies the most subtle forms of attachment for the objects of the suffering world.

Jamyang Shepay Dorje (1648-1721) explains this term as referring to negative emotions which are conducive to remaining in the desire realm, which is the “bottom end” of the three realms.  See f. 39b of the fifth volume of his commentary to the Treasure House of Higher Knowledge (B15, S19100-5).

lemma: All the rest are realized beings
text: See f. 91a of Master Asanga’s Compendium of Higher Knowledge (S1, TD04049).

In Sanskrit, Dipankara.  Our Buddha’s time spent studying under this Buddha many eons ago was an important point during his progress to enlightenment.  It is said that our Buddha, Gautama, first experienced the true Wish for enlightenment during a birth in the hell realms.  From that point, up to the point that he became enlightened, three “periods of countless eons” passed.  These consisted, respectively, of 75,000; 76,000; and 77,000 eons.  Gautama’s time with the Buddha named “Maker of Light” marked the beginning of the third period.  See Sera Jetsun’s explanation at ff. 2b-3a in his overview of vowed morality (B33, S06848).

lemma: In the future, you will become
text: The entire episode is found in a sutra named The Predictions Granted by Light-Maker; see ff. 306b-313b of S34, KL00188.  The young man receiving the prediction here seems to be called simply “The Cloud.”
See ff. 349a-349b of the sutra (S43, KL00156).
Both the Sanskrit and Tibetan expressions for “perfection” in the present context literally mean “gone to the other side”: in Sanskrit, param-ita; and in Tibetan, pha-rol tu phyin-pa.
A Buddhist technical term for someone who has not yet reached enlightenment.

lemma: Different usages of the term “perfection of wisdom”
text: Briefly, “natural perfection of wisdom” is just another word for emptiness.  “Textual” perfection of wisdom refers to classical literature of the the greater way which treats the subject of the wisdom with which we perceive emptiness, either directly or intellectually.  “Path” perfection of wisdom refers to paths (realizations) of the greater way which incorporate this same wisdom.  “Result” perfection of wisdom is the wisdom of an enlightened being.  See Choney Lama’s own commentary to the Heart Sutra (f. 3b, B9, S00220), and also Kedrup Je on the Jewel of Realizations (ff. 16b-17a, B3, S05461)
Referring of course to giving; keep an ethical way of life; refraining from anger; joyful effort in goodness; and meditation—all leading to the sixth, the perfection of wisdom.
See, respectively, the sections starting at f. 11b and f. 12a of Arya Asanga’s classic (S15, TD03786).

Choney Lama here includes an explanation of a word which will first occur in a version of this section to come below (see section K89). Different editions of the text spell the Tibetan word here ‘bri-ba or ‘dri-ba, or even mix the two in this section (they are pronounced identically).  The sutra itself, in the version we have it, gives a tense of the former; but note that the reference to The Middle & Extremes (found on f. 44a, S14, TD04021) has a form of the latter.  Happily, the verb “to write” is accepted in either spelling; as are the verbs ‘brid and ‘drid, which mean to redirect, or to mislead.  These are pronounced almost identically to the former pair of words and are evidently what Choney Lama is referring to here.

lemma: That one of the four powers
text: The “four powers” are four steps used to purify oneself of the power of a negative karma.  The one mentioned here is the fourth and final one.  Briefly, the four consist of (1) re-connecting with ones understanding of how things work, and with the traditional places of shelter; (2) feeling sincere regret motivated to stop the negative karmic seed, and prevent its powerful daily growth; (3) a commitment not to repeat this kind of negative deed; and (4) a commitment to some positive karmic action to “balance” the karma.  A classic presentation may be found in Pabongka Rinpoche’s Gift of Liberation, Thrust into Our Hands, at ff. 111b-112b (B29, S00004).

lemma: No more than a simple headache
text: For the treatment in Master Bhavaviveka’s Blaze of Reasoning, see f. 173a of the work (S12, TD03856).  We haven’t located the original source of the verse here; some of its content may be found on f. 424a of a sutra called Reaching the Attainment of Buddhahood by Cleaning Yourself of Bad Deeds Using that Pure Form of Regret which Leads to Great Liberation Spreading in All Directions, and this is presumably the text being referred to here (S36, KL00264).

These different types of results are a major topic in the second chapter of the Treasure House of Higher Knowledge (Abhidharma Kosha).  A “result consistent with its cause” here refers to a result which is of the same class as its cause; especially with regard to the three realms (desire, form, formless). An “owner” result is one which comes from a specific cause named a “doer” cause; this refers to everything in the world whose arisal is not prevented by a specific factor.  In this sense, the birth of a baby in Britain could result from a surfer riding a wave in Indonesia.  A “result of separation” refers to the state achieved by eliminating specific negative qualities from our being. For details see ff. 129a-129b of Choney Lama’s own excellent commentary to the Treasure House (B8, S00027).

This refers to levels in our spiritual development where we have yet to see emptiness directly, and our understanding of this concept is so far based largely upon belief in the descriptions we receive from our teachers and the scriptures; thus, we are still for example on one of the first two of the five paths: the path of accumulation, or the path of preparation (see also footnote 44).  The term is described by Geshe Drolungpa (c. 1050) in his Great Book on the Steps of the Teaching, a prototype for Je Tsongkapa’s own Great Book on the Steps of the Path, written three centuries later (see f. 425b of Vol. 2, B30, S00070).
For Je Rinpoche’s annotation, see f. 455a of his commentary on the Secret Collection (B16, S05282).
See also footnote 88 above for details of the story.

lemma: “Mastery” stage of the path of preparation
text: Third of the four stages of this path; famous for being the point at which our intellectual understanding of emptiness is so strong that we can no longer ever take a lower rebirth.  See for example Jamyang Shepa’s End of All Error, Vol. 2, f. 142a (B14, S00839).

lemma: Anything which cannot be a thing
text: See ff. 458a-458b of the sutra (S29, KL00118).

lemma: Before it is given the name
text: See f. 18b of the famed text by Master Asanga (S2, TD04048).  A nice explanation of this verse comes in another work by Choney Lama, an explanation of emptiness meditation called Light on the Path to Freedom (see ff. 6b-7b, B6, S25002).  This translation of this text is included in the present Diamond Cutter Classics Series.

The ultimate source of this quotation is an interesting question.  It is used frequently in the Tibetan literature and almost always attributed simply to “sutra,” and understood to be the Buddha speaking.  Je Tsongkapa gives the citation several times in the “modern” version found here and mentions that it comes from a “listener” or lower-way sutra (see his Essence of Eloquence, on the Art of Interpretation, f. 72a, B17, S05396). An older version is found twice in the abhidharma literature (which belongs in fact to the lower way) of the Tengyur, and in some other sections.  The first of the two from the former gives a partial form of the “early” version of the verse (see f. 86a of Master Vasubandhu’s autocommentary, S17, TD04090).  A full form of the early version is found in the commentary to his Treasure House by Master Shamathadeva (see ff. 82a-82b of the second part of S21, TD04094). To understand it, we need to know that a female arhat (a person who has already reached the high goal of nirvana) named simply Brag in the Tibetan is spending the summer retreat near Shravasti, where by coincidence the Buddha taught the Diamond Cutter Sutra.  Brag (pronounced Drak) can mean “Lady of the Mountain Cave,” and it could well be that she is the lady saint Ri-ma of the Udrayana epic, since both names in the original Sanskrit are Shaila. In the abhidharma account, this nun is sitting practicing in the forest.  A demon sees her and determines to distract her.  He takes the form of a handsome young man and walks up to her and asks her a question about where living beings have come from, and where they are going. In reply, she gives the extended form of the verse, which includes: ,bdud kyi sems-can snyam sems nas, ,'di ni lta-bar gyur-pa ste, ,'du-byed phung-po 'di stong ste, ,'di la sems-can rnyed ma yin, ,ji-ltar yan-lag tsogs la ni, ,shing-rta'i 'du-shes dran-pa 'byung, ,de-bzhin phung-po'i nyer-len las, ,kun-rdzob tu ni sems-can brjod, Demon, I can read your thoughts! This is the way you should see it: This mountain of causes is empty— No living being is here. When we look at the parts Of a wagon, the thought Of a wagon comes to us; It’s the same with beings, Since only deceptively We can speak of the parts We have taken at birth As being a living being. In some of the later literature, the demon is properly equated with the misunderstanding of how we see ourselves in our parts, due to our karmic seeds.
See f. 114a of Arya Nagarjuna’s great String of Jewels (S11, TD04158).
See f. 10b of Master Vasubandhu’s Treasure House of Higher Knowledge (S18, TD04089).

lemma: Put a stop to the seed
text: See f. 16a of his 400 Verses (S3, TD03846).

This is a reference to the eighth chapter of the classic sutra What I Really Meant—a chapter which is dedicated to a question by Maitreya.  See the discussion beginning on f. 46b (S41, KL00106).

Several of the Sanskrit versions include the final line found here in the Sanskrit, but it is not found in the Tibetan, which is quite authoritative; the line would read something like “Thus it is taught, and taught well.”  Max Müller however gives a version of the line based on a Japanese version of the sutra which would seem to fit the entire theme of the sutra perfectly.  This is kathaṃ ca saṃprakāśayet yathā na prakāśayet tenocyate saṃprakāśayet, which would be: As much is taught is also not taught; and thus can we say it is taught.

See f. 39a of the Arya’s Commentary on the Wish for Enlightenment (S9, TD01800).  The “Cousin of the Sun ” here is an epithet of Gautama Buddha; this version of the final line does not appear in this particular work but does in a text called the Jewel Lamp of the Middle Way written by Master Bhavya, who says that he is “closely following Nagarjuna” (see f. 266b, S13, TD03854).
See f. 267a of Master Kamalashila’s commentary (S4, TD03817).
This verse seems to be a summary of the section of the sutra beginning at f. 72a (S44, KL00080).

lemma: To the north through the north
text: This would seem to be a reference to fairly numerous statements of this kind in the perfection of wisdom sutras.  See for example f. 200b of the 8,000 Lines (S25, KL00012) and ff. 55b-56a in part 4 of the 100,000 Lines (S49, KL00008).
A reference to Je Tsongkapa (1357-1419).  The “Father and Son” are the realized being Nagarjuna and his spiritual son Aryadeva (both 3rd century).

lemma: “Root Text on Wisdom” and “Entering the Middle Way”
text: The two most important works from ancient India upon the subject of emptiness, composed respectively by the realized being Nagarjuna (c. 200ad) and Master Chandrakirti (c. 650ad).
A poeticism for the bird, which is born once when the egg comes out of its mother, and again when the egg breaks open.

A reference to the realized being Nagarjuna (c. 200ad), and his heart disciple Master Aryadeva, but by extension to the entire lineage of masters and their spiritual sons and daughters of the tradition of the emptiness teachings.  A “realized being” in this context is someone who has seen emptiness directly, called an arya in Sanskrit.

Refers to the teachings on emptiness and compassion, respectively; all three of the lands can refer either to above, below, and upon the earth, or else to the desire realm, form realm, and formless realms.  Lord of the Able is an epithet of Lord Buddha.

Traditionally the word innovator is reserved for those greatest teachers who have founded a major tradition in this world; the great Changkya Rolpay Dorje for example identifies the “three innovators” as Maitreya, Arya Nagarjuna, and Arya Asanga (see Part Three of his famed Survey of the Schools of Philosophy, bibliography entry %B1, ACIP catalog #S00062, f. 2b).  In this case though we can assume that Je Tsongkapa is honoring the three sages he has just mentioned: Master Buddha Palita; Master Chandrakirti; and Master Shantideva.

In Tibetan, rgya-chen spyod-pa’i phyogs, referring to the teachings upon the Wish for enlightenment, as opposed to the teachings upon the profound view that all things are empty (zab-mo lta-ba’i phyogs).  For a nice explanation see ff. 118a-118b of the first volume of Yongdzin Yeshe Gyeltsen’s famed biography of the teachers of the tradition of the steps to enlightenment (%B@, S005985).

lemma: Four major languages of ancient India
text: Je Tsongkapa himself lists these four in his "Commentary of the Commentary of the Names”: A Revelation of the Meaning of the Words in "The Lamp of Illumination," an Extensive Commentary upon the King of All Secret Teachings, the Glorious Secret Collection (Guhyasamaja) (bibliography entry %B2, ACIP S05282, f. 1b):

lemma: “In India there were four great language groups
text: Prakirta, the natural or native language of each different locality; Avabhransha, or corrupted dialects; Pishacha, or the language of the spirits [called meat-eaters, or pishacha]; and Sanskrit, the well-formed language—the Tongue of the Gods.”  Note that the Tibetan translation for the word sanskirta is typically literal: sam for well and kirta (the correct pronunciation of the vocalic r) for formed.  The correct spelling of the third language listed is apabhransha, or literally “languages that have wandered away,” and this line has been the apparent victim of a miscarving {@Ven J check}.  Please note that throughout this translation we will be presenting the prenasal sound in its correct pronunciation, dependent upon the quality of the following consonant, rather than confusing the pronunciation with the transcription (for example m with a dot under it), as is unfortunately often the case among many modern Sanskritists.

The current rules of euphonic combination (sandhi) would require that these two words of the title be combined into one word with a long a between, and in fact the title appears this way for example in the ancient Tibetan transcription of the Sanskrit name of the commentary by Master Jayananda (see the opening lines at ACIP TD03870).  We also observe though several other instances of the variant found here, with the short final a followed by a break and an then an initial short a (see for example the opening lines of the original text at ACIP TD03861, and of the autocommentary at ACIP TD03862).  It is interesting to speculate that this may be some Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit variant for the common conversion of a final e to a before vowels other than a short a; that is, “entering into the middle way,” with the use of a final e to indicate the locative, and the space between the two words retained after the change {%check this last with Buddhist Hybrid grammar}.

lemma: Classical Commentary on the Middle Way
text: A popular nickname for Arya Nagarjuna’s masterpiece, The Foundational Verses on the Middle Way entitled “Wisdom” (ACIP TD03824, bibliography entry %S4).
From the opening lines of Master Chandrakirti’s autocommentary (ACIP TD03862, entry %S3, f. 220b).

See for example f. 121a of the Autcommentary, where Master Chandrakirti uses this wording to reference the 18th chapter of Wisdom; f. 243a, where he references the 24th; and f. 252a, where he references the 20th (ACIP TD03862, entry %S3).

Master Bhavaviveka’s commentary upon Arya Nagaruna’s Wisdom; compare for example the two usages of “middle way” at f. 46a (dBu-ma’i bstan-bcos bshad par bya’o, or I shall undertake to explain the “Classical Commentary on the Middle Way”) and at f. 136b (dbu-ma smra-ba rnams, or those who belong to the school of the Middle Way) (ACIP TD03853, entry %S5).

The great Jamyang Shepay Dorje of Drepung Monastery (1648-1721), in his Entry Point for Those of Great Virtue: A Dialectical Analysis of “Entering the Middle Way” which is a Veritable Treasure Trove of Scriptural Reference and Reasoning that Clarifies Every Profound Point of the Work (ACIP S13000, %B3, f. 4a), identifies this position as belonging to Master Jayananda, and in the latter’s commentary on Entering the Middle Way we do find the statement, “The Classical Commentary on the Middle Way [doesn’t] describe, in detail, the deceptive and ultimate natures of things; here though they are so described, and this is in fact why Master Chandrakirti wished to compose Entering the Middle Way, which is how this classical commentary thus enters into the other” (TD03870, f. 2b).  The negative particle is missing in the Derge carving!  (@JIK check carving)

lemma: This is a truly unique system
text: From f. 347a of the Autocommentary (entry S3, TD03862).

lemma: Present suchness in an unerring way
text: From f. 347b of the Autocommentary (entry %S3, TD03862).  With this spelling of the quotation especially, the second commentary mentioned is Master Chandrakirti’s own Entering the Middle Way.  Although this edition of Je Tsongkapa’s Illumination (the Trashi Hlunpo edition, ST05408) and the other two in the ACIP database (Kumbum edition, SK05408; and Gurudeva {@Jiki check, 267ff total} edition, SA05408) give the phrase by Master Chandrakirti here spelled as bstan-bcos kyis, the spelling in the Derge edition of the Tengyur referenced here is bstan-bcos kyi {@Jiki check carving}, which might then be translated as “to present in an unerring way how the Classical Commentary [of Arya Nagarjuna] teaches suchness.”

lemma: The way in which things are projected
text: See f. 23a (entry %S6, TD03860) of Master Chandrakirti’s other classic treatment of Arya Nagarjuna’s verses, where he says, “This too I have presented in great detail in Entering the Middle Way, so please go and find it there.”  The brief title of this second work in Sanskrit, by the way, is Prasanna Pada.  Prasanna means clarified, and pada can mean either words or verses.  The former, in Tibetan, is translated as tsig; and the latter as tsigs-su bcad-pa, which is sometimes abbreviated to tsigs.  The Tibetan translation of the title of the work in our reference edition of the Tengyur (the Derge) uses the latter spelling (f. 1b) {Jiki check carving}, and in the opening section we see Master Chandrakirti promising to clarify (gsal) the verses (here tsig-le’ur byas-pa), and not the words (ff. 1b-2a).  As such, the correct English translation of the title would seem to be A Clarification of the Verses, although subsequently the Tibetan abbreviation Tsig-gsal (A Clarification of the Words) basically became universal, and we see this spelling even at the end of the Tengyur version.  Later Tibetan commentators will also make statements such as: “Master Chandrakirti’s Clarification of the Words covers the wording of the Foundational Verses called ‘Wisdom,’ whereas Entering the Middle Way covers its intent” (Kyabje Pabongka Rinpoche, 1878-1941, in The "Key that Opens the Door to the Excellent Path," being Notes of an Explanation Granted when the Holder of the Diamond, the Good and Glorious Pabongka, Granted Profound Teachings upon "The Three Principal Paths," entry %B4, S00034, f. 30b).
I.e., (1) to grasp how the presentation is unique within our own school, the Middle Way; and (2) to understand how the Mind-Only presentation is mistaken.
That is, the Greater Way (the Mahayana) or the Lesser Way (the Hinayana).
See f. 228a of the Autocommentary (%S3, TD03862).
Here referring to Entering the Middle Way.

That is, people who have yet to see emptiness directly.  The “three qualities” referred to here are compassion; the Wish for enlightenment; and the wisdom which is beyond all duality, as the exist in a person at this point in their spiritual evolution.
A reference to beings who have not yet reached full enlightenment.
I.e., the eleventh bodhisattva level, called “Light Everywhere,” at which one is now fully enlightened.

lemma: Two different types of the lack of a self-nature
text: That is, the lack of a self-nature to the person, and the lack of a self-nature to things.
Referring to a wisdom which has arisen from the direct perception of emptiness, leading to a direct experience—individually—of the Four Higher Truths.

Higher Knowledge, or Abhidharma, as the lowest of the four great schools of ancient India is not itself the subject of Master Chandrakirti’s work.  Rather, the subject is “abhidharma” in its ultimate form, which is described as follows by great Cho-ne Lama Drakpa Shedrup (1675-1748), an author of important textbooks for the incomparable Sera Mey Tibetan Monastery: “Consider the paths of seeing, of habituation, and of no more learning—along with the unstained components which accompany them.  These are the ultimate [don-dampay] form of higher knowledge [abhidharma, or chos mngon-pa in Tibetan].  And that is because they either consist of the ultimate [don dampa], or derive from it; and because a person on these paths is either headed towards [mngon du phyogs-pa] those objects [dharma] which are the higher truths of the end of suffering and of the path to this end; or because they have directly [mngon-sum-du] perceived them.  Thus these kinds of knowledge are called both ultimate [don dampa] and higher [mngon-pa]” (see ff. 5b-6a of his Sun that Illuminates the True Intent of the Entire Mass of Realized Beings, the Victors and All Their Sons and Daughters: A Commentary upon the “Treasure House of Higher Knowledge,” entry %B5, ACIP S00027). In the same work (at f. 6b), Cho-ne Lama contrasts this ultimate form of higher knowledge with its nominal form, which he describes in the following words: “The nominal form of higher knowledge consists of two different things: (1) any spiritual path which one engages in, in order to reach the resultant forms of higher knowledge that we just spoke of; and (2) higher knowledge as it is presented in scripture: in the classical commentaries which take such things as their subject matter.”

A reference to the traditional classification of the teachings of the Buddha into three sections, or baskets (in Sanskrit, the tripitaka).  These are the sections on vowed morality (Skt: vinaya); on the classics (Skt: sutra); and on higher knowledge (Skt: abhidharma).  One of the traditional three “extraordinary trainings” is the primary subject matter of each of these three sections—respectively, the extraordinary training of morality; of concentration; and of wisdom.

lemma: I have done what I needed to do…
text: A common phrase found in the teachings of the Buddha himself, where disciples who have listened to and followed his advices have reached their goal.  See for example multiple uses of the phrase in Part Two of The Foundation of Assorted Topics of Vowed Morality (Vinaya Kṣudraka Vastu, or ‘Dul-ba phran-tsegs kyi gzhi, %S50, KL00006-2), at ff. 39a, 304b, 364b, and 492a-b.
Tibetan, mtso-skyes; Sanskrit, saroja; a common poeticism for the lotus.

The Autocommentary, at f. 221a, entry @S3, TD03862.  The actual wording in our reference edition is: sangs-rgyas kyi de-nyid nyan-thos dang rang-sangs-rgyas dang bla-na med-pa yang-dag-par rdzogs-pa'i sangs-rgyas gsum-car la yang 'jug ste.

All three editions of Je Tsongkapa’s text give the spelling as tatva buddha, the tatva being a universal variant by the time of the native Tibetan commentarial tradition; whereas tattva is much more common for example in the titles of works in the Tengyur rendered in the Tibetan transcription of Sanskrit.  Bodhisattva for example is given universally as bodhisatva in both cases.  Whitney, in his incomparable Sanskrit Grammar, points out that both treatments of tva following a vowel are traditionally permissible (section 232a, p. 80, @E1, ACIP R00011).

The latter of the two correlations is found verbatim in the Tengyur, in The Compendium of Sanskrit Roots (f. 76a, @S7, ACIP TD04277), except that the buddha is rendered as budha {@Jiki check}.  The former sounds as though it must come from the same work, but we haven’t yet located it there.  The point it makes though is repeated in the same section of the Kangyur (Works on the Study of Sanskrit) a number of times; see for example A Clarification of the Categories of Grammar, a Commentary upon “The Proclamation of the Lady of Song,” a Major Treatise upon the Construction of Sanskrit, ff. 32b, 115a and 35b (this folio in fact includes a treatment of tattva buddha) (@S8, ACIP TD04298); as well as The Source of Jewels, a Book of Composition, f. 356a (@S9, ACIP TD04303).

lemma: This idea about objects which are grasped
text: A well-known line from the Ornament of Realizations, by Lord Maitreya and Arya Asanga, explaining the distinction between practitioners of the three levels in terms of the subtlety of their realizations of selflessness (f. 5a, @S10, ACI TD03786).
I.e., Lord Maitreya, and by extension Arya Asanga.

See f. 91a of Master Haribhadra’s renowned Commentary to “The Ornament of Realizations, a Book of Advices upon the Perfection of Wisdom,” commonly referred to as A Commentary which Clarifies the Meaning (%S12, ACIP TD03793).

All three editions of Illumination give the same spelling, saṃbhara; the spelling now current is sambhāra.  The root here is √bhṛ, which as Whitney (in his invaluable Roots, Verb-Forms, and Primary Derivatives of the Sanskrit Language, p. 114) notes most often has the connotation of to bear—while the Tengyur lexicons will commonly describe it as ‘dzin-pa, or to hold (see for example f. 169a of Master Anubhutisvarupa’s Clarification of the Categories of Grammar, %S8, TD04289).  This verb plays prominently in the current discussion, as the word embrace; thus Je Rinpoche’s comment about the literal explanation of the Sanskrit.
Sanskrit, arhat; meaning one who has permanently destroyed the enemy of negative emotions, and thus reached nirvana.
Since, as already described, they reach their enlightenment in a lifetime in which they do not rely upon the instructions of another master.

See f. 10a of Master Aryadeva’s classic on emptiness (%S13, ACIP TD03846).  Our reference edition of the text, incidentally, reads “in the next life” (skye-ba phyi-mar) rather than “within another life” (skye-ba gzhan du).

See f. 11a of Arya Nagarjuna’s Wisdom (%S4, TD03824). All three editions of Illumination give the latter rendering; the corresponding Sanskrit is @Jiki get Skt edition & check.

Here is the section of the Autocommentary in question: “Now it is admittedly the case that some practitioners who only listen to a teaching on how things are created in dependence might become masters in perceiving the ultimate, and yet still fail to attain nirvana in the life which they are presently experiencing.  Nonetheless, those practitioners who do receive such teachings will, beyond a shadow of a doubt, see the fruits they so ardently hope for ripen in other, future lives—in the same way that certain karmas are sure to produce a specific future result” (%S3, TD03862, ff. 220b-221a).

Skt, Jina; that is, an Enlightened Being.  His Holiness the First Panchen Lama explains the name as follows: “Why do we refer to the Conquerors, the Buddhas, as ‘Victors’?  Because they have conquered the cause—meaning things which are bad deeds; and because they have as well attained victory in the battle against the demon of the result of these wrong actions” (see f. 6b of A Party to Open Up Excellent Things, %B15, S05941).

The native Tibetan catalog to the Derge edition of the Tengyur, in listing The Exalted Sutra named “The Perfect Compendium of All Things” (Skt: Āryasaṃgīti Nāma Mahāyāna Sūtra, Tib: ‘Phags-pa Chos yang-dag-par sdud-pa zhes-bya-ba theg-pa chen-po’i mdo, %S15, KL00238), says that “Some have explored the question of whether this is the same work as The Exalted Sutra on the Discussion of All Things [note the slight but significant difference in the Tibetan here: ‘Phags pa Chos kun bgro-ba’i mdo], which is mentioned in The Great Catalog” (see f. 131a of %B8, KL04568).
