These will be based primarily on traditional commentaries of the ancient literature of the Higher Knowledge School (Abhidharma), which is a major source for the first period of Lord Buddha’s teaching career.

lemma: As for the “parts of a person,” there are five
text: (1) the physical body (which is sometimes also expanded to the physical world of which the person is a part); (2) the capacity of feeling; (3) the capacity of discrimination; (4) a group of “other factors” including for example the person (“John”) and the seeds or potentials within their mind; and (5) the capacity of awareness.  For a complete discussion see for example the one beginning at f. 11a of the brilliant commentary by Choney Lama Drakpa Shedrup (1675-1748) at %B8, ACIP digital text number S00027. The traditional term here for “parts of a person” is “heaps”; the Abhidharma literature explains this as meaning that each of the five parts itself includes many different components.  See lines I.77-78 of the Treasure House of Higher Knowledge (Abhidharma Kosha) at f. 2b of %S14, TD04089, and f. 22a of Choney Lama’s commentary.

These number twelve, consisting of ten physical members and two mental members.  The ten physical members are the five objects of sense (visible form, sounds, smells, tastes, and touches) and the five physical sense organs which detect them (eye, ear, nose, tongue, and skin of the body).  These ten trigger five different kinds of physical sense consciousness, which combined with our mental sense consciousness (and you could even throw in here our general mental awareness of the moment before) become the object of our general mental awareness, and are given the name of “the door of sense called ‘things’”).  These two then—our sense consciousnesses all combined, and our general mental awareness of them—are the two mental members.  This is the presentation of Je Tsongakapa’s close disciple Gyaltsab Je (1364-1432) in his commentary to the Compendium of the teachings of Higher Knowledge (Abhidharma) (see f. 54a, %B15, S05435).

lemma: Process of how things occur in dependence upon each other
text: The famed twelve links of dependence, each link triggering the next in a cycle of suffering, and later depicted in the well-known painting of the Wheel of Life.  The twelve are (1) misunderstanding; (2) fresh karma; (3) consciousness; (4) name & form; (5) the sense doors; (6) contact; (7) feelings; (8) initial desire; (9) advanced desire; (10) ripe karma; (11) birth; and (12) aging & death.  See the discussion in Choney Lama’s commentary to the Treasure House beginning at f. 70b (%B8, ACIP digital text S00027).

These are traditionally listed as four.  The first is “sustenance taken in portions,” a reference to physical food such as rice.  The second is the “sustenance of contact,”  meaning contact of the mind with the outside world, whose objects sustain the various mental functions.  An example would be where love is increased by contact of the mind with the sight of a child.  The third is the “sustenance of thought,” as when sustained thought of a child sustains and increases the love.  And the fourth is the sustenance of consciousness, which in perceiving objects allows the sustaining just described.  See the discussion in Choney Lama starting from f. 77a (%B8, ACIP S00027).

lemma: A useful oral monastic tradition is to also list the four as
text: physical food; sleep (which we need to sustain both body & mind); focus (which also sustains us, whereas a lack of a chance to focus or concentrate—being interrupted frequently in our tasks at work with different tasks, for example—hurts both body & mind); and hope (which always sustains us deeply).

A reference to the four truths of a realized being—meaning the standard realizations that a person has in conjunction with seeing emptiness directly.  Such a person is called, in Sanskrit, arya; the common translation here of arya as noble (i.e. “Four Noble Truths”) is a gross mistake.  These four are (1) the truth that our life is pain; (2) the truth that this pain has a source that we can identify; (3) the truth that this source—and thus the pain it causes—can be shut off; and (4) the truth that there is a path or method that we can follow to shut off this source. It is also important to note that “truth” here means more “experience” than “correct statement”; a headache itself, for example, is the first truth.  For a general treatment see Choney Lama, starting from f. 160b (%B8, ACIP S00027).

Along with the parts of a person and the doors of sense, the third of the great classic divisions of reality presented, for example, in the teachings of Higher Knowledge (Abhidharma).  Here they are very commonly found as 18 in number; this count is arrived at by splitting the six sense powers and their six objects within the presentation of 12 doors of sense mentioned previously—which along with the six corresponding consciousnesses makes for the total of 18.  See Choney Lama starting from f. 20b (%B8, ACIP S00027).  The additional meaning of a “variety” of categories and “many different” categories will be treated by our commentators below.

These are counted as four: close awareness of the body; the feelings; the mind; and of other objects.  In the tradition of Higher Knowledge they are emphasized at the path of accumulation—an early stage in spiritual development—and act as  supports for the deep state of meditation which is conducive to the perception of emptiness; they involve an awareness of qualities such as the impermanence and a lack of a self-nature of the objects they focus upon.  See the discussion in Choney Lama beginning from f. 164b (%B8, ACIP S00027), and in Jamyang Shepay Dorje (1648-1721) at f. 57a of %B12, ACIP S19100-6.

Also counted as four; as pointed out by Chim Jampay Yang (b. 1280), a renowned commentator upon Higher Knowledge, they are aspects of joyful effort which may most usefully be equated to the famous four forces of confession and renewal, for stopping negative karmic seeds: (1) reviewing our foundational knowledge of the teachings, especially of emptiness; (2) resolving to stop these seeds before they multiply; (3) pledging not to repeat the kinds of actions that planted the seeds; and (4) performing some positive action to “balance” the negative karma.  See f. 356b of The “Chim” Commentary to the “Treasure House of Higher Knowledge” (%B9, ACIP S06954-2).  Jamyang Shepa points out how the Higher Knowledge School relates this primarily to the “warmth” stage of the path of preparation, a level of practice which leads to the direct perception of emptiness (see again f. 57a of %B12, ACIP S19100-6).

A reference to four aspects of meditative concentration, which in turn supports miraculous abilities.  The four are clarified by the great textbook writer of Sera Mey Monastic University, Kedrup Tenpa Dargye (1493-1568), in his Overview of the Perfection of Wisdom as antidotes to the famed five problems that can occur in meditation.  The four are: a thirst to achieve successful meditation; the effort needed to do so; the meditative flow which comes from practice; and acting on advices for how to meditate (f. 14a, %B10, ACIP S00009).  Jamyang Shepa ties these to the “peak” stage of the path of preparation (at f. 57a of %B12, ACIP S19100-6).

Referring to five different practices that are said by the great Abhidharma commentator Gyalwang Lobsang Trinley Namgyal (c. 1850) to be important at the “mastery” stage of the path of preparation.  The five are faith; effort; awareness; meditative focus; and wisdom (see f. 51a of %B11, S00044-6 and f. 33a of %B8, S00027).
The same five practices as the five powers, except as emphasized at the “highest experience” stage of the path of preparation (see f. 57a of %B12, ACIP S19100-6).

Seven practices relating primarily to the path of habituation—the stage of spiritual development following the direct perception of emptiness, when we are getting used to what we saw and incorporating it into our life (again see Jamyang Shepa, as above).  These seven are: (1) “recollection” as the ability to pull back a lost meditation object; (2) intellectual discernment; (3) effort; (4) practiced ease; (5) joy; (6) meditative focus; and (7) equanimity (see ff. 52b-53a of Jamyang Shepa in another text at %B13, ACIP S19092-1).

lemma: Eight components of the path of the realized ones
text: These eight then relate to the path of seeing—the direct realization of emptiness (Jamyang Shepa, as above); they consist of (1) a correct view of reality, during the stage of the path of seeing subsequent to the direct perception of emptiness; (2) correct thinking at this point, which leads to (3) correctly describing ones experience of emptiness; (4) an ultimately informed observation of morality—the laws of karma; (5) a correct livelihood based on this moral code; (6) continued effort to progress even higher along the path; (7) recollection in the form of great meditation, feelings of equanimity, and so on; and (8) meditation to achieve further spiritual skills such as the various types of clairvoyance (following Kedrup Je’s presentation of Lord Maitreya and Arya Asanga’s Ornament of Realizations, %B14, S05461, f. 130a). Note that all of the spiritual practices and qualities listed here in the sutra starting from the four types of close recollection add up to a total of 37; and these are sometimes referred to, together, as the “37 Components of Enlightenment”—spiritual components for reaching enlightenment—and we will see Master Yuance and Je Tsongkapa referring to them this way in their commentaries.

The three qualities or natures of the Mind-Only school—being dominated; being imaginary; and being established—have just been presented in previous chapter of the sutra (Chapter 6).  They will be discussed more as we go, especially by Je Tsongkapa in his Essence.
The original name of the bodhisattva in Sanskrit, Paramartha Samudgata, breaks down into paramartha, meaning ultimate; and samudgata, meaning born of.

A famed work of the Mind-Only School written by Master Asanga (350ad) (%S15, ACIP TD04048).  Master Yuance seems to be referring to the discussion at f. 25a; the theme of rising to preeminence is strong in the text from its first pages.

lemma: Difference in viewpoint of the translators
text: Unfortunately the different translations to which Master Yuance is referring to may no longer be extant for comparison; this point is relevant elsewhere in the text.

The Compendium is a famed presentation by Arya Asanga on the teachings of Higher Knowledge (Abhidharma) from the viewpoint of different schools.  See f. 102b (%S16, TD04049) for the reference by Master Yuance.

See f. 3a of Master Vasubandhu’s classic on Higher Knowledge (Abhidharma), at %S14, TD04089; as well as ff. 42b-43a of the first volume of the autocommentary at %S17, TD4090—both composed around 350ad.
See f. 5a of the Treasure House (%S14, TD04089).

As we will see, the thirteen topics of the five groups are as follows: (1) the five parts to a person; (2) the twleve doors of sense; (3) the twelve links in the process of how things occur in dependence on each other; (4) the four types of sustenance; (5) the four truths; (6) the 18 categories; (7) the four types of close awareness; (8) the four perfect freedoms; (9) the four legs of the miraculous; (10) the five powers; (11) the five forces; (12) the seven components of enlightenment; and (13) the eight components of the path of the realized ones.

Several sutras give a list of mini-definitions of the five parts to a person like this.  The ones not mentioned here are the second part (or “heap”), the capacity of feeling, there defined as “the capacity of experience”; the third part, the capacity of discrimination, defined as “separating”; and the fourth part, the other factors of body & mind, defined as “other things which affect things.”  See for example The Perfection of Wisdom in 100,000 Lines (f. 227b, %S18, KL00008, Part 3), as well as Bringing to Mind the Holy Teachings (f. 236b, %S19, KL00287, Part 1).
See footnote %4, in the section above presenting the original sutra, for a full explanation.

The Levels of Practice is an important classic of the Mind-Only School written by Arya Asanga; it discusses the twelve links of dependence (only the first and last are mentioned here) throughout, but the present reference by Master Yuance seems to be the one at f. 109a (%S20, TD04035).  For a listing of the twelve, see footnote %5 in the translation of the original sutra above.
Again, only the first and last of the four types are mentioned here.  For a complete listing see footnote %6 in the section above, of the original sutra.

lemma: Chapter on the Nature of Ultimate Reality
text: That is, the second chapter of the sutra, which begins with a question from the bodhisattva named “Born of the Dharma” (Dharmodgata).

The four truths of a realized being have been listed above in note %7 for the translation of the original sutra.  Note that the Tibetan translation of the sutra in the Kangyur (see section S7.6 above) says only “qualities” (mtsan-nyid) of the various truths, and not “self-natures” (rang gi mtsan-nyid).  There are many such distinctions between the Tibetan of the sutra in the Kangyur edition we are using, and the Tibetan of it found in the Tengyur edition of Master Yuance’s commentary.  We will point out only ones that seem particularly significant, with reference to the original Sanskrit where available.@{check Skt on this one}
This seems to be a reference to f. 100a of the work (%S20, TD04035).
See footnote %9 in the translation of the sutra for a description of the four.

The original Sanskrit for “close awareness” is smirtyupasthana, where smirti means “awareness” and upasthana means “standing close.”  The “closeness” here refers to a fine level of attention which is considering qualities such as the impermanence and the emptiness of the object it focuses upon.  Again, see footnote %9 above.  We have not located any separate discussion of the six connotations mentioned.
These have all been described in detail above, in footnotes %10-%14.

The “last seven” mentioned are (1) the four types of close awareness; (2) the four perfect freedoms; (3) the four legs of the miraculous; (4) the five powers; (5) the five forces; (6) the seven components of enlightenment; and (7) the eight components of the path of the realized ones.  This makes for a total of 37: a famous group of practices and qualities which mark our progression through five spiritual paths that lead to enlightenment.  For details on these paths follow the Master’s advice here and see the individual notes for these seven as mentioned in the footnotes just above.

We haven’t located a sutra by this name {@available in Chinese?}, or the citation given.  In a number of sutras on the perfection of wisdom, this perfection is also given this same name of “achieving limitless goals”; so perhaps this is a term used for one or all of the perfection of wisdom sutras.  Master Yuance again refers to this same sutra immediately below. A similar thought though is expressed in the Sutra Requested by Purna (f. 424a, %S22, KL00061), where Lord Buddha states that he “taught sutras of the greater way at the Deer Park, to listener disciples”—who are usually described as disciples of the lower way, and students of the first turning of the Wheel.
Six famed bodhisattva practices, each performed with a solid awareness of emptiness: giving, leading an ethical life, patience, joyful effort, meditation, and wisdom.

We haven’t located this particular reference, but a similar idea with the same wording appears in a secret teaching of a Diamond Angel; pointing out that what is secret declares itself clearly to people of sufficient wisdom (see f. 83a of %S23, TD01417).  In a previous chapter of his commentary, Master Yuance has already noted that the “highly secret” here refers to teachings of the bodhisattva way (of which the Second Turning was a part), while “clearly declared” is a reference to teachings given to disciples of the listener (lower) way (those of the First Turning).  See f. 83a of the first part of his commentary (%C1, TD04016).

text: Again the wording of the sutra seems off a bit here, but the point seems to be that the act of thinking to ask the question, and the act of actually asking it, were both awesome karma.

“Gentle Voice,” or Manjughosha (commonly known as Manjushri), is the embodiment of the wisdom of all Enlightened Beings.  Je Tsongkapa is being literal when he refers to this Buddha as his teacher, since during his lifetime he was able to make contact with this being and seek his direct guidance.  For the story of their first meeting, see p. 185 of his illustrated biography, King of the Dharma (%E1).

lemma: The likes of Source of Bliss
text: This and the other names here are poeticisms referring to powerful but impermanent beings who live in the temporary god-realms; in appearance and powers they are very similar to the superheroes seen in modern movies.  Here are the more familiar Sanskrit titles, according to the Great Dictionary (%B16, R00002): “Source of Bliss” is Ishvara; “Cloud-Horse” is Shakra; “Golden Womb” is Brahma; “Lord of the Disembodied” is Ratishvara; and “Cord Around The Waist” is Vishnu.
Reference to an ancient belief that many gemstones first came from the bottom of the sea.
A reference to the three traditional divisions of the physical universe: the desire realm; the form realm; and the formless realm.

An epithet of the realized beings Nagarjuna and Asanga, who in ancient India innovated masterful systems of interpreting the Buddha’s teachings: the Middle-Way School and the Mind-Only School, respectively.
All great Indian commentators on the teachings of Lord Buddha, and dating from about the second to the seventh centuries.

lemma: Never accept what I say from respect
text: A popular verse in the ancient literature.  The earliest version of this particular wording seems to be the one in The Compendium on the Essence of Wisdom, by Master Aryadeva (c. 200ad) (see f. 27b of TD03851, %S4, as well as f. 35a of Master Bodhibhadra’s commentary, %S5, TD03852).  It was later used by both Master Shantarakshita and his famed disciple Kamalashila, both masters of the group within the lower Middle-Way School which tilted towards the Mind-Only; and thus it would make sense that their writings would be on Je Tsongkapa’s mind as he composed the current work (see ff. 130b-131a of %S6, TD04266; and f. 93a of %S7, TD04232). We have not found any versed version in the Kangyur, but there are various presentations of the components here; for the tests of gold see for example The Sutra on the Great Nirvana (%S8, KL00119-1, ff. 347a-347b); and for not relying only on respect for the Buddha see the Foundation of Assorted Topics of Vowed Morality (%S9, KL00006-1, f. 75b).  For the logical and experiential tests of the gold metaphor, the best example is our own What I Really Meant, the very sutra being discussed by Je Tsongkapa below (see ff. 81a-82b), %S2, KL KL00106).  Sections such as these are no doubt the source for the combined, versed version later.  We also see a nice reference for the three tests of gold in evaluating ideas in the Jataka tales; see Stories of the Past Lives of the Buddha (%S10, TD04156, f. 87a). The way in which the firing, cutting, and filing of the gold correspond respectively to testing an idea against our direct personal experience; our logic; and consistency with other ideas from the same source is found throughout the later Tibetan literature; a good ancient source for it is for example Master Shantarakshita’s Commentary to the “Jewel of the Middle Way” (%S11, TD03885, f. 83a).  The famed Longdol Lama Ngawang Lobsang (1719-1794) gives a fascinating description of how the test actually works: the three processes produce different colors in the gold being tested (red from firing; white from cutting; and yellow from filing); this may be found in his Brief Instructions on the Evaluation of Gems and Precious Metals (%B2, S06559, f. 708b). The verse incidentally is also found at least six times in the Diamond Way section of the Tengyur, with a particularly famous occurrence in the Kalachakra (Wheel of Time) literature (%S12, TD01347, f. 232b).  In his commentary, Kedrup Je (at %B7, S05463-1, f. 355a) attributes this to the sutra called Paradise of the Clouds (Ghana Vyuha, %S13, KL00110), but we have not located it there; subsequent writers have also wrestled with this problem, and the question of the original Kangyur source (see for example Gungtang Konchok Tenpay Drunme [1762-1823], %B4, S00045, f. 7a; the same author at %B5, S00911, f. 16b; and Jigme Damchu Gyatso [1898-1946], %B6, S00302, f. 49a-49b).

text: The former is a reference to the illustrious half-brothers, Arya Asanga and Master Vasubandhu; the latter refers to Arya Nagarjuna and his spiritual son, Aryadeva.

That is, all the things we ourselves need and all the things that others need; and only a Buddha has accomplished both.  Perhaps the most famous discussion of this concept is that found in the opening lines of Master Dharmakirti’s Commentary on Valid Perception; see f. 94b of bibliography entry S8, corresponding to ACIP digital text TD04210.  See as well Gyaltsab Je’s renowned explanation of these lines at f. 3b of his Unerring Illumination of the Path to Freedom (B12, ACIP S05450).
The Tibetan here includes the required letter for euphonic combination.

The Sanskrit original that we are using divides the original sutra into 32 sections; these section numbers will be included at the beginning of each section in parentheses.  We supply the Sanskrit in the online version of this translation for the interest of students, from several sources, most often referencing Max Müller (S40) and including the page numbers of his edition; it has not been our goal to create a definitive Sanskrit version, and there may be errors or inconsistencies; that task will have to wait for a later date. Sanskrit scholars please note that with certain exceptions, such as vowel combinations, we have deconstructed the euphonic combination (sandhi) here in order to assist students of the Sanskrit language, who we believe will be the primary users of the native Sanskrit presented in this volume.  Basically this decision makes it infinitely more interesting and easier for these readers to follow the Sanskrit and compare it to the other languages used here, at the cost of confusing internal and external sandhi for the expert.  But since we have relied greatly on the Müller version in the Devanagari, and it is so commonplace now online, we encourage our expert friends to consult the original spacing there, if desired.

The three sentences in the Sanskrit here are not found in the Tibetan; nor does Choney Lama comment upon them.  They would be translated thus: And why is that?  Because, o Subhuti, the very words “One Gone Thus” are an expression that refers to the unborn nature of reality.  The very words “One Gone Thus,” o Subhuti, are an expression that refers to the ending of things; these very words are an expression referring to the fact that nothing ever begins at all.  And it is for precisely this reason, o Subhuti, that the fact that nothing happens is itself ultimate reality.
In Sanskrit, Tathagata—where tatha means thus, and gata means gone.

We have inserted the root text of the sutra from the Lhasa Kangyur edition (S23, KL00021) at the relevant lines in Choney Lama’s commentary.  Where he “weaves” the root text into his explanation, we use italics within the English of the commentary, and bold in the Tibetan. We present the Sanskrit in both technical diacritics and, for general readers, in the closest normal English pronunciation (in italics).  We also capitalize proper names, and references to Enlightened Beings, in the Sanskrit.  We further break the individual Sanskrit semantic units out of their compounds to help students of our main language here—Tibetan—locate the corresponding Sanskrit for each Tibetan word, and thus learn more about these two languages.  This is done with the exception that we do not break out these units where that would change the meter.  For notes on the Sanskrit edition used, please see the bibliography entry for S23, KL00021.

lemma: Four language groups of ancient India
text: Je Tsongkapa describes these four, in a commentary to the secret teaching called the Secret Collection, as follows (B10, S05282, f. 1b):

lemma: In India there were four great language groups
text: Prakirta, the “natural” or native language of each different locality; Apabhransha, or corrupted dialects; Pishacha, or the language of the spirits [called “flesh-eaters,” or pishacha]; and Sanskrit, the “well-formed” language—the Tongue of the Gods. Note that the Tibetan translation for the word sanskirta is typically literal: sam for “well” and kirta (the correct pronunciation of the vocalic r) for “formed.”  The name of the third language listed, apabhransha, literally means “languages that have wandered away.” Please note that throughout this translation we present the prenasal sound in its correct pronunciation, dependent upon the quality of the following consonant, rather than confusing the pronunciation with the transcription (for example m with a dot under it), as is unfortunately often the case among many modern presentations of Sanskrit.

Note that, unless otherwise necessitated, we use the closest English pronunciation for foreign words in the text and in the footnotes; and in the bibliographies, the technical transcription.  Please also note that we distinguish between the two!  Which means, for example, the vocalic ṛ is transcribed with ir, and not ri—as is sometimes seen when transcription and pronunciation are confused or intermixed. The reader may enjoy some cognates, or English words which have derived from the Sanskrit here.  As we will see, Bhagavan—which originally means “having a share”—relates to the Sanskrit root /bhaj, which itself means “to share,” or “divide.”  English cognates are “fracture” or “vagina,” which reflect a split or divide.  The prefix pra- connotes “to a high degree,” or “up front,” and thus the English cognates “prow” of a boat or “proud”—the desire to be in front.  The root /jna, meaning “to know,” is responsible for that unexpected “kn-“ spelling in English.  To go “to” the “edge” or “limits” all around—param—relates to the “peri-“ in “perimeter” and “periscope.”  And ita is the past participle of the root /i, meaning “to go;” it is found in our English word “exit,” meaning “place to go out.”  Hirdaya or “heart” is of course related to that word, and to “cardiac.”

The original, prose version of the list is found on f. 368 of the original tantra (S32, KL00381). See f. 35a of the work, which is one of the Five Books of Maitreya (S16, TD04020).  Here the word “great” is being described with reference to the “greater way”—the path as practiced by those who wish to become a fully enlightened Buddha in order to help all living creatures in the universe.  Gungtang Lodru Gyatso explains these seven by saying that the “great focus” refers to embracing the entire corpus of the greater way, and that the “two great accomplishments” are achieving all of one’s own needs, and all those of others.  “Great wisdom” is the realization of both the lack of a self-nature to things, and to people.  “Great effort” is the willingness to make spiritual efforts for three “countless” eons; and the great form of skillful means refers to love which will never give up on beings in the cycle of pain.  “Great practice” means the development of enlightened qualities such as the ten powers; while “great deeds” means to display, over and over again, the holy deeds of attaining nirvana and enlightenment.  See f. 217a of the work (B19, S00967).

See f. 33b of Je Tsongkapa’s classic explanation of the secret teachings (B10, S05282); as well as Master Chandrakirti’s original commentary (f. 9b, S3, TD01785).  “Obstacle Destroyer” (Skt: Sarva Nivarana Vishkambhin) is the name of one of the Eight Close Sons, bodhisattvas who were especially close to Lord Buddha.  And so Choney Lama is saying that Shariputra was not, as is generally reported, a disciple on the “listener” track of the lower way, but rather on the bodhisattva or higher-way track.

It’s worth noting here that the English translation of the original Sanskrit chatur arya satya as “four noble truths” is a gross error.  The word translated as “noble” in this case is arya, which is rather meant to indicate that the content of these truths is perceived directly only by an arya, or “realized person”: a person who has experienced the direct perception of ultimate reality.  The fact of this perception immediately pushes such a person up to the next step in the evolution of sentient life, to a higher state of being.  Thus, the “four higher truths.”

“Rongtikpa” literally means “commentator from the Rong area of Tibet” and is a reference to Rongtun (“Teacher from Rong”) Sheja Kunrik (1367–1449), a writer of the Sakya lineage of Tibet who produced many commentaries on the Buddhist classics, including one on the Heart Sutra entitled A Complete Clarification of the Meaning of the Mother (Yum don rab-gsal)—referring to the Mother Sutras on the perfection of wisdom.  The reference here is found on f. 5a of the work (B21, BDRC W28942).

Choney Lama is playing with the Sanskrit verbal roots that go into the word mantra, or the “sacred words” here.  As Je Tsongkapa notes in his commentary to the famed Fifty Verses on Lamas, drawing from the literature of the Secret Collection (Guhya Samaja), the word mantra breaks down into two parts: man meaning “mind” and tra meaning “to protect.” The latter comes from a Sanskrit verbal root /trā, meaning “to rescue” or “protect.”  This in itself is a secondary root whose primary form is /tṛ (pronounced tir), meaning “to pass” or “cross over.”  This sense of tra is the point of Choney Lama’s wordplay here, since the perfection of wisdom (or more properly perhaps, the perfectionizer of wisdom) is literally something that helps us “cross over” and thus escape the ocean of pain.  The very word “perfection,” or paramita in the original Sanskrit, of course literally means “gone” (ita) “to” (-m) the “other side” (para). For Je Tsongkapa’s etymology see A Commentary to the Fifty Verses on Lamas, ff. 26a–26b (B14, S05269).  His reference from the Secret Collection may be found at ff. 526a–526b of the Latter Secret Teaching (S20, KL00443).  As always, the roots are presented masterfully by Dwight Whitney in his Roots, Verb Forms, and Primary Derivatives of the Sanskrit Language (E2, R00013); see pp. 64 and 67.

See f. 193a (S21, KL00013).  Here is the entire passage: The perfection of wisdom Of the Victorious Ones Is a great mantra of knowledge; It takes even beings Who have no aptitude, And puts to rest in them All grief, all pain. All those who have gone beyond— The protectors of the worlds In every corner of the universe— Became Kings of Benefit By learning these sacred words. Those sages who live a life Hoping to help others, Acting in compassion Towards others, And who train themselves In this knowledge mantra, Reach and touch Their enlightenment.

The classic source for these seven is a verse from a secret book of the teachings known as “Tip of Diamond” (see f. 341b of S27, KL00480).  Here is how it reads; the “source of wealth” by the way means “the world,” and so this sacred sound is being called the most precious thing in the world: And now I will explain to you The meaning of Om, The heart of the source of wealth. It has meanings of “supreme”; And “granting wealth”; and “glory”; And “fortune”; “one who possesses Their share of goodness”; “Making a commitment”; And “auspiciousness.” Go to the enlightenment of a Buddha!  The “enlightenment of a listener” or of a self-made buddha is not full enlightenment; it is only a reference to lower nirvana: the permanent ending of negative emotions, not combined yet with omniscience.  The third enlightenment mentioned here is full enlightenment, of the greater way.

Again, a reference to the Detailist and Sutrist Schools; see footnote 15 above at section 32.  In conjunction with the comments by Konchok Tenpay Drunme there, it’s helpful as well to note another difference he draws between these two groups and the Mind Only School.  Here he refers to the way that the Objectists describe the two realities, a standard topic in Buddhist philosophy.  They say that things which can be further deconstructed belong to deceptive reality, whereas things which cannot be so deconstructed—meaning indivisible atoms—are therefore ultimate reality.  He notes finally how the Mind Only School denies that outer objects are physical matter; and in so doing, focusses mainly on consciousness (see f. 12b, B2, S00918).

lemma: The Powerful One, and so on
text: These are different names for a single worldly god that would have been familiar to students in the author’s time who were versed in the ancient Indian literature.  “Powerful One” in Sanskrit is “Ishvara”; “Destroyer of a Hundred Cities” is “Shatakratu” (sometimes also called “Indra”); and “One with a Thousand Eyes” is “Sahasraksha.”
Choney Lama says “Tashi” here, which is a common Tibetan name.

See ff. 185a–185b of this famous sutra, spoken by Lord Buddha (S36, KL00107).  Our readers may enjoy reading the entire context, from the original: ,BDAG MED PA YI MNYAM PA STE, ,BZHI PA RNAL ‘BYOR RNAL ‘BYOR PA’I, ,LTA BA THAMS CAD RNAM BZLOG PA’I, ,RTOG DANG BRTAG PA SPANGS PA STE, ,DMIGS MED SKYE BA MED PA NI, ,SEMS TZAM DU YANG NGAS BSHAD DO, The fourth way things are all equal Is in the way they are not themselves: The practitioner who puts a stop To all the ways practitioners see things Rids themselves of thoughts, Rids themselves of thinking: They see nothing, nothing starts— For I have declared It is all only mind. ,DNGOS MED DNGOS MIN MA YIN PA, ,DNGOS DANG DNGOS MED RNAM PAR SPANGS, ,DE BZHIN SEMS LAS GROL BA NI, ,SEMS TZAM DU YANG NGAS BSHAD DO, Things were never things, Nor were they ever not; Give up thinking things Are things, and give up Thinking things are not. Free yourself From the mind itself: For I have declared It is all only mind. ,DE BZHIN NYID DANG STONG PA’I MTHA’, ,MYA NGAN ‘DAS DANG CHOS KYI DBYINGS, ,SNA TSOGS YID KYI LUS RNAMS NI, ,SEMS TZAM DU YANG NGAS BSHAD DO, The end of all things Is the way things are; The end of all things Is emptiness. This is nirvana, the Realm of Is; And all these different bodies Are just your different thoughts— For I have declared It is all only mind. ,RNAM RTOG BAG CHAGS ‘BREL PA YI, ,SNA TSOGS SEMS LAS BYUNG BA STE, ,MI RNAMS LA NI PHYI ROL SNANG, ,’JIG RTEN PA YI SEMS TZAM MO, All the kaleidoscope of things Is flowing from your imagination; Linked to the seeds inside, The outside appears to people— But all of it is only the mind Of those who live in this world. ,PHYI ROL SNANG BA YOD MED DE, ,SEMS NI SNA TSOGS RNAMS SU SNANG, ,LUS DANG LONGS SPYOD GNAS ‘DRA BAR, ,SEMS TZAM DU YANG NGAS BSHAD DO, It’s not that anything at all Is appearing on the outside: The mind itself is appearing As the kaleidoscope of things. Your body, and everything you possess, And the place you live are all the same: For I have declared It is all only mind.
The discussion by Kedrup Je may be found in his Great Interlude on Emptiness; it begins on f. 150a (B7, S05459).
That is, the simultaneous ability of the mind to perceive itself as it perceives something else—a concept accepted only by certain Buddhist schools, such as the Mind Only.

The “two” here are for example a blue which is indeed an outer object; and the perception which holds it that way.  See f. 18a of Lord Maitreya’s work (S25, TD04020).  In the translation available to us, incidentally—in the Derge Tengyur—the position of the word “always” would change this reading to “neither of the two could ever exist as…”

See f. 439a of the work (S51, KL00442).  Readers may really enjoy the entire context, which we translate here: ,DNGOS PO THAMS CAD DANG BRAL BA, ,PHUNG PO KHAMS DANG SKYE MCHED DANG, ,GZUNG DANG ‘DZIN PA RNAM SPANGS PA, ,CHOS BDAG MED PA MNYAM NYID PAS, ,RANG SEMS GDOD NAS MA SKYES PA, ,STONG PA NYID KYI RANG BZHIN NO, What is the nature of emptiness? It’s that the world is devoid Of any object at all— It is free, forever, Of the different parts of a person; Of the categories, and doors of sense; Of anything to perceive, Or anything to perceive it. Everything there is Is one and the same, In the sense that nothing Can be itself. Thus it is that we can say That our minds, for time With no beginning, Have never started at all.
See f. 46b of Je Rinpoche’s commentary upon the Secret Collection (Guhya Samaja) (B21, S05302).
Again, this is a technical term which refers to someone who has not yet experienced a direct perception of ultimate reality.

Buddhism describes two classic types of obstacles.  The first type are called “negative-emotion obstacles,” or obstacles that prevent us from reaching nirvana—which is defined as the permanent ending of negative emotions.  The second type are called “obstacles to omniscience,” or things which prevent us from reaching full Buddhahood, and gaining thus the ability to help all beings in the universe simultaneously.  A great discussion of these two may be found in the section starting at f. 118b of the dialectic analysis of the beliefs of the Consequence branch by Kedrup Tenpa Dargye (1493–1568).  See B30, S00022.

The “commentary” mentioned is a reference to Je Tsongkapa’s classic Illumination of the True Thought (B20, ST05408), in commentary to Master Chandrakirti’s Entering the Middle Way.  Distinguishing the Literal from the Figurative (B17, S05396) is of course Tsongkapa’s Essence of Eloquence, on the art of interpreting the words of the Buddha.  Interlude on Emptiness is again Kedrup Je’s classic on the topic (B7, S05459).

The atoms that make up a physical object are being pictured here as packed into a configuration where our one atom is at the center, with atoms at the same level touching each of its four sides (in the four directions), and then one atom touching it from above, and another from below—for a total of six.

See f. 3b of the work (S28, TD04056), a popular text of the Mind Only School.  In situ, the author is identified as Master Asanga’s half-brother and frequent collaborator, Master Vasubandhu (see f. 4a).

lemma: Truth of the end of suffering
text: Like the other two existing entities not born of causes and conditions, this one—if you think about it—is an absence and therefore unchanging: you can’t have more or less of nothing and still have nothing.  This truth of the final end of pain (which in this case just means fact or condition) is one of the four higher truths enunciated by Lord Buddha in his first teaching: (1) every normal thing in the world is pain; (2) the pain has a cause; (3) the pain can be stopped by stopping the cause; and (4) there is a way or path to do so.

lemma: Extending to space inside a vase
text: This is a delicate point, since the concept of empty space being referred to in this section of the text is that of the place occupied or vacated by a physical object (such as a vase).  “Empty space” in this sense is not what we think of as “space” when we consider the distance between two walls of a room, or two sides of a vase; rather, it is the unmoving and indestructible position in which the whole room and its walls are standing.
Choney Lama is confirming the relationship between the subject and the second part of the reason in the logical argument at section 210.
A technical way—from the Buddhist logic tradition—of saying that to be one is to the other.

The first has just been discussed; the second proof—also known as the “King of Reasoning”—reads as follows: Consider a sprout. It does not exist in truth, Because it occurs in interdependence. See for example the excellent summary of logical proofs for no-self by Sera Jetsun Chukyi Gyeltsen at ff. 30a–30b in his review of the Jewel of Realizations, in Volume 1 of B25, S06814.

This is a term used in Buddhist formal logic to refer to an easily-understood example presented at the very end of a classical syllogism to help the opponent understand the truth of our proof.  The example is called “combined” because it should incorporate both the quality to be proven, and the quality expressed in the reason.  In the current example, a reflection in a mirror combines the qualities of not really existing (in the sense that the reflection is not the actual person standing in front of the mirror), and being neither one thing nor more than one thing that exists in reality.

See f. 133a of Chandrakirti’s work (S13, TD03865).  The edition available to us, from the Derge Tengyur, again reads brtags for btags, without change of basic meaning; the same with some other variations. text: Some Tibetan carvings have btags here rather than brtags—again, a common confusion.  Choney Lama himself uses this same standard expression repeatedly in other works with the correct spelling—see for example his commentary to the Heart Sutra—so perhaps it’s a carving error.

lemma: The true intent of the Enlightened One
text: See f. 238b of the same work (B20, ST05408).
In the first set, the first self cannot exist, and the second must.  In the second set, the first “me” is fine and the second one is a disaster.
That is, the form of a worldly god; a demigod; a human being; an animal; a hungry ghost; and a hellbeing.

This is a technical term for the belief that I myself, and the things that relate to me, have some nature of their own.  It is the precise kind of misunderstanding which sets into motion the self-perpetuating Wheel of Life, or Wheel of Pain. lemma: The reality body of an Enlightened Being
text: A Buddha can be divided into two most basic parts, referred to as the “form body” and the “reality body.”  The former consists of the physical part of their being, which refers both to the bodies that they emanate throughout the universe, and the body in which they reside within their own paradise.  The latter consists of both their omniscient state of mind, and the emptiness of everything that makes them up.  See the discussion by Sera Jetsun starting at f. 15a of his Seventy Topics (B24, S06827).

lemma: That type of meditation called “fixed” meditation
text: This is a reference to three broad categories of meditation that are traditionally presented.  The first is called a “list meditation” (bshar-bsgom), where we review, in order, a standard list of concepts.  The second is “analytical meditation” (dpyad-bsgom), which is basically a problem-solving exercise.  The third is “fixed meditation” (‘jog-bsgom) where we keep the mind one-pointed on a single concept or object of visualization.  See for example the discussion beginning at f. 7a of Kyabje Pabongka Rinpoche’s commentary to the Three Principal Paths (B33, S00034).

lemma: Master of the ten great books
text: A title in former times similar to that of “geshe,” or “master of Buddhism.”  According to the Great Dictionary (p. 50, Vol. 1, B44, R00002), the ten books consisted of the five works focused upon in the geshe course, along with a major commentary on each.  These five are as follows: 1) The Jewel of Realizations by Lord Maitreya (with Arya Asanga as secretary, c. 350ad), for the study of the lower branch (the Independent) of the Middle Way, a 12-year program of instruction (including ancillary work in the Mind Only School) commonly referred to in the monasteries as the “Perfection of Wisdom”; 2) Entering the Middle Way, by Master Chandrakirti (c. 625ad), for studying the higher branch (Consequence) of the Middle Way, a 4-year program of instruction also called “Middle Way”; 3) A Commentary on Accurate Perception, by Master Dharmakirti (c. 600ad), for the Sutrist School, the program (annually for about 20 years, during the three months of winter) called simply “Accurate Perception”; 4) A Brief Presentation of Vowed Morality, by Master Gunaprabha (c. 650ad), for the ethical teachings of the Detailist School, a 2-year program called “Vowed Morality”; and 5) The Treasure House of Higher Knowledge, by Master Vasbandhu (c. 350ad), for the philosophical teachings of the Detailist School, a 2-year program called simply “Treasure House.”

lemma: Sever the three kinds of flow
text: This expression is found in the sutra called A Journey to Langka (see for example f. 92b, S36, KL00107); it has been variously interpreted, but one solid explanation is presented on f. 22a in the commentary to the sutra by Master Jnana Vajra (S16, TD04019).  Here the three flows are related to three separate progressions within the twelve links of the interdependence found for example in the teaching of the Wheel of Life. The first is called the “flow of negative emotions,” consisting of misunderstanding (link #1); initial desire (link #8); and advanced desire (link #9).  The second is the “flow of the progression of karma,” consisting of fresh karma (link #2) and ripe karma (link #10).  The third is the “flow of the progression of pain,” consisting of all the rest of the twelve links—which would be consciousness (link #3), name & form (link #4), the doors of sense (link #5), contact (link #6), feeling (link #7), birth (link #11), and aging & death (link #12).

These are four different possibilities for something to start through some nature of its own; if we eliminate the four, then we come to the conclusion that things never start this way.  These are (1) things that could already exist, ultimately, and then start; (2) things that could start after not already existing, ultimately; (3) things that could both already exist and not already exist, ultimately, and then start; and (4) things that could neither already exist nor not already exist, ultimately, and then start. The second is where we recognize the way of the listeners; the way of the self-made buddhas; and the greater way, of the bodhisattvas.  These latter three are traditionally divided according to their explanation of no-self, which is more relevant here.

Please note that ancient Sanskrit manuscripts were copied by hand—often by illiterate scribes—rather than carved on blocks that were most often carefully checked by scholars and then reproduced from there, as were the Tibetan classics.  This means that we will see a lot of lacunae, variant spellings, and differences between Sanskrit manuscripts.  We have done our best to strike a balance between preserving the original and correcting obvious errors, but would be happy to receive comments for further refinement of the text.

(1) “All-inclusive” meditation objects consist of general categories and come in four different types.  The first are topics analyzed by both quietude and insight that we have heard about and seek to learn more of, but which we have not yet experienced directly—especially emptiness.  The second are objects of analysis for both quietude and insight that relate to focusing directly on emptiness itself.  The third are objects upon which we train both the wisdom which perceives how things are, and the wisdom which perceives all the things there are.  The fourth are objects that relate to the ability to transform all things. (2) The “object of the master” refers to mastering fundamental spiritual topics such as the different traditional ways of dividing up reality—heaps, doors of sense, categories, and so on—so that we can go deeper in our understanding. (3) The “activities” object refers to initial objects that the deep practitioner utilizes as an antidote to negative emotions, or as an antidote to excessive thinking in general.  Practices utilizing these objects would include the following five: meditating on horrific sufferings and sad events (as an antidote for desire); meditating on love (as an antidote to hatred); meditating on the chain of events that creates the cycle of pain (as an antidote to misunderstanding life); meditating on the billions of things we don’t know yet (as an antidote to pride); and meditating on our breath (as an antidote to too much thinking). (4) The “object used for cleaning away negative emotions” refers generally to different forms of deep concentration itself—both aimed at objects within this world and at those which transcend this world.
