See ff. 44a–44b of the sutra entitled The Various Manifestations of the Single Nature of All Things, the King of Concentration (S45, KL00127).

The five objects of the senses are of course visual objects; sounds; smells; tastes; and things to touch.  The three poisons are best represented by the three animals found at the very center of the famed illustration of the Wheel of Life: ignorant liking represented as a lascivious pigeon or rooster; ignorant disliking portrayed as an angry snake; and ignorance itself, represented by a pig.
See for example ff. 4a–4b of the work (B35, SP05939).
Results of a lower practice—such as temporarily shutting down our gross thought processes, without any spiritual benefit.
See f. 50b of his classic on the three sets of vows (B43, S25123).

The eponymous topics of one of the most illustrious works of all Tibetan Buddhism, by Je Tsongkapa.  These three are to grow tired of the suffering of the cycle of pain; to develop the Wish for enlightenment to save all beings; and to reach an accurate view of the way all things really are.  See B23 (S05275-85).
The technical spelling of the Sanskrit is Ārya Sapta Tathāgata Pūrva Praṇidhāna Viśeṣa Vistāra Nāma Mahāyāna Sūtra.

“One Who Has Gone That Way” is a common way of referring to an Enlightened Being.  The idea is that one has become totally enlightened due to their complete mastery of emptiness, also known as “the way that things are.”  See for example f. 232b of Gyaltsab Je’s famed explanation of the perfection of wisdom, A Jewel for the Essential Explanation (bibliography entry B5, ACIP digital text S05433).
The count of quantities of translated lines was employed by the ancient translators, in part to prevent later, unapproved additions to the text.
The original teachings of Lord Buddha were written down only after his passing.  Eminent disciples gathered to recite from memory those they had personally attended.

An ancient city in India located in the far northeast.  “Conqueror” is a common epithet for an Enlightened Being, since they have conquered their negative emotions, impure karma, a rebirth into suffering, and all impediments to omniscience.  See for example the expanded explanation of this point by Choney Lama Drakpa Shedrup (1675–1748) at f. 4a of his wonderful commentary to the Heart Sutra entitled Sunlight on Suchness, translated in the present Diamond Cutter Classics Series (B1, ACIP digital text S00220).

lemma: Bodhisattva who is a great being
text: A bodhisattva is someone who is working to become a totally enlightened being so that they can help and serve countless suffering beings.  When we say that a particular bodhisattva is also a “great” being, we are saying that they are one of those very special bodhisattvas who also has a deep grasp of ultimate reality, or emptiness. See for example f. 29a of the magnificent explanation of the Diamond Cutter Sutra by Choney Lama (B2, ACIP digital text ST00024); also translated in the present series.

The original Sanskrit for some of the names will be familiar to a number of our readers: “Holder of the Diamond” is Vajrapani; “Loving Eyes, Lord of Power” is Avalokiteshvara; and “Loving One” is Maitreya.

lemma: The last of the five hundred
text: This is a reference to a Buddhist tradition which says that the teachings of our Buddha, Shakyamuni, will last in this world for a total of 2,500 years: for five periods of five hundred years each.  The final period is said to be our present times, during which the teachings themselves steadily deteriorate, and then disappear completely. The classic reference to these periods is found in the Diamond Cutter Sutra; see for example ff. 9b–10a of Choney Lama’s commentary (B2, ST00024).

Note that the word “god” in the sutra refers to a powerful worldly being, on the level of a Greek or Norse god who could move a planet or drink a sea.  Existence as this kind of god is, in the end, considered very undesirable, since it uses up all of our stored good karmic seeds and thus leads directly to a rebirth in the realms of hell.

This Buddha is commonly known simply by the name of “Good Name,” where the word for “good” was originally part of the expression “to the corners of the universe.”  Since the original Sanskrit names of the Buddhas described in the present sutra are so crucial, we will present them in footnotes for each Buddha.  Here the general pronunciation of the Buddha’s full name is Supari Kirtita Nama Shri Raja.  The precise pronunciation is Supari Kīrtita Nāma Śrī Rāja.

Generally speaking, bodhisattvas can be found at ten different spiritual levels.  The last three of these are known as “levels of purity,” since by this point the bodhisattva is free of even the most subtle seeds for misunderstanding reality, along with every other negative thought there is. See for example the explanation by the great textbook writer of Sera Mey Monastery,  Jetsun Chukyi Gyeltsen, at f. 5b of his description of the levels and paths entitled A Necklace for the Wise (B18, S06826).

It is said that particularly virtuous individuals can be born, as finished adults, from the center of a great lotus flower.  The seven precious jewels are traditionally listed as ruby, sapphire, lapis lazuli, emerald, diamond, pearl, and coral.  See for example f. 182a of the annotated commentary of Je Tsongkapa (1357–1419) on the practice of the Secret Collection (B14, S05282).
An allusion to female and male bodhisattvas, who are “children of the Buddhas.”  See for example f. 5b of Choney Lama’s commentary to the Heart Sutra (B1, S00220).
The Tibetan ending of the sentence here, btab-bo, is also seen spelled as btab-po in different sections.  Both seem acceptable, so we have retained them.

Five of the most serious bad deeds there are; so named because after one’s death they are thrown—immediately, without any other, intervening rebirth—into the lowest of the realms of hell.  These include (1) killing one’s father; (2) killing one’s mother; (3) killing an enemy destroyer; (4) causing a schism in a spiritual community; and (5) injuring a Buddha—drawing blood from a Buddha in malice. For the list, see for example f. 55b (B7, S06411) of the specialized treatment of the Offering to Lamas by Lama Quicksilver, Ngulchu Dharma Bhadra (1772–1851).  For the literal explanation, refer to p. 244 of the famed explanation of Higher Knowledge by Jampay Yang of Chim (B12, SP06954).
That is, a rebirth in the realm of hell; or that of the hungry ghosts; or that of the animals.

The reference here is to two types of disciples who have already achieved a personal nirvana—an extraordinary achievement—but who have not yet entered the way of the bodhisattva.  These disciples themselves are divided into two types. “Listeners” are practitioners who have attended teachings on the bodhisattva’s path, and can even describe to others what they heard—but who have no attraction to practicing this path themselves. A “self-made buddha” is a practitioner who can reach nirvana in this life without necessarily taking themselves to a spiritual teacher—but only because they have closely followed their personal teacher in countless former lives.  They are called “buddhas” because they have reached this lower approximation of enlightenment, and its attendant understandings; but since it is not full Buddhahood, we use the lower case.  See the typically brilliant explanation of the point by Je Tsongkapa (1357–1419) at f. 5b in his Illumination of the True Thought (B17, ST05408).

The general pronunciation of the Buddha’s full name in Sanskrit is Ratna Chandra Padma Pratimandita Pandita Tejah Svara Ghosha Raja.  The precise pronunciation is Ratna Candra Padma Pratimaṇḍita Paṇḍita Tejaḥ Svara Ghoṣa Rāja.

The teachings of the Buddha are divided into the “lower way” and the “greater way.”  The primary focus of the former is a personal nirvana, or state of inner peace permanently free of negative emotions.  The focus of the latter is becoming a full Buddha so that we can help every living being in the universe.

This is a crucial topic for understanding just how the names and secret words (mantras) of the Medicine Buddha practice can actually affect people and their karma.  Please see the discussion of this topic, in the appendix, called Gateways to the Secret Words of Holding: How the Medicine Buddha Really Works.

This is a period of many millions of years traditionally marked by four different events.  The destruction of the existing world lasts for twenty “intermediate” eons.  This is followed by a period of equal length during which there is nothing.  The formation of a new world then occurs, across twenty more such eons.  This is followed by twenty intermediate eons during which the world remains, and the majority of human history unfolds.  Thus, the “greater eon” mentioned here lasts for eighty intermediate eons.  See the explanation by Gyalwa Gendun Drup, His Holiness the First Dalai Lama (1391–1474), starting at f. 102a of his Light on the Path to Freedom (B3, SL05525).

This is a reference, found in the literature of Higher Knowledge (Abhidharma), to how beings living on a higher level of this planet witness the destruction of the lower level (where we ourselves live now) by a fire that spreads across the entire world.  See for example the poignant account by Gyalwa Gendun Drup, again in his Light on the Path to Freedom, ff. 76a–76b (B3, SL05525).

lemma: One-day vow of eight different parts
text: The eight are divided into four foundation commitments, and four secondary ones.  The foundation four are to refrain from (1) sexual activity of any kind; (2) stealing; (3) taking life; and (4) lying.  The secondary four are refraining from (5) utilizing luxurious objects; (6) drinking alcohol or using drugs; (7) dancing and similar activities performed in a heedless fashion, and ornamentation or such; and (8) eating after noon. The vow is described in the seminal summary of ethical behavior by Je Tsongkapa (1357–1419) entitled The Essence of the Ocean of Vowed Morality (B13, S05275-63).  A wonderful and thorough commentary to this work by Gyal Kenpo Drakpa Gyeltsen (1762–1836), including also the root text, may be found among the titles translated into English as part of the Diamond Cutter Classics Series of the Mixed Nuts Translation Group (for the eight parts see ff. 5a–6a, B4, S25101).

This third Buddha’s name in Sanskrit is Suvarna Bhadra Vimala Ratna Prabhasa Vrata.  The technical spelling, for more precise pronunciation, is only slightly different: Suvarṇa Bhadra Vimala Ratna Prabhāsa Vrata.

Master Yi Jing adds here, “They will take birth in the hells, and suffer from all kinds of pains.  Even if by some remote chance they find themselves back in the human realm, they won’t live very long…”  See p. 410c29 (S8, CBETA T14, no. 451).

Master Yi Jing adds, “They will fall to the lower realms; and even if by some remote chance they find themselves back in the human realm, they are born into a poor household.”  See p. 411a4–6 (S8, CBETA 2021.Q3, T14, no. 451).
Our own Buddha, Shakyamuni, is famed for having achieved his own enlightenment sitting at the base of a tree by this name.
Master Yi Jing’s early Chinese translation specifically mentions here “a sudden, untimely death.”  See p. 411b5–6 (S8, CBETA T14, no. 451).
Master Yi Jing here specifically adds that “Whoever keeps this mantra will harvest great benefits in this very life, and be free of all forms of pain.”  See p. 411b6–9 (S8, CBETA T14, no. 451).

Here is the technical form of the dharani, for those who would like to pronounce it more perfectly: Tadyathā, siddhe siddhe, susiddhe, mocani, mokṣaṇi, mukte, vimukte, amale, vimale, māṃgalye, hiraṇya garbhe, ratna garbhe, sarvārtha sādhani, paramārtha sādhani, manase, mahāmanase, adbhute, atyadbhute, vitabhaye, suvarṇe, brahma ghoṣe, brahmādhyuṣite, sarvārtheṣu aparājite, sarvatra apratihate, catuḥ ṣaṣṭhi buddhe, koṭi bhāṣite, namaḥ sarva Tathāgatānām svāhā.

Powerful worldly gods whom we will meet again further on, as making a commitment to help practitioners.  The protectors mentioned here have nothing to do with the current, unfortunate controversy concerning a traditional Buddhist protector.
Master Yi Jing’s translation includes here, “dry up the ocean of the negative emotions, to help them step out upon the shore of nirvana.”  See p. 411b23–24 (S8, CBETA 2021.Q3, T14, no. 451).

lemma: Eight components of the path of the realized ones
text: A “realized one” (arya in Sanskrit, or pakpa in Tibetan) is a person who has seen emptiness directly.  The eight special spiritual practices associated with them are described as follows by the great Rendawa Shunnu Lodru (1349–1412), who was a major teacher of the matchless Je Tsongkapa (see ff. 28a–28b of his String of Jewels, upon the Higher Knowledge School; B27, S19153): (1) Pure view, where the realized one is able to pinpoint what they saw during the direct perception of ultimate reality; (2) Pure conception, where the realized one is able to express what they have pinpointed about what they perceived at that juncture, in a way which others will comprehend.  (From here, all the rest as well relate to realized beings.) (3) Pure speech, the ability to speak in such a way that others can believe they possess an accurate view of things; (4) Pure conduct, speaking and acting in such a way that others can believe they conduct themselves in an ethical way; (5) Pure livelihood, speaking and acting in such a way that others can believe they have given up impure ways of making a living, and are following instead an honorable livelihood; (6) Pure effort, where they delight in the good work of gradually overcoming those spiritual obstacles which are removed on the “path of habituation”—the period subsequent to their seeing emptiness directly; (7) Pure awareness, where they are cleaning themselves completely of the negativities associated with mental dullness and agitation during a meditation session; and (8) Pure focus, where they are eliminating within themselves obstacles to clairvoyance, and reaching other such extraordinary achievements. Please also note that the translation of Master Yi Jing here mentions the “vow of eight components”; for a description, see footnote 23 at section 134 above.  For the reference in Yi Jing, see p. 411b29 (S8, CBETA 2021.Q3, T14, no. 451).
The fourth Buddha’s name in Sanskrit is Ashokottama Shri.  The technical spelling, for more precise pronunciation, is Aśokottama Śrī.
So called because there is not a moment spent there without extreme torment.
Master Yi Jing’s translation here adds, “And they will as well have to endure relationships with unkind family members, friends, and followers.”  See p. 411c28 (S8, CBETA 2021.Q3, T14, no. 451).
Master Yi Jing’s translation here adds, “And may they enjoy relationships with family members, friends, and followers who are kind to them.”  See p. 412a1–2 (S8, CBETA 2021.Q3, T14, no. 451).

The fifth Buddha’s full name in Sanskrit is Dharma Kirtti Sagara Ghosha.  The technical spelling, for more precise pronunciation, is Dharma Kīrtti Sāgara Ghoṣa.  Note that the spelling here differs from that of the name of the famous Buddhist logician, Dharma Kirti.
Master Yi Jing expands here, “…of the way that things are impermanent, suffering, empty, and never themselves.”  See p. 412a23–24 (S8, CBETA 2021.Q3, T14, no. 451).
Note that this refers not to lands far from civilization, but rather to parts of the world not yet reached by the teachings of an Enlightened Being.
Master Yi Jing’s translation adds here, “May they always be accompanied by a good spiritual guide, and never fall to the lower realms.”  See p. 412b9–10 (S8, CBETA 2021.Q3, T14, no. 451).

Our reader will have noticed, by now, that many of the prayers made by our seven Buddhas seem to overlap.  But when you think about it, they were different bodhisattvas, presumably on different planets, and could well be wishing for the same good things to happen.
Master Yi Jing continues with, “May they embrace the infinite thought of joy, and the infinite thought of equanimity.”  See p. 412b20–21 (S8, CBETA 2021.Q3, T14, no. 451).
The sixth Buddha’s full name in Sanskrit is Dharma Sagaragra Mati Vikriditabhijna Raja.  The technical spelling is Dharma Sāgarāgra Mati Vikrīḍitābhijñā Rāja.

lemma: Path of the ten bad deeds
text: These begin with three negative actions committed physically: taking the life of any being; stealing; and sexual misconduct, especially adultery.  Those are followed by four bad deeds committed verbally: lying; divisive speech; harsh words; and idle talk.  Finally come three negative deeds committed within the mind: being unhappy when others get something they want; being happy when something they don’t want happens to them; and harmful, mistaken views.

These are the opposite of the ten just mentioned.  In body, then, protecting life; respecting others’ possessions; and respecting others’ personal relationships.  In speech, telling the truth; speaking in ways that bring other people together; speaking gently; and always speaking of things that are helpful and meaningful.  In thought, sharing in others’ happiness when they get something they wanted; sharing in their sorrow when something happens to them that they did not want; and finally holding correct, unmistaken views.

The translation of Master Yi Jing here continues with the following section: “There will be certain beings who commit various kinds of bad deeds which cause them to lose their faith in the Three Jewels.  They will follow wrong views; they will abandon correct views; and they will enjoy the company of bad disciples.  They will denigrate the holy books of Buddhism, claiming that they are not the words of holy beings.  Instead, they will honor and follow the texts of the other schools, and also teach them to others—creating confusion for both themselves and others.  Such people will fall to the hells, with no opportunity escape.  And even if they somehow do, and take a rebirth as a human, then they will have to endure the eight lacks of leisure—far from the true path, and living blind, since they lack the eyes of wisdom.”  See p. 412c20–25 (S8, CBETA 2021.Q3, T14, no. 451).

The three “higher” rebirths: as a human, as a demigod, and as a worldly god.  Master Yi Jing’s translation then adds, “And when they have heard that name, may they come to keep correct view as they approach the end of their life, and be freed from every form of suffering.  May they be born in central lands, where the teachings thrive.  May they then be cleaned…”  See p. 412c26–27 (S8, CBETA 2021.Q3, T14, no. 451).

lemma: Holy names of the seven Buddhas
text: Since the seven Buddhas have not yet all appeared, this section seems to be out of place in the Tibetan version that we have used, from the Lhasa edition of Kangyur.  A study of Master Yi Jing’s translation helps clarify the correct order of the sections. The prayers of Sea Dancer end, as here, at section 264.  Then come the twelve prayers and other sections concerning Medicine Buddha himself, found here at sections 270–361.  After section 361, there is an additional section in Master Yi Jing’s translation not found in the Tibetan; see the note below, at this juncture.  Sections 265 to 268 in the Tibetan here then follow after this additional material; and finally section 268 leads into our section 368 here, with the subsequent parts the same in both the Tibetan and the Chinese.

In Master Yi Jing’s translation, this section begins with an added sentence: “They first use the brushing stick to clean their teeth; and then bathe themselves, so that they are cleansed.  They then make offerings…”  See p. 414c15–16 (S8, CBETA 2021.Q3, T14, no. 451).

Traditionally explained as relating together to the three extraordinary trainings.  The two strong legs are the foundation of the extraordinary trainings of morality and meditative concentration.  “Knowledge” is the extraordinary training of wisdom—an understanding of how reality works, and of ultimate reality.  See for example f. 168a of Fantastic Food for Faith, by Changkya Ngawang Lobsang Chunden (1642–1714), B6, S00147.

These are traditionally listed as (1) the vows of individual liberation—basically, commitments to refrain from harming others; (2) the vows of the bodhisattva—commitments that inevitably make us a person who can be of help to every living creature in the universe; and (3) the vows of the Diamond Way, or highest teachings—which enable us to provide this help within a single lifetime of practice.

lemma: Drop to the three lower realms
text: Master Yi Jing’s translation here adds, “And even should they break this ethical code, may they make a sincere confession, and speak my name wholeheartedly.  With this they will be able to restore the purity of this code, and continue such up to the day of their own enlightenment.”  See p. 413a22–24 (S8, CBETA 2021.Q3, T14, no. 451).
Previously described in our sutra as the enlightened paradise of the Buddha named Amitabha, or Limitless Light.  Connected as well later in the sutra to the Buddha named Amitayus, or Limitless Life.

lemma: World of the Lord of Death
text: This is an alternate name—not infrequently found in lists of the five or six types of rebirths—for the world of the hungry ghosts.  See for example f. 91b of the biography of Pabongka Rinpoche at B24, S00992.

Master Yi Jing’s translation includes an additional part at this point.  It reads, “They honor the code of ethics, never transgressing it; they keep to the correct view of things, and listen to a great many teachings.  They rid themselves of pride, and never denigrate the pure teachings.  Nor are they found in the company of evil friends.”  See p. 414a12–14 (S8, CBETA 2021.Q3, T14, no. 451).

lemma: The eight bodhisattvas of greatest power
text: A reference to the “Eight Great Sons,” a group of bodhisattvas who were particularly close to Lord Buddha; that is, (1) Gentle Voice (Manjushri) himself; (2) the Holder of the Diamond (Vajrapani); (3) Loving Eyes (Avalokiteshvara); (4) Essence of the Earth (Kshitigarbha); (5) Destroyer of Obstacles (Avarana Vishkambhi); (6) Essence of the Sky (Akashagarbha); (7) Loving One (Maitreya); and (8) Ever Pure (Samanta Bhadra). See for example the practice of fasting for Loving Eyes in his form with eleven faces at B23, S05929, f. 6a.  These eight are sometimes represented by eight petals in the corresponding lotus flower; see for example f. 366a of the treatment of secret empowerments by Dzeme Rinpoche (1927–1996) at B25, S12111. Incidentally, the number eight with bodhisattvas here is as well significant in that among eight qualities possessed by bodhisattvas at the eighth of the ten bodhisattva levels (essentially equivalent to nirvana on the track of the greater way, or mahayana) there is counted “so intense a love that they can display miracles upon countless worlds” (see f. 23a of the Great Commentary to Lord Maitreya’s Jewel of Realizations by the great Kedrup Tenpa Dargye of Sera Mey Monastery [1493–1568], B20, S00189). As a final note, another early Chinese translation lists another eight.  This text is The Sutra of Empowerment Spoken by the Enlightened One who Rescues Us from Bad Deeds, and Brings us Liberation from Birth & Death, rendered by Master Po Shrimitra (d. 343), from the Dong Jin Dynasty (317–420ad).  Here there are eight Holy Ones who guide the deceased to the Buddha paradise they hope for: (1) 文殊菩薩 Gentle Voice (Manjushri) himself (2) 觀世音菩薩 Loving Eyes (Avalokiteshvara) (3) 大勢至菩薩 Master of Tremendous Power (Mahasthama Prapta) (4) 無盡意菩薩 Remover of Every Obstacle (Avarana Vishkambhi) (5) 宝檀华菩萨 Precious Flower of Sandalwood (Ratna Chandana) (6) 藥王菩薩 King of Medicine (Bhaishajya Raja) (7) 藥上菩薩 Pure Birth of Medicine (Bhaishajya Samudgata) (8) 彌勒菩薩Loving One (Maitreya) See CBETA 2021.Q3, T21, no. 1331, p. 533c2–8.

lemma: The secret words of the holding
text: Here is the technical transcription, for those who may wish to follow the precise pronunciation: Tadyathā.  Om namo Bhagavate, Bhaiṣajya Guru, Vaiḍūrya Prabhā Rājāya.  Tathāgatāya, arhate, Saṃyak Saṃbuddhāya, Tadyathā.  Om Bhaiṣajye Bhaiṣajye Mahābhaiṣajye Rāja, samudgate svā hā.

lemma: Write it out as a book
text: This would include, in modern times, reproducing the sutra in print, on paper or digitally.

Master Yi Jing’s translation refers at this point not just to the name of the Medicine Buddha, but to the names of all seven Buddhas here; see p. 414c23–24 (S8, CBETA 2021.Q3, T14, no. 451).  This difference occurs repeatedly between sections 371 and 440.

The first of these is “Guardian of the Land” (Dhirta Rashtra), a powerful worldly being who has special authority over certain types of wandering spirits.  The second is “Eminent One” (Virudhaka), with authority over certain denizens of the sea.  The third is “Bad Eye” (Virupaksha), lord over the water dragons; while the fourth is “Prince of Learning” (Vaishravana), chief over specific harmful spirits.

lemma: The Three, the five, and the ten
text: The “Three” here are, of course, the Three Jewels: Buddha, Dharma, & Sangha.  On the deepest level, the refuge of the Dharma—the Teaching—consists of remembering that nothing comes from its own side: If our spouse yells at us in the kitchen, it is never something that doesn’t come, for example, from our yelling at the children last week.  When we realize this kind of absence directly in a deep meditation, we have truly achieved this Jewel. The refuge of the Sangha—the Community—consists of taking ourselves to those who have already had this direct experience, so they can help us to achieve it ourselves.  And the refuge of the Buddha—the Totally Enlightened One—is trusting ourselves to those who have reached omniscience, and the ability to directly help all living beings in the universe, so that we can in time join them in their efforts. These points are covered in an incomparable way by the great Kedrup Tenpa Dargye in his commentaries to Lord Maitreya’s Jewel of Realizations; see for example the section at ff. 41b–52a in Part Two of his Garland of White Lotuses (B19, SE00001-2). The five most basic trainings here are (1) refraining from the act of killing any other living being, or fetus; (2) refraining from stealing anything more valuable than an inexpensive sweater; (3) refraining from hurting a committed personal relationship, such as that between a husband and wife; (4) refraining from lying, especially about our spiritual life; and (5) refraining from the use of intoxicants—whether alcohol or drugs.  See for example f. 5b of the excellent commentary by Quicksilver Lama, Ngulchu Dharma Bhadra (1772–1851), to Je Tsongkapa’s Essence of the Ocean of Vowed Morality (B9, S06361). The ten trainings, as mentioned briefly earlier, consist of the first four of the five, and then (5) refraining from divisive speech; (6) refraining from harsh words; (7) refraining from idle talk; (8) refraining from being unhappy when others get something they wanted; (9) refraining from being happy when something happens to others that they didn’t want; and (10) refraining from mistaken view of the world—by believing, for example, that there is no law of karma & its consequences; or no future life; no Three Jewels, and no combination of cause & effect and emptiness. Some of the greatest explanations of these ten are to be found in the literature on the “steps of the path,” or lam-rim.  See for example the sections starting at f. 232a in A Gift of Liberation, Thrust into Our Hands, by Pabongka Rinpoche (B21, S00004); and at f. 107b in The Great Book on the Steps to the Path, by Je Tsongkapa (B16, S05392).

Current tradition lists 18 root downfalls, and 46 secondary offenses, for a total of 64 guidelines—although many of these can be broken down further.  The Indian commentator Master Kirshna Pada says, in his commentary to difficult points in Master Shantideva’s Guide to the Bodhisattva’s Way of Life, that the mention of 400 is not meant to refer to a specific number.  See f. 95a, S1, TD03875.

Again, these appear to be descriptive numbers, and not definitive.  The current tradition lists 253 guidelines for full monks, and 364 for full nuns.  See for example ff. 61b–62a of Je Tsongkapa’s Essence of the Ocean (B13, S05275-63).

These two heavenly bodies were even, in ancient times, sometimes perceived as worldly gods of great power.  See for example the description by Arya Nagarjuna at f. 44a in his famed Letter to a Friend (S3, TD04182).

The translation of Master Yi Jing says here that we should “Make 49 colorful banners, and one longer banner of 49 feet; and we should release 49 animals from captivity.”  See p. 415c22–23 (S8, CBETA 2021.Q3, T14, no. 451). The ancient Chinese translation of the shorter Medicine Buddha Sutra by Master Xuanzang (602–664ad) states that we should “Make a five-colored banner of 49 hand widths, and release 49 different types of animals from captivity.”  See p. 407c10–11 (S7, CBETA 2021.Q3, T14, no. 450). Master Yi Jing’s translation then concludes this section with: “In this way, all disasters and adversities may be avoided; negative forces and spirits will have no power over such persons.  O Revered One, O Joyful One, this then is how a person should make offerings to Those Gone Thus.  Those who make offerings even to a single one of these seven Enlightened Beings accumulate countless virtue, and see all their hopes come true.  What need mention then the result of making offerings to all seven of these Buddhas?”  p. 415c23–27 (S8, See CBETA 2021.Q3, T14, no. 451).

The translation of Master Yi Jing includes an additional paragraph after this last sentence, to conclude the section.  It reads, “O Revered One, O Joyful One, consider any king or queen; any princess or prince; any official of the realm; any male servant or maid; or any other man or woman who is tormented by sickness, or any other adversity.  Suppose that they fashion images of the Seven Buddhas; or read this sutra out loud; or keep offering lamps burning; release captive animals; or make offerings of incense sticks or flowers.  Should they do so, then all of their illness will come to an end; and all their adversities be put to rest.”  See p. 416a9–13 (S8, CBETA 2021.Q3, T14, no. 451).

The translation of Master Yi Jing adds here: “And has the Conqueror not thus taught us of various secret words and medicines; and medical treatments; as well as the practices of offering butter lamps, and making banners, and accomplishing various good deeds?  For when people collect merit, they will be able to extend their lifespan.’  Then did Joyful One request the bodhisattva named Freedom Shelter to list for him these nine different types of an untimely death; and so Freedom Shelter replied…”  See p. 416a15–19 (S8, CBETA 2021.Q3, T14, no. 451).

Master Yi Jing’s translation adds at this juncture the following section: “They believe the misleading words spoken to them by teachers of evil paths, who speak of good fortune or bad fortune; and so they become frightened.  They ask after omens—good or bad—and they kill living animals in sacrifices, hoping that the gods will fulfill their wishes.  They invoke negative spirits to grant them blessings that will extend their lifespan.  And yet they die, due to this ignorant confusion and completely mistaken viewpoints—and then fall to the realms of hell, with no chance of escaping.”  See p. 416a21–25 (S8, CBETA 2021.Q3, T14, no. 451).

Master Yi Jing’s translation adds a number of words here: “…lifestyle which is equally vulnerable, including activities like hunting, amusing themselves, and addictions to sex or alcohol.  And so as a result…”  See p. 416a26–27 (S8, CBETA 2021.Q3, T14, no. 451).

The translation of Master Yi Jing adds an additional paragraph at this juncture.  It reads as follows: Moreover, Ananda, the Lord of Death keeps a book of the names of every living being.  If there are people who have not honored their parents; or who have committed the five immediate deeds; disparaged the Three Jewels; or broken the code of society, then the Lord of Death will sentence them to punishments according to the degree of their bad deeds.  Therefore, today I advise all people to offer butter lamps; make banners; liberate animals; and accumulate merit—which will save them from various sufferings. See p. 416b5–9 (S8, CBETA 2021.Q2, T14, no. 451).

The name of this first of the leaders, and the name of the eighth, are missing in the longer Medicine Buddha sutra as found in the Kangyur scriptural collection; and so we have supplied them from the shorter version.  There is not currently available any Sanskrit version of the longer, and we have located only one version of the shorter—and taken the Sanskrit names directly from there as listed.  See f. 432a of S7, KL00504, for the Tibetan of the names; and for the Sanskrit pp. 29–30 of Dr. Dutt’s work for the original Sanskrit versions, at the same bibliography entry.
Note that the Sanskrit listed here is only Vikala, but Avikala seems more correct, given the Tibetan—which is usually quite accurate.

In the translation by Master Yi Jing, this last sentence continues with:  “Whosoever wishes to be freed from any trouble or sickness should read this sutra out loud, and tie knots on a five-colored cord to represent our names.  And then once their wishes are fulfilled, they should untie the knots.”  See p. 416b25–27 (S8, CBETA 2021.Q3, T14, no. 451).
The translation of Master Yi Jing here reads “…the kindness shown to you by the Seven Buddhas.”  See p. 416b28–c1 (S8, CBETA 2021.Q2, T14, no. 451).

The point of the name is that the holy beings living in this enlightened realm no longer tolerate any negativities within themselves.  See the wonderful etymology by the esteemed Buton Rinpoche (1290–1364)—who did much of the work of assembling the nearly 5,000 ancient texts of the Kangyur and Tengyur collections—at f. 40a of his history of early Buddhism (B22, S12060).
The translation of Master Yi Jing says here, again, “the vow with eight components”—and also repeats that in the next section.  See p. 417b3–5, and p. 417b9 (S8, CBETA 2021.Q2, T14, no. 451).
That is, a holy being of the secret traditions of the Buddha, which are also known as the “Diamond Way” (Vajrayana).
Master Yi Jing adds, “They will live in a state of love, one for the other, as though they were each other’s mother, or father.”  See p. 417b15–16 (S8, CBETA 2021.Q3, T14, no. 451).

The translation of Master Yi Jing adds after this sentence the following: “When people fall ill because of the influence of ghosts or spirits, then they should write this mantra down on paper and tie it behind their elbow.  Once they have recovered, the paper should be stored in a clean place.”  See p. 417c7–8 (S8, CBETA 2021.Q2, T14, no. 451).

The technical pronunciation of the mantra is: Tadyathā, oṃ vajre vajre mahāvajre, vajra pāśa dhāraṇī, samasama samanta, apratihata vajre, śama śama praśamantu, sarva vyādhayaḥ, kuru kuru kuru sarva karmāṇi, samayam anusmara Bhagavān Vajrapāṇi, sarva āśāṃ me paripūraya svāhā!
In Master Yi Jing, the sentence goes on: “Every hope of their heart, so that these foundational secret words will never fade from this world.”  See p. 416b25–27 (S8, CBETA 2021.Q3, T14, no. 451).

The translation of Master Yi Jing includes two further names here: the “Sutra Requested by Gentle Voice (Manjushri)”; and “A Detailed Account of the Prayers of the Medicine Buddha, Lapis Light.”  See p. 418a19–24 (S8, CBETA 2021.Q2, T14, no. 451).

Readers who would like to pronounce this word dharani more precisely can follow the technical pronunciation, dhāraṇī.  The macron over a vowel means that we hold it for twice the length: dhaa-ra-nee.  The “underdot” below the n indicates that we say the letter as a retroflex, turning the tip of the tongue up under the back of the top front teeth.  If you’re doing it right, you will sound a bit like a person from modern-day India!
See f. 117a of Master Chandragomi’s commentary (%S2, TD04279).
Okay, okay, for real Dharma nerds out there, here are the Sanskrit comments, away from the main body of our essay, where they would be confusing for the average reader.

lemma: In the case of tantra, the comment is prabandhākhyā
text: “an explanation of the composition.”  For mantra, it is mantre gupti bhāṣane: “in that it is spoken secretly in the mantra.”  For vidya (another common word for tantra), it is vidjñāna: “wisdom of knowing.”  For dharani, it is artha grantha dhārayati dhāraṇī: “dharani by virtue of holding both meaning and word.”
See f. 4a of his Lamp Which Sheds All Light (B8, S06351).
See f. 344b of the first volume of the teaching (S9, KL00009).
That is, in technical spelling, saṃskṛta, which is made of sam (“perfectly”) and kṛta (“formed”).  When the two come together in a single word, the rules of Sanskrit require an s letter inbetween.
See for example f. 433a of the native catalog to the Derge edition of the Tengyur, which is a highly accurate edition, and the one that we most often use in this and other writings (B26, TD04569).
Careful readers of the sutra will easily figure out this plural.
See ff. 146b–147a of Master Vasubandhu’s commentary (S5, TD03808).
For those who would like to pronounce the mantra more precisely, the technical spelling is only slightly different from the simplified pronunciation: Om akaro mukham sarva dharmāṇām adyanutpannatvāt.

For our explanation of the meaning of the mantra, we are relying heavily upon a wonderful explanation again by the great Quicksilver Lama.  See f. 136a of his Secret Treasure of the Angels (B10, S00202).

Here is the technical pronunciation, for those who would like to say the mantra more precisely: Ye dharmā hetu prabhavā hetun teṣān Tathāgato hyavadat, teṣāñ ca yo nirodha evaṃ vādī Mahāśramaṇaḥ.  We have based this rendering on the ancient text devoted to the mantra; see ff. 324b–325a of S6, KL00521.

An easily understood and still accurate rendering of the full title, which is An Exalted Sutra of the Greater Way Entitled “Unraveling the True Thought.”  For text details, see bibliography entry S35 below.
For text details see bibliography entry B102, ACIP catalog number S25001.
That is, in technical Tibetan spelling, Blo-bzang ‘jigs-med.

The reference to our author as Rikdra Rikpay Reldri (Rigs-grva rig-pa’i ral-gri) may be found for example in A Catalog of Some of the Great Books of Tibet (B109, R00004, p. 616).  He refers to himself as “Lobsang the Fearless” (Blo-bzang ‘jigs-med) in the colophon to the edition used in this volume (f. 14b, B102, S25001). We should not confuse him with a teacher of the same name, Rikpay Reldri, dated 1227–1305; it would seem that the “Rikdra” has been historically used to distinguish them, as this is never added to the name of the earlier one.
The technical spelling of the former is rnam-thar; and the latter, rtogs-brjod.

Dates, names, and incarnations are from the entry devoted to him in the Buddhist Digital Resource Database (BDRC), accessed January 6, 2021.  His name is technically spelled Reb-rtza (also seen as Reb-tsa) bKa’-’gyur-ba dKon-mchog dam-chos yar-’phel.

See p. 102 of the Treasury of Names (B2, S12327), as well as p. 84 of A Catalog of Some of the Great Books of Tibet (B109, R00004).  For the comments by Mi-nyak Gunpo, see pp. 248–252, “A Brief Biography of Rikdra Lobsang Jikme,” in Brief Biographies of the Procession of Master Sages Who Have Appeared in the Land of Snows (B85, S25114).
It says “Da-pa,” which refers to the eleventh volume of a set.  This is sometimes an error for “Nga-pa,” which looks very similar, and refers to the fourth volume.
See entry 13534, p. 601, in the Materials (B111); and entries 51488–51490 (corresponding to the original Institute numbers B10020/1 to B10020/3) in the Institute catalog (B113).
See f. 58b of the commentary (B3, S25117).

See f. 82a of the biography (B95, S25115).  To get a taste of the original incarnation’s writings, readers may wish to refer to his extraordinary biography of Je Tsongkapa, meant to be the basis for painting the events of the Master’s life onto thangka scrolls.  Refer to B40 (S00072), as well as the English translation of this work (and presentation of the paintings themselves), included in the present Diamond Cutter Classics Series.  For this, see p. 295 of King of the Dharma: The Illustrated Life of Je Tsongkapa, Teacher of the First Dalai Lama (E2).
See p. 248 of the author’s Brief Biography (B85, S25114).

text: See BDRC article for The Blade (p. 285 of B85, accessed January 5, 2021) and f. 35 of B104.
Difficult technical spelling, Thu’u-bkvan.

text: For the original by Ngawang Tashi, see B30.  For the commentary by Konchok Jikme Wangpo, see B5.  The Blade is mentioned there at f. 26a.
The original prayer is by Sumati Abhyashasanasya Dhvadza; see B107.  For the commentary by The Blade, see B101.

See for example the lists in the Questions & Answers of the great Pabongka Rinpoche Dechen Nyingpo (1878–1941); refer to f. 35b (B66, S00505).

That is, in technical spelling, Po-ti lnga—where po-ti often has a connotation more of the physical volume.
Readers with a knowledge of Tibetan may like to know the formal spelling: skyid-sdug gcig-pa.

Jang (technically spelled ‘Jang) is a monastery not far from Lhasa where these debates were traditionally held, before the destruction of the Cultural Revolution.  Modern monks often mis-hear the name as Jamyang, which is not so bad, considering this word refers to Manjushri, the embodiment of all the Buddhas’ wisdom.

Incidentally, our entire essay here relates to a young monk.  But—finally!—in very recent years the geshe study program, after centuries of foot-dragging, has been opened up as well to nuns, in convents of the Tsongkapian tradition.

This way can correctly be referred to also as tantra, or the “secret lineage” for helping others in the fastest manner possible.  Yet this sacred term has sadly accumulated such a filthy connotation in the modern world that we will have to avoid it here.
See, for the Kalachakra text, B96.  For Sarvavid, see B90.
See f. 36b of the Rinpoche’s record of oral transmissions and instructions received, at B69.
See f. 200a of the Rinpoche’s record of oral transmissions without accompanying teachings, at B68.

lemma: In your love, care for us
text: There are some classical poeticisms here.  “Summer drums” refers to rumbling sounds of thunder, which for some reason peacocks—according to ancient Asian tradition—find particularly enjoyable.  “Those with crowns” is a name for peacocks, referring to the antenna-like tufts on their heads.  “Glorious Gentle Voice” is the translation of the name of Manjughosha, with its equivalent Manjushri: the embodiment of the wisdom of all the Buddhas—a wisdom which we require to understand this book. A full list of the Sanskrit, Chinese, Tibetan, and English names of divine beings is included in Appendix A.  The “three realms” are the three sectors of the Buddhist universe—desire realm; form realm; and formless realm; the phrase can also refer to all creatures in the sense of those who walk upon the earth; those who burrow below it; and those who fly above.
Throughout Fearless Blade’s commentary, we have inserted Tsongkapa’s root text in bold.
Where Fearless Blade weaves the words of Je Tsongkapa’s root text into his commentary, we have italicized them.

An excellent presentation of the four appears in a commentary to the Jewel of Realizations by Choney Lama Drakpa Shedrup entitled The Cloud of Offerings (see ff. 75a–75b, B21, S00195-4).  He divides them into two versions: a less subtle, and a more subtle.  The less subtle are (1) the five impure parts to a person that we have taken on at birth; (2) the negative emotions which block us from achieving nirvana; (3) a certain powerful spirit known as “Lord of Desires,” who tends to distract us from doing good things; and (4) the Lord of Death, which actually refers to the fact that—because of our past deeds and negative emotions—the power of our life force must one day end. The more subtle are (1) the five parts of a person that we are born into due mainly to the seeds of misunderstanding our world; (2) our subtle negative emotions, referring to our subtle seeds of misunderstanding (here Choney Lama also adds forms of unstained karma); (3) the Lord of Desire, considered actually as the same thing as the subtle seeds just mentioned; and (4) the discontinuation—due to the seeds of misunderstanding, or even unstained karma—of a homogenous form of the five parts of a person.
Here referring to high practitioners who have not yet committed to the task of saving every living being in the universe from suffering.

There are a few Buddhist technical terms here.  “What is always good” is a phrase used to describe nirvana and enlightenment.  The “three collections” are three groupings of the Buddha’s teachings, sometimes called the “three baskets” from the Sanskrit, tri-pitaka.  These three are described nicely by Tsongkapa’s disciple Kedrup Je in his brilliant work, Great Presentation of the Interlude on Emptiness (f. 8a, B18, S05459). The collection of vowed morality (vinaya) features teachings on the extraordinary training of an ethical life; the collection of sutra (sutra) features teachings on the extraordinary training of meditation; and the collection of higher knowledge (abhidharma) features teachings on the extraordinary training of wisdom. The “three ways” mentioned here can refer either to the lower way, the open teachings of the higher way, and the secret teachings of the higher way; or to the three tracks through the five paths: listener, self-made buddha, and bodhisattva.

lemma: Chujey Dundrup Rinchen and Lord Rendawa
text: Two of Je Tsongkapa’s principal teachers.  The former (1308–1385) tutored Je Rinpoche from childhood, and gave him his first ordination vows; the latter (1349–1412) guided him, for much of his life, through major subjects such as vowed morality; higher knowledge; the Mind Only School; and Middle Way philosophy.  See Je Tsongkapa’s illustrated biography, King of the Dharma, for details throughout (E2).

lemma: Those who believe there is nothing but conceptualization
text: A reference to the “Conceptualists” of the root text, meaning followers of the Mind Only School.

This wording represents a traditional preliminary to the composition of a scripture wherein the author expresses humility: “I am just writing this for myself; I would never assume that it would help someone else.”  But of course it does!

A reference to Arya Asanga and Master Vasubandhu, who had the same mother.  The Explanation of Secret Points is a text found in the Mind Only School Section of the Tengyur Collection of classical commentaries from ancient India (S41, TD04052).  It is described in the native catalog to the Derge edition of the Tengyur as “as much as we could find of a commentary to the first chapter of [Arya Asanga’s] Summary of the Greater Way; it is said in earlier catalogs to have been composed by Master Vasubandhu, but it would seem that this is mistaken” (see f. 446a, B87, TD04569).  From his syntax in the Tibetan here, Fearless Blade would appear to agree, although he does not identify the true author.

Please note that Je Tsongkapa’s root text is not divided regularly; it is so brief that he is using traditional Tibetan divider symbols (tseg-shad) to isolate sections even in half-lines, as here.  We therefore number each section that he divides out with these symbols with a separate reference number.

The reference in the Journey to Langka may be found on f. 265a (S33, KL00107); that in the Root Secret Teaching of Gentle Voice (Manjushri) is located on f. 408a (S31, KL00543).  Both citations (the latter only in part) are given by Je Tsongkapa in his autocommentary, which is found in the second volume of the present translation; see f. 5a (B54, ST05414B). The “two lower ways” mentioned here are the way of the listener, and the way of the self-made buddha.  Both are included, more generally, within the lower way.  That is, Buddhism in general is broadly divided into the “lower way” (called hinayana in Sanskrit) and the “higher way” (mahayana); and these two are contained within the former.  The difference between the lower and higher ways in general is that the latter emphasizes the bodhisattva ideal of trying to reach full enlightenment, in order to help every living being in the universe.  The higher way also presents the idea that nothing is itself (emptiness) in a more correct and comprehensive way. A “self-made buddha” is a person who achieves nirvana (not full Buddhahood, thus the lower case) without needing to study under a master in this life—but only because they have completed such study in countless former lives.  See for example the commentary to Master Asanga’s Compendium of Higher Knowledge by Gyaltsab Je (1364–1432) (f. 194a, B26, S05435).

A “realized one” (arya in Sanskrit) is one of those rare persons who has seen emptiness directly; Nagarjuna is possibly the most famous of them in history, and is sometimes simply called “The Arya” (“The Realized One”).

The “dragons” mentioned here are called nagas in Sanskrit; their actual appearance (as they have assumed identities as well) resembles that of the western idea of a dragon, and they are often associated with bodies of water.  Like dragons as they are presented in western literature of the past, they are attracted to treasure of all kinds, including fine scriptures.  Nagarjuna’s name actually means “Lord of the Nagas,” since in his lifetime he found a way to travel to the lands of these beings and recover precious scriptures that had gone missing during the centuries between the passing of Lord Buddha and Nagarjuna’s birth.

A translation of the Sanskrit word Madhyamika, which has come to refer to the highest of the four classical schools of ancient Indian Buddhism.  More generally, it represents a middle approach through the two extremes of believing—mistakenly—that things exist the way they seem to us; and that if they don’t exist that way, then they can’t exist at all.  Gungtang Konchok Tenpay Drunme (1762–1823) gives a brief beautiful explanation of the name at ff. 23b–24a of his Light on the True Nature, tracing it back to a group of teachings by Lord Buddha himself entitled A Pile of Rare and Precious Gems.  (For the former, see B7, S00901; for the latter, see f. 229b of The Account of Kashyapa, S29, KL00087).
See ff. 408a–408b of the Manjushri tantra (S31, KL00543).
That is, The Jewel of Realizations, The Jewel of the Sutras, Distinguishing the Middle from the Extremes, An Analysis of the Sphere of Reality, and The Higher Line.

Meaning an object that will neither produce a positive karmic result nor a negative karmic result.  The technical term here is avyakirta in the Sanskrit and lung ma bstan in the Tibetan, both meaning “not clarified.”  The basic idea here is that if Lord Buddha during his life did not clarify an action as being positive or negative, then it is neutral—although obviously he did not clarify every single possible action, and this distinction is more descriptive than definitive. For a nice explanation of the “unclarified” concept, see Gyaltsab Je at ff. 37a–37b of his commentary to the Compendium of Higher Knowledge (B26, S05435).  For the concept of karmic neutrality, see Choney Lama’s commentary to the Treasure House of Higher Knowledge (f. 106b, B22, S00027).  For a good general description see Jamyang Shepa’s analysis of the Jewel of Realizations (f. 256a, B41, S19088).

Again, a pile of Buddhist technical terms here.  “Linked mentally” refers to a situation where the main mind is linked to one or more mental functions, in five different ways: they share the same support (sense power); the same object of focus; the same aspect (for example, “bluish”); same duration; and same substance (mental stuff).  For a clear explanation see Kachen Lobsang Supa’s excellent modern Logic Topics (ff. 22a–22b, B15, S00978). The “ever-present five” are five mental functions which always accompany main mind.  These are the capacity of feeling; capacity of discrimination; mental movement; contact (between consciousness, related sense power, and its object); and attention.  They are pictured as being “in attendance” on main mind, in the way that attendants might sit in a circle on the ground before a king seated on a throne.  See for example the famed Collected Topics of Ngawang Tashi (1678–1738) (f. 36a, B29, S00217). The “group of six types of consciousness” consists of consciousness of the eye; ear; nose; tongue; body; and thought.

lemma: Lower two of the three realms
text: The Buddhist universe is pictured as including three sectors: the desire realm, form realm, and formless realm.  The desire realm (where we live) is one inhabited by beings attracted to gross physical objects, such as food and sex. The form realm is distinguished by extraordinary physical forms; the beings there, for example, look a lot like the superheroes in modern movies.  Beings in the formless realm possess no manifest physical form—thus the debate here. We are reborn into one of the higher two realms by engaging in deep meditations, and thereby avoiding our usual constant flow of small negativities.  Unfortunately the good power that sends us to these two inevitably wears out, and we always fall then into the lower realms.  The classic presentation of these realms is the third chapter of Master Vasubandhu’s Treasure House of Higher Knowledge (S25, TD04089).
See the discussion beginning at f. 9a of Je Tsongkapa’s autocommentary (B54, ST05414B).

This is one of the meditations just described in footnote 86 (Section G47 above) as projecting us into a rebirth in the formless realm.  “Infinite space” is the name of the first of the four levels of this type of meditation.

We don’t know a lot about him, or his dates; some references might place him about a millennium ago.  Sometimes we see “Jahu” mistakenly written for “Jahnu,” an ancient Indian king and sage who is said to have drunk the oceans. One very possible identification is a Nepalese scholar named Ja-hung mentioned in the Blue Annals at p. 465 and p. 1,004 of volumes 1 and 2, respectively (B25, S25006).  He is said to have been a teacher of Kirshnapada, which would put him in the right time frame.  Ja-hung is Sanskrit (Dza: h’uṃ in the Tibetan) and is coincidentally the first part of a mantra of unification in the Vajra Yogini literature (see for example f. 17a of Pabongka Rinpoche Dechen Nyingpo’s commentary, B65, S00046). In any event, Jahu’s position on this point—as well as the second position here—are quite clear, from the commentary to this same text of Je Tsongkapa written by Konchok Tenpay Drunme (1762–1823) (see ff. 25b–26a, B11, S00910).
In the present context, a reference to the first of the four schools of ancient Indian Buddhism, as typified by the teachings found in Master Vasubandhu’s famed Treasure House of Higher Knowledge.
A Buddhist technical term for the physical world and all the creatures who inhabit it.
A particular Buddha paradise (Skt: Mārīcī; Tib: ‘Od-zer-can gyi zhing-khams).
That is, the famed bardo, where people between births live in a kind of spirit form.

lemma: Links of the cycle of pain
text: Referring to the twelve links of the Wheel of Life, or dependence.

lemma: Twelve different divisions of the holy word
text: These are twelve traditional divisions of the Buddhist teachings, according to a mixture of subject matter, format, and style.  The classic reference to the twelve is found in Master Haribhadra’s Illumination of the Jewel (see f. 23a, S40, TD03791).  The traditional names for each division are obscure; they are nicely explained as follows by the great Mongolian sage Chujey Ngawang Pelden in the first volume of his Lamp for the Jewel of Realizations (B31, S00982):
Original, concise, prose presentations of the teachings.
Sutra presentations which are embellished, either at the beginning or ending, by verse; also any sutras which are not to be taken literally.
Explanations concerning how people die and move on, and where they will take rebirth; also any sutras which are to be taken literally.
Sutras where the entire presentation is made in verse.
Presentations dedicated to the purpose of the teachings remaining in this world for a very long time.
A description of the location; the person(s) involved; the negative emotions involved; and the problems involved, when Lord Buddha decided to prohibit a certain action.
Situations where examples, or real cases, are related to illustrate a particular point.
Teachings where the correlations between certain activities and their karmic consequences are described.
Occasions where our Teacher described the activities and hardships he went through as a bodhisattva striving for enlightenment.
Detailed descriptions of the path of the bodhisattva.
Descriptions of the wondrous good qualities of Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and other holy beings.

Detailed descriptions of either the general, or specific, defining characteristics of specific entities. Je Tsongkapa, in his String of Golden Beads, connects these twelve to the famous “three collections” or “three baskets” (tripitaka) of the Buddhist teachings: divisions #1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 relate primarily to the collection of sutras for the lower way; divisions #6, 7, 8, and 9 to the collection of vowed morality; divisions #10 and 11 to the collection of sutras for the higher way; and division #12 to the collection of higher knowledge—both in the version relating to the higher way, and the lesser.  See f. 38a of Vol. 1 (B55, S05412).

lemma: Holding objects in an illumined way
text: This phrase is as arcane in Tibetan as it is in English.  But it can be easily understood by the most common reference to it, which occurs in the study of meditation—and specifically the four levels of meditation which result in a rebirth into the formless realm.  (These are similar to the four levels of meditation, already discussed, which result in a rebirth into the form realm.) During the third and fourth levels of these “formless realm” meditations, we purposely try to “shut down” our own consciousness—much in the way that we would turn out a light, except here the “light” is awareness itself, in the sense of holding things in an illumined way.  These two forms of meditation incidentally are not a true spiritual goal and have—over the entire history of Buddhism, and in many meditation studios in the present day—been mistaken for the gloriously useful meditation on emptiness. For a great presentation on “the tendency to illumine,” see the magnificent Interlude on Emptiness by Je Tsongkapa’s close disciple Kedrup Je (1385–1438), f. 60b (B18, S05459).  For a neat discussion of mistaking these “shut down” meditations for emptiness meditations, see the extended discussion by Je Rinpoche’s other close disciple, Gyaltsab Je (1364–1432), in his commentary to Arya Nagarjuna’s Sixty Verses (starting at f. 4b, B27, S05443).  The translation of the former will be volume 97 in the present Diamond Cutter Classics Series; and the latter volume 87.

Karmically neutral entities, already discussed in footnote 84 (at section G37), are divided into two types: one which does block us from reaching our spiritual goals, and another which does not.  The type that does is said by the great Mongol sage Chujey Ngawang Pelden (b. 1797) for example to always be involved with negative emotions; while the type that does not block us is not (see f. 10a, B32, S12161).

Generally speaking, there are two traditional presentations of the functions of the mind.  The general literature on higher knowledge (abhidharma)—specifically Master Vasubandhu’s Treasure House of Higher Knowledge—presents them in six groups (five “fixed” groups and one “not fixed” group) totaling 46 functions. The specific higher-knowledge presentation emphasizing the Mind Only School and best known from Master Asanga’s Compendium of Higher Knowledge gives 51 mental functions in six groups.  Naturally, Je Tsongkapa and Fearless Blade are here using the latter, which also became the standard used for the famed Collected Topics of Logic presentations of these functions associated with the Sutrist School. For the interested readers, we have provided a complete, traditional listing of the 51 mental functions, according to their six groups, in Appendix B.  We have included the functions’ original names in Sanskrit, Pali, Chinese, and Tibetan.

Meaning that whether they are karmically virtuous, non-virtuous, or neutral depends upon the mental context in which they occur.  We have numbered the four in these sections to make it easier for our readers to identify them.

The Tibetan used here, len-pa, can be read as the traditional nye-bar len-pa, meaning “a part of us taken on at birth” as karma ripens.  At the same time it shades towards “grasped as a self,” in the sense covered in the immediately preceding verse.

lemma: Enemy destroyer with nothing left over
text: An “enemy destroyer” is a person who has put a permanent end to their negative emotions, and thus reached nirvana.  In the teachings of the lower-way schools of Buddhism, a person attains this state but still possesses the old body and mind created by their previous karmic seeds.  When the flow of this body & mind is discontinued, it is then referred to as “nirvana with nothing left over.”  See for example the discussions in the commentary to the Treasure House of Higher Knowledge by the esteemed Gyalwang Trinley Namgyal (c. 1850) at ff. 6b–7a of Vol. 1 (B80, S00044).

lemma: Adamantine concentration of the path of habituation
text: A state of meditation which leads directly into complete Buddhahood, and is thus associated with the eighth of the twelve great deeds of Shakyamuni Buddha—his full enlightenment.  See for example f. 6a of the overview of vowed morality by Sera Jetsun Chukyi Gyeltsen (1469–1546) (B108, S06848).

That is, the six states of consciousness common to all Buddhist schools (visual consciousness through mental consciousness), along with the famed “number seven”—or negative consciousness, which is unique to the present, Mind Only School.  Specific mental functions for example would be “attendants.”

Buddhist philosophy posits two kinds of existing entities: one type which is changing, and a second which is unchanging.  The latter type is often described as “any entity which exists, but which has not been brought about by the convening of causes and conditions.”  Such an entity—something like the empty space or position occupied by an object—could not be changed by imprinting it with something new.
Most often referring to a state of awareness which is operating in the normal world, and not actively perceiving that world’s true nature.

These two, along with “imaginaries,” constitute the famed “three defining qualities” of existence, according to the Mind Only School.  Put simply, we can understand the three almost as an equation.  We start with “contingents”—which refers to all objects which are contingent upon others in a cause-and-effect sense; that is, entities which are results and depend for their existence upon their causes and conditions. Normal people though entertain misconceptions about these contingent objects—they imagine, for example, that objects which are actually appearing within the mind itself exist, instead, on the outside.  If we can strip away these imaginary ideas from the contingent objects (subtract im from co), the process culminates in, or establishes, the concept of emptiness (that is, co-im = cu).  This “formula” is the subject matter of much of Je Tsongkapa’s brilliant Essence of Eloquence, on the Art of Interpretation (B51, S05396).

There are a number of technical terms here.  The “view of destruction,” broadly speaking, is the tendency to believe that either “me” or “mine” has some nature of its own: it focuses on the five parts of a person, which are bound for destruction.  Thorough treatments of this viewpoint may be found in discussions of the first link of the famous Wheel of Life, for example in the treatment by Kedrup Tenpa Dargye included in the present Diamond Cutter Classics Series (see the section starting at f. 2b, B59, S00015). In general, mistaken views in Buddhism are often divided into those which we are born with, and those which are learned, in this life, from mistaken explanations of the world which we receive from others. “Whichever form of grasping to a self-nature” is a reference to the fact that this grasping is traditionally divided into grasping to a self-nature of the person, or to a self-nature of the person’s parts. The concept of a mental link between main mind and its various mental functions has been discussed in footnote 85 (at section G38 above).
A reference to the twelve links of dependence, which are portrayed for example in the famed painting of the Wheel of Life: twelve steps in a chain reaction which brings us all our pain.

This is a reference to a concept found in the teachings on higher knowledge.  The roots of our hair for example are “held by consciousness” since, when we pull out a hair, it hurts; the tips though are not thus held, since we can get a haircut without the same sting.  See for example f. 32b of the commentary to the Treasure House by His Holiness the First Dalai Lama, Gendun Drup (B23, SE05525).

Secret Points, as found at present in the Tengyur collection of early Indian commentaries, is again an incomplete commentary to the first chapter of Master Asanga’s Summary of the Greater Way (itself at S2, TD04048).  A discussion of the different types of mental seeds may be found there beginning at f. 335a (S41, TD04052).  As noted in footnote 76 (at section G16), the native catalog to the Derge edition of the Tengyur states that some earlier listings attribute the work to Master Vasubandhu, but that this is questionable (see f. 446a, B87, TD04569). The Explication is also a commentary to the Summary of the Greater Way, composed by an Indian master whose name is listed in Tibetan as Ngo-bo-nyid med-pa, which in the original Sanskrit was Nihsvabhava, or some similar variant.  Here the relevant discussion begins on f. 205a (S20, TD04051).  Lord Tsongkapa’s treatment, which will be included in the second volume of the present work, begins at f. 16a (B54, ST05414B).
Two sets of entities famous for having the very same members; that is, if something has been created, it is constantly changing—and vice versa.

lemma: All three qualities must be present
text: This is a reference to the classical definition, in Buddhist logic, of “an object to be defined” (technically called a “definiendum,” or “subject of a definition”).  We might wish to define, for example, what a “water pitcher” is.  The traditional definition of a water pitcher, in ancient Buddhism, reads this way: “A rounded vessel, with a flat base, which can perform the function of holding water.” To be valid, this and any other definition must have three substantial (as opposed to nominal) qualities.  First, it must—in general—be a definition of something. Secondly, it must be perceived, with an accurate perception, as applying to an actual, typical example of what it defines.  This could be, for example, a particular glass pitcher sitting between us on a table right now. Thirdly, this particular definition should not be applicable to any other object we wish to define: it must be unique to what we are defining at the present moment. Why are these three qualities said to be “substantial”?  More particularly, why would elements of the definition of a water pitcher be considered more “substantial” than the water pitcher that they define?  If you think about it, the rounded shape; flat base; and water-holding exhibited by a water pitcher are more concrete or “substantial” than the idea of “water pitcher”—and this is the point here. From this point of view, the object being defined would be considered more “nominal” than “substantial.”  Thus, the three elements required of an “object being defined” are referred to as the “three nominal qualities.” These three elements, by the way, are listed as follows.  First, “water pitcher” must in general be an object which we can define.  Secondly, we should be able to perceive—with an accurate perception—that “water pitcher” applies to a particular object, or objects, in the universe.  Third, “water pitcher” should not be something that definitions other than its own particular definition could apply to. The point of raising this difficult subject here in the commentary is to compare the lack of substantiality of mental seeds, or potentials, to the lack of substantiality of these elements of something defined.  To put it more easily, “water pitcher” is an idea, and not a physical reality.  The elements that we look for when we try to decide whether something is a water pitcher or not are, rather, more substantial: certain shapes, or function. The definition of definition itself is an important topic in the classical Buddhist literature on logic and perception, typified by Master Dharmakirti’s Commentary on Accurate Perception.  For clear textbook presentations, see f. 16b of the work by Jamyang Shepay Dorje (1648–1721) entitled Colors, White & Red (B37, S19076); as well as f. 34b in Vol. 2 of the Collected Topics of the great tutor, Purbuchok Jampa Tsultrim Gyatso (1825–1901) (B70, S06857).
See, for example, ff. 61a–61b of Master Asanga’s Compendium of Higher Knowledge (S1, TD04049).
See the section in Je Rinpoche’s autocommentary starting from f. 23a (B54, ST05414B).

That is, the great Buton Rinpoche Rinchen Drup (1290–1364), who was instrumental in the assembly of the Indian Buddhist canon in Tibetan translation.  The latter two Sanskrit names in this sentence are attempted reconstructions from the Tibetan.  We have not been able to locate this statement in Buton Rinpoche’s works; Jamyang Shepa (1648–1721) (f. 283b, B38, S19028) also complains that he has trouble doing so.  Gungtang Konchok Tenpay Drunmey (1762–1823) (f. 32b, B11, S00910) says that the attribution to Buton Rinpoche is found in “the great book on philosophical systems,” which most often applies to that by Changkya Rolpay Dorje (1717–1786), but we haven’t found it there either.

The Blue Annals identify the master translator from Pang as Lodru Tenpa (1276–1342) (see f. 58a of the section on the Lineage of Marpa, B25, SP25006 [pecha version input]).  Sasang Ngakgi Wangpo was a contemporary of Je Tsongkapa.  The Sanskrit names here as well are attempted reconstructions of the Tibetan.  It seems to us that the “great book” mentioned at this point is in fact the work on comparative philosophy by Jamyang Shepa that we’ve cited in footnote 117 (at section G144).
See f. 24b of Tsongkapa’s autocommentary (B54, ST05414B).

This eminent lama was the reincarnation of the illustrious Jamyang Shepay Dorje (1648–1721), and is himself dated by the Buddhist Digital Resource Center as having lived 1728–1791.  BDRC also lists here Fearless Blade, our author, as one of Konchok Jikme Wangpo’s students; and the high honorifics used for him here in The Blade’s text are typical (even required) for referring to one’s own direct teacher. This would mean that The Blade was actively studying around 1775.

lemma: Facts of suffering and its source
text: This is an allusion to the four well-known “higher truths” which in fact constituted the first teaching of Lord Buddha in this world.  These are (1) the truth of suffering; (2) the truth of the source of suffering; (3) the truth of the end of suffering; and (4) the truth of the path to the end of suffering. The original Sanskrit word for “higher” here is arya, which refers to a person who has seen emptiness directly.  The root meaning of this word is “higher” or “superior,” in the sense that such a person has—by seeing the ultimate nature of reality directly—thereby entered an infinitely higher stage of human evolution.  The common translation of “Four Noble Truths” here is incorrect. In the present context we have used the word “fact” rather than “truth,” since—very importantly—these are not four statements about the way things are, but rather refer themselves to the actual realities expressed; thus, the pain of a dentist’s drill, or of losing a loved one, itself constitutes the “truth” or fact of suffering.  For all these points see the discussion beginning at f. 6b of the dedicated treatise on the four truths by Jamyang Shepay Dorje (1648–1721) (B43, S19026).

Note that Fearless Blade is using the Tibetan word ngo-bo (“nature”) here for the word dngos-po (“functioning thing,” or more broadly just “existing thing”) in Je Tsongkapa’s original verse, as we find it in the editions of his work available to us.  Keep in mind that both connect back to the Sanskrit word bhava, which happily covers all these connotations.

As noted here, this is an expression that generally refers to a bodhisattva at the eighth or higher bodhisattva levels.  In some works the emphasis of “attaining power” is to make substantial progress in ten different spiritual powers; see for example f. 319a of Gyaltsab Je’s Jewel for the Heart (B28, S05433).  This text itself references a sutra as a source for equating the “attainment of power” and the eighth bodhisattva level; the source is given in Kedrup Je’s masterful Great Interlude on Emptiness (at f. 82b, B18, S05459) as a sutra entitled The Lion’s Roar of the Goddess Shrimala; see for example f. 435b of that work (S34, KL00092). Further clarification of Je Tsongkapa’s thinking on this point may be found in The Union of Sun and Moon, a commentary to his current work by Keutsang Lobsang Jamyang Munlam (b. 1689), where this stage of spiritual realization is referred to as ending obstacles created by the negative emotions (see f. 230b, B1, S06514).  Other important works mention, in this context, attaining extraordinary power over wisdom where we no longer perceive things as self-existent; see for example f. 225b of Je Tsongkapa’s famed Great Book on the Steps of the Path (B49, S05392L), and f. 90a of Jamyang Shepay Dorje’s Entry Point for Those of Great Virtue (B44, S13000).

lemma: Not clarified as good or bad
text: This is the traditional term—alluded to in footnote 84 (at section G37 above)—which is used to describe something as karmically neutral; again, the general point is that if Lord Buddha, during his time on this earth, did not feel compelled to describe an action as good or bad, then quite likely it is neutral: it is an action which does not ripen into an experience of pleasure, or of pain. Obviously though the Buddha did not cover all possible actions, and so this term is but a general description.  See for example f. 107b of the wonderful commentary on vowed morality by Panchen Lodru Leksang (c. 1510) (B73, SB00059).

These five are listed in footnote 85 (at section G38 above) as the capacity of feeling; the capacity of discrimination; movement of the mind; contact; and attention.  Their functions relative to foundation consciousness are treated nicely by Keutsang Lobsang Jamyang Munlam in his commentary to Tsongkapa’s present Difficult Points (see f. 205a, B1, S06514).
We arrive at nine by adding the ever-present five just listed in footnote 125 (at section G159).
There is a related treatment of the conundra here by Panglung Lobsang Tukje (c. 1770–1835) which is so helpful that we have added it in toto as Appendix C, below.

lemma: Ninth degree of the negative emotions
text: This is a standard set of nine, used in different contexts, where negativities are divided into blatant; medium; and subtle—and each of these again divided into three degrees.  The “ninth degree” of a negativity then would be the most subtle of the subtle versions; for example, the deepest and most subtle traces of jealousy that actually require the correspondingly more powerful versions of their antidotes, which themselves are inevitably tied up with perceiving the true nature of things. See for example f. 18b of Kedrup Tenpa Dargye’s overview of the meditations of the form and formless realms (B62, S00016).  The complete permutations involving various negative emotions may be studied starting from f. 53b of Konchok Tenpay Drunme’s commentary to Je Rinpoche’s Difficult Points (B11, S00910).

The Blade here drops into a traditional debate format, where certain responses are considered so standard that they are most often not included in the text.  We have supplied them here in italics, for the benefit of the general reader.
See f. 2a of Master Vasubandhu’s standard on the Mind Only School (S26, TD04055).

This is a technical term which refers to a meditation which is so deep that mind and mental functions are temporarily very close to erased.  (Note that this is not a spiritually desirable place!)  See for example the discussion by Choney Lama Drakpa Shedrup (1675–1748) at ff. 27b–28a in the fourth chapter of his Cloud of Offerings (B21, S00195). “Person who is still learning” is another technical term used for a person who has not yet reached the fifth of the five paths, and is not yet an enemy destroyer—who is said to have attained a point of “no more learning.”
Explained previously at footnote 104 (at section G91).

This refers to bodhisattva levels eight, nine, and ten.  Reaching level eight is the higher way’s equivalent of nirvana, marked by the destruction of our seeds for seeing things as self-existent. The levels are, in one way, referred to as “pure” realms because we are now able to stay, at all times, in deep meditation on a special form of emptiness known as “the ultimate form of purity”; for details, see for example f. 14b of the illumination of Master Haribhadra’s famed explanation of the perfection of wisdom by Je Tsongkapa’s close disciple Kedrup Je (1385–1438) (B19, S05461).  At these levels as well we are free of certain impurities that accompany us even from the womb; see for example f. 5b of the outline of the levels and paths by Sera Jetsun Chukyi Gyeltsen (1469–1546) (B56, S06826).

That is, they would have had to achieve full Buddhahood.  This wisdom is one of the five types that we obtain upon our enlightenment.  Each of the five wisdoms relates to the ultimate purification of one of the five “heaps,” or parts of our body & mind complex. “Equivalent” wisdom represents the final purifying of our capacity to feel, and its special cause is treating others equally: the habit of putting ourselves in other people’s minds to stay aware of how they feel, and acting accordingly.  See f. 140a of Master Sthiramati’s treatment of the topic in his commentary to the Jewel of the Sutras (S37, TD04034). Perhaps the greatest explanation ever of these five wisdoms, a difficult subject, is to be found in Sera Jetsun Chukyi Gyeltsen’s overview of the eighth chapter of the Jewel of Realizations; see the section starting from f. 9b (B57, S06814-11).

See the discussion starting at f. 38b of Je Tsongkapa’s autocommentary (B54, ST05414B). Adherents of the Conceptualist School who follow after scripture: The classic division here in a more general context would be between members of a school who tend more to follow scriptural authority, and those who tend more to follow reasoning.  We see members of the Mind Only School who follow after scripture described in various sources as holding a number of typical beliefs.
