Kedrup Tenpa Dargye (1493–1568) reports that they assert that—when a listener reaches nirvana without remainder—their body & mind discontinue; while that Masters Dignaga and Dharmakirti (from the Sutrist School, just below the Mind Only School) would disagree (f. 23b, Vol. 1, B61, S00009).  He also describes them as accepting the idea that, in the end, there are three different spiritual ways—as opposed to a single sea into which all paths flow (a belief of higher schools) (f. 8b, Vol. 2, B61, S00009). Jamyang Shepa (1648–1721) agrees with this description of the members of the Mind Only School who follow after scripture, lumping them on this point together with those of the Sutrist School who follow after reasoning (f. 58b, B41, S19088). Kedrup Jinpa Dargye (b. 1558) makes the point that members of the Mind Only School may be divided into those who “hold that the aspect is true” and those who hold “that it is false”; and he equates the former to those who follow after scripture (f. 9a, B83, S00467).  This distinction is explained by Kedrup Je as referring to those who believe that objects held by consciousness exist in a substantial way, and those who say they exist only in an imputed way (f. 49b, B17, S05501).

The Sanskrit here for “deep practice” is yoga charya.  These four levels involve crucial viewpoints on the ultimate nature of objects, and would seem to form an important part of Master Asanga’s famed Levels of Deep Practice (Yogacharya Bhumi, beginning from S9, TD04035).  They are so important that an alternate name for the Mind Only School itself is “The School of Deep Practice” (Yogacharya).  Je Tsongkapa’s disciple Kedrup Je (1385–1438) gives a great presentation of the four in his commentary to Master Haribhadra, and we have shared it with our readers in Appendix D below. The Summary of the Greater Way is a much briefer presentation of the Mind Only School by Master Asanga at S2, TD04048.

These eight are treated at greater length in Je Tsongkapa’s autocommentary, and this will appear in our second volume.  To assist our readers, we have included, in Appendix E—“Eight arguments on the existence of the foundation consciousness,” a very good explanation of intermediate length on this important topic by the great Mongol scholar, Chuje Ngawang Pelden (b. 1806) (B31, S00982).  We suggest reading that appendix before returning to this point in The Golden Key.
See f. 125a of the famous presentation of logic & perceptual theory by Master Dharmakirti, c. 650ad (S16, TD04210).

This is a group of seven essential works on logic & perceptual theory composed by the great Dharmakirti.  These are named (1) A Commentary on Accurate Perception; (2) Ascertaining the Nature of Accurate Perception; (3) Just a Touch on Accurate Perception; (4) Just a Touch on Logical Statements; (5) An Examination of the Concept of a Relationship; (6) A Proof that the Mind Streams of Other People Really Do Exist; and (7) The Logic of Debate.  A deep but accessible commentary upon the content of the seven is the subject of a translation included in the present Diamond Cutter Classics Series; that is, the treatise by Je Tsongkapa’s close disciple Kedrup Je (1385–1438) entitled Destroying the Darkness Where Our Minds Have Yet to Understand the Seven Books.

See f. 9a of the Jewel Lamp by Jamyang Shepay Dorje Ngawang Tsundru, 1648–1721, on comparative school systems (B39, S19027).  The opening line here, “It is not explained that way,” is just a piece of a longer thought that begins in the lines previous; the whole thus reads as, “The division of consciousness into a collection of eight types is a position taken by those who follow the Esteemed Brothers—Masters Asanga and Vasubandhu—but is not here explained that way.”
This is, in fact, why we have here used the translation “eight arguments on foundation consciousness” rather than “eight proofs of foundation consciousness.”

Meaning Je Tsongkapa’s autocommentary, which our readers will find translated in the second volume of the current translation.  Je Rinpoche for example mentions a direct reference to foundation consciousness by this sutra on f. 38a of his work (B54, ST05414B).

The classic reference here appears in Je Tsongkapa’s autocommentary, where he cites Arya Asanga’s Summary of the Greater Way referring itself to the sutra mentioned.  In the autocommentary, see f. 48a (B54, ST05414B).  In the Summary, see f. 4b (S2, TD04048). Although the original sutra mentioned is no longer available in the Kangyur Collection itself, we do see other sutras and classical commentaries with the same wording.  See for example f. 71b of The Sutra Requested by Brahma Vishesha Chinti (S30, KL00160); f. 394a of A Box of Precious Jewels (S32, KL00117); or f. 158b of Master Shamatha Deva’s explanation of the Treasure House of Higher Knowledge (S28, Vol. 9, TD04094).

Again, the classical source for the reference is the citation within Arya Asanga’s Summary of the Greater Way.  See f. 5a of the work (S2, TD04048).  The “Majority Group” is one of the four main groups within the Detailist School of ancient Indian Buddhism, a lower-way school.  A nice explanation of the structure of the groups within this school may be found at f. 16b of the translation, found here in the Diamond Cutter Classics Series, of the study of the schools of philosophy by Choney Lama Drakpa Shedrup (1675–1748) entitled A Brief Essence of All Schools of Philosophy (B20, S25008).

The citation is, again, drawn from Arya Asanga’s Summary; see f. 5a (S2, TD04048).  The “Elder Group” is another of the four main groups within the Detailist School; they are so called because they descend from a master elder by the name of Arya.  See again f. 16b of the translation of Chone Lama’s Brief Essence (B20, S25008).

Yet again drawn from f. 5a of Arya Asanga’s Summary (S2, TD04048).  Note that the spelling rnam for “aspect” here (which can often connote a state of mind, and is also the spelling used in Je Rinpoche’s autocommentary) is in the Derge Tengyur rendered as rnams, which changes the translation to simply “parts of a person which last as long as cyclic life”—still conveying the meaning intended, but not as strongly.  The Sanskrit, which could be used as confirmation at this point, does not seem to be available. The “Earth Teacher” (Mahīśāsakā) group is one of seven among the first of the four major groups just mentioned, this one called “Those Who Profess All” since they teach that all three times exist in a substantial way.  Again, reference the same page in Choney Lama’s translation.  We haven’t found any clear explanation for the name “Earth Teacher”; the Sanskrit name is also seen in Tibetan as “Earth Protector” (Sa-srung).

In this context, simply referring to the followers of the lower way.  The name “listener” is sometimes explained as referring to disciples who can listen to the teachings on the greater way, and even relate these teachings to others, but who feel no attraction towards following this path of ultimate compassion themselves.  See for example the extensive explanation at f. 4b of Je Tsongkapa’s masterpiece on emptiness, Illumination of the True Thought (B50, SA05408), a translation of which is also included in the present Diamond Cutter Classics Series.

The three positions taken are described, again, in Arya Asanga’s Summary of the Greater Way; see ff. 5a–5b (S2, TD04048).  They are not here attributed to particular masters; but we do see the attribution in an explanation of the Arya’s work entitled simply A Commentary to the “Summary of the Greater Way”; see ff. 325b–326a (S41, TD04052).  This is in fact the Explanation of the Secret Points that we’ve seen Fearless Blade refer to earlier—see footnotes 76 (at section G16) and 112 (at section G121).  Again, this text is sometimes said to be composed by Master Vasubandhu, but with the authorship disputed.  It seems thus that Je Tsongkapa is relying upon this commentary regularly for his own presentation. The one name, “Vamana” in Sanskrit, is reconstructed from the Tibetan (Mi’u-thung), and later research may establish it with more certainty.  Here is a bit about each of the three. Vasumitra was a sage of the Detailist School who is counted as one of the “Seven Defeaters of the Foe” who compiled collections of the Buddha’s wisdom during the period after his passing.  These are called the “Seven Books of Higher Knowledge,” and Master Vasumitra’s contribution was known as The Great Composition.  He is also mentioned for early work on the details of vowed morality.  For all this, see the history of Indian Buddhism by the great Buton Rinpoche, Rinchen Drup (1290–1364) (refer to ff. 19a–19b, and 155a–155b, B71, S12060). Information about Vamana, whose name literally means “The Dwarf,” is hard to come by.  He is mentioned in an early Sanskrit language study in the same breath as Master Chandragomin, who is believed to have lived in the 7th century; whereas presumably Vamana would have to be at latest 4th century.  In any case, this reference would indicate that he may have also been a linguist of Sanskrit (see ff. 24a–24b of S23, TD04287).  This is corroborated through a brief mention by Jamyang Kyentse Wangpo (1820–1892) of a rare Sanskrit work, with this personal name in the title, on poetics (see p. 187 of B35). There is also one ancient lexicon which indicates that the word used for his name, technically spelled vāmana, is a synonym for the mythical “elephants of the directions.”  The term for these elephants happens to be dignāga, but it would seem a long shot to equate this thinker with the 6th-century father of Buddhist logic by the same name, who is again probably too late (see f. 202b, S38, TD04454).  On the other hand, Vamana is included in a list of ancient sages of the Sutrist School—to which Master Dignaga belonged—found in a work by Jamgon Kongtrul Lodru Taye (1813–1899) (see section Ae 121 at B34). Ghoshaka is most closely associated with the study of higher knowledge (abhidharma) from the Detailist School, and is mentioned in many of the ancient commentaries on this topic found in the Tengyur Collection, in contexts such as the study of time and the levels of deep concentration.  As such he most likely predates Arya Asanga.  He is also referenced in later Tengyur works on the birth stories of the Buddha; a commentary to Lord Atisha’s Light on the Path; Master Bhavaviveka’s famed Blaze of Reasoning; and in a treatise devoted to Buddhist logic & perceptual theory. The “view of destruction,” by the way, refers to a belief in the self-nature of “me and mine”—a destroyable view towards things that will meet their destruction.  This is the specific misunderstanding which functions as the first of the famous twelve links of the Wheel of Life; for an extensive explanation, see the translation of the brilliant dialectic commentary by Kedrup Tenpa Dargye (1493–1568) (B59, S00015) included in the present Diamond Cutter Classics Series; as well as the ancient commentary by Master Vasubandhu in the same series (S27, TD03995).
That is, which could stand on its own within the mind.
The Sanskrit for “realized being” is arya, which in classical Buddhism denotes any one of those extremely rare persons who has seen ultimate reality directly.
Note that the order of this and the following argument is reversed, relative to the order in Je Tsongkapa’s root text.  Students of the topic of foundation consciousness might find a reason for this!

The quotation is massaged in the Tibetan just as it is in the English.  It’s common in the ancient texts—since the Sanskrit language is based so strongly on verbal roots—to give an explanation of a word that stresses its original root.  The point being made here is that the original root for the word “consciousness” (manas, in Sanskrit) also shows up in the expression “thinking I am me” (manmatā), around which the idea of negative consciousness (which mistakenly takes “me” as being a me from its own side) is itself built.  For the original Sanskrit in situ, see verse 102 (and the footnote correction there), p. 278, in the Sanskrit edition of the Journey to Langka edited by Bunyiu Nanjio (S33, KL00107).

lemma: If you would like to learn more
text: Again, this autocommentary is translated in the second volume of the present work.

This sage’s dates are given as 499–569ad; he was born in central India, and—having become famous for his erudition—was invited to the Chinese imperial court, where he came to head a team that translated numerous classics of Indian Buddhism into Chinese (Wikipedia article on “Paramartha,” E4).  These works included for example The Treasure House of Higher Knowledge, and the famed sutra, What I Really Meant (see Jikme Damchu Gyatso, 1898–1946, ff. 66b–67a of Part One of A Point of Entry, B45, S00302).  He is best known for his presentations on the group of nine types of consciousness; the Buddha’s three turnings of the wheel of the Dharma; and the different ways, or vehicles, of Buddhism.  Je Tsongkapa, in various works, singles him out for criticism on each of these topics (see for example f. 12b of his famous Essence of Eloquence, on the Art of Interpretation, where he refuses to even describe Paramartha’s positions; B51, S05396).

One of the three classical ways of splitting up all the things in the universe—consisting of the six objects of perception; the six instruments of perception; and the six awarenesses of what is perceived.  This is a major topic in the first chapter of the famed Treasure House of Higher Knowledge (Abhidharma Kosha); again, composed by Master Vasubandhu in the 4th century ad.  See S25, TD04089.

This is a technical term for the self-existence of the parts of the person.  So here in this section we have two kinds of belief in self-existence: that which perceives the person as being self-existent; and that which perceives the parts of the person as being self-existent.
This is a technical expression, most often associated with the lower part of the Middle Way School, for the true nature of things.

This is a technical term which refers to very rare, high bodhisattvas—ones who have seen emptiness directly—who in the course of human history have been able to present the core concepts of Buddhism in revolutionary new ways.  The Tibetan term is shingtay sulje (shing-rta’i srol-’byed), which means “inventor of the wooden horse,” or wagon; the equivalent of “inventor of the wheel” in English, as referring to a person who pioneers an extraordinary innovation.  See the technical definition in the dialectical analysis of Lord Maitreya’s Jewel of Realizations by Kedrup Tenpa Dargye (1493–1568) at f. 6a (B60, S00001-1).

lemma: Bodhisattvas who assert that it is only one
text: This is a difficult name that could be read in several different ways.  Lobsang Tadrin (1867–1937) refers to it specifically as a “group within the Detailist School”; see f. 51b in his dialectical analysis on the subject of mind and awareness at B76, S25110.  The great Ngawang Pelden (b. 1806) also specifies that the byang-sems here refers to people and not a state of mind; see f. 49a of the third volume of his overview of the Jewel of Realizations (B31, S00982-3). And Chim Jampay Yang (c. 1280), a great master of the philosophy of the Detailist School, attributes the specific arguments coming below to a group including the great masters Nanda and Nagasena, who may thus be the bodhisattvas mentioned (see f. 53 of his magnificent Treasure House of Chim, B33, Vol. 1, S06954).  All this, despite the fact that the very concept of a bodhisattva appears only very rarely in the literature of Detailists themselves. It would be intriguing to see if this name might somehow rather derive from the parallel belief that the Wish for enlightenment (also called byang-sems) is composed of the single main mind, and not of a mental function—an idea which will be mentioned soon in our text.

A reference to what we know as The Collection of Tailored Teachings, copies of which are found both in the Kangyur and the Tengyur Collections.  See f. 385b of the former (S17, KL00326) and f. 44a of the latter (S18, TD04099).  Important references to the citation are also found in Arya Asanga’s Summary (f. 15a, S2, TD04048), as well as in his famed Levels of Deep Practice (f. 256b, S9, TD04035). Again Chujey Ngawang Pelden, as he so often does, describes the intent of the ancient line here in a very helpful way.  He asks us to think of a small cabin with a number of windows all round.  Then imagine a hyperactive monkey inside, racing from window to window to take a peek out—a metaphor for the idea of but a single consciousness, availing itself of multiple sense supports such as the eye, ear, etc.  He and other authors say we can also think of it in terms of a person inside the cabin, at night, walking from window to window and holding up a lamp at each, to see what’s outside.  See once more ff. 49a–49b of the third volume of his overview of the Jewel of Realizations (B31, S00982-3).

This is a reference to a reference in Arya Asanga’s Summary; see f. 15b (S2, TD04048).  That reference could be a discrete sutra of this name which no longer exists; or simply similar passing statements throughout the Kangyur Collection.

lemma: Those who don’t accept the mental function
text: A reference to the argument that the Wish for enlightenment—since it includes two different points of focus (me becoming a Buddha and me helping every living being)—must consist of main mind, which then contains these two mental functions.  A description of why Arya Asanga insists rather on a mental function may be found for example at f. 21a of Kedrup Je’s Illumination of the Difficult (B19, S05461).

For the Mind Only, a typical example of this type of emptiness would be the idea that an accurate perception which holds to a visible form, and the very form that it holds to, never come from two separate karmic seeds—which is to say, they always grow from one and the same seed.  See for example f. 53b of the first volume of the dialectical analysis of the Jewel of Realizations by the great textbook writer of Sera Mey, the greatest of Tibetan monasteries—Kedrup Tenpa Dargye (1493–1568) (B60, S00001-1).
This is the ordination name of Je Tsongkapa, who was born and raised in the environs of Tsongka, in eastern Tibet.

Je Tsongkapa’s biographies describe a vision of the Two Brothers of the Mind Only School—Masters Vasubandhu and Asanga—which occurred in 1393; see for example p. 345 of King of the Dharma (E2).  Apart from this, it doesn’t seem that the details of specific early sessions with his teachers on the subject of the Mind Only School have been recorded.

Three traditional metaphors for the intellectual processes of testing an idea (in the way that we would test a coin offered to us as gold) against our direct personal experience; our logic; and consistency with other ideas from the same source.  A good ancient source for the three is for example Master Shantarakshita’s Commentary to the “Jewel of the Middle Way” at f. 83a (S36, TD03885).

Those who are familiar with the writings of Je Tsongkapa will be reminded here, as certainly the author intended, of extraordinary lines of verse he composed in a ritual dedicated to the glorious Union of the Spheres (Chakra Sanvara), utilizing the image of his meditation as a paintbrush.  See ff. 5a–5b of B52, S05382.

The ordination name of our author, which itself means “Lobsang the Fearless.”  For more details of this and his teacher, see “The Golden Key, and the Fearless Blade” in the introduction to the present volume.

The lines here include very frequently repeated sentiments found in the final prayers at the close of a text.  We haven’t found these exact ones though elsewhere, and the “Panchen Rinpoche” could simply be a reference to a high lama in the area when the work was completed who was asked to contribute a closing prayer—a very common occurrence. There is a possibility though that the lines were composed especially for the work by His Holiness the Third Panchen Lama, Pelden Yeshe, whose dates (1738–1780) would work well—and who was actively involved, as we see from the introduction to this volume, in the founding of the monastery where Fearless Blade once served as abbot.

“Kumbum” is the name of a monastery built at the site of Je Tsongkapa’s birth; it is so named because a tree grew at the exact spot, and each of the thousands (bum) of leaves on the tree has a natural image (ku) of Tsongkapa imprinted upon it.  See for example f. 8a of The String of Pearls, a history of the monastery, at B4, S12134. “Jampa Ling” means “A Center for the Study of Love for All Beings.”  Abaga Wangshok seems to be a monastery whose name is variously spelled, in Tibetan, Aa-ba-ga wang-shog; Aa-bha-ka-t’a wang-shog; possibly Aa-ba-gatpa pi-li’i shog, and so on.  Parts of the name at least seem to be in the Manchu language.
These are three common mantras with special connections to the compassion; the wisdom; and the secret teachings of the Buddhas, respectively.
Corresponding to the modern Western year of 1974.  See also our notes on the connection to Gomang College, “Blade undertakes his studies” in the introduction to this volume.

It is a custom, at the beginning of a classical text from ancient India translated into Tibetan, to give first the Sanskrit title—to honor the perfect language spoken by all Enlightened Beings, and the extraordinary achievement of the ancient translators; as well as the “Mother Land” of Buddhism.  When a Tibetan author inserts a faux Sanskrit title at the start of a native composition, it is meant to invoke these same feelings.  The title, given here as Je Tsongkapa does and in simplified pronunciation for the general reader, would in modern times be transcribed as Mano Vijñānālaya Vijñānaṃ.
Text information may be found in the bibliography at B63, S00019.

“That which is clear and which knows”—meaning something which is physically invisible and possesses the quality of awareness—is the traditional definition of consciousness itself.  The “clear” here is sometimes explained as referring to how the mind illuminates or clarifies an object and then knows its particular features; see for example ff. 35a–36a of Panchen Lama Pelden Yeshe’s teaching on the Path to Bliss (B79, S12239).  The point is that we would then possess general awareness not linked to any form of individual mental functions at all—an impossibility.

This is a technical term (full Tibetan spelling bdag-po’i rkyen) which here refers to a genre of condition which is included within the person—as opposed to something outer like the blue color of a cup, as it provides a condition for the arisal of visual consciousness.  See for example f. 16b of Gyaltsab Je’s explication of the Compendium of Higher Knowledge (B26, S05435).

lemma: Negative emotions of the desire realm
text: See f. 51b of the commentary (B26, S05435).  Gyaltsab Je is referring to the Thirty Verses of Master Vasubandhu, an important source for the Mind Only School (see f. 2a, S26, TD04055).  The Compendium of Higher Knowledge is a Mind Only take on the topics of higher knowledge (abhidharma) composed by Arya Asanga (see S1, TD04049).

The “three tracks” are three approaches for attaining nirvana and Buddhahood: that of the listeners, who can listen to the highest track, and even repeat it to others, but not follow the track themselves; the self-made buddhas, who are not full Buddhas but who attain nirvana without following a teacher in this life (although they have had countless teachers in their past lives); and the bodhisattvas of the supreme track, who act out of a desire to reach enlightenment for all living beings.  For respective explanations see the classic Great Book on the Steps of the Teaching by Geshe Drolungpa (c. 1100ad), f. 374b (B72, S00070); the commentary to Master Asanga’s Compendium of Higher Knowledge by Gyaltsab Je (1364–1432) (f. 194a, B26, S05435); and the classic definition of bodhichitta in Lord Maitreya’s Jewel of Realizations (f. 2b, S21, TD03786).

This is a reference to one of the five types of wisdom which we obtain upon our enlightenment; what’s being said then is that the practitioner at this point has still not achieved Buddhahood.  For further details on “equivalent” wisdom, please see footnote 134 (at section G171 above).

In the Mind Only School, the “seventh state of mind” is counted as negative consciousness; and the “eighth consciousness” is foundation consciousness.  See for example f. 30b of Master Panglung’s sister commentary on the Difficult Points (B64, S00018).  Only this school accepts these two on top of the traditional set of six consciousnesses accepted by all schools.
For Kedrup Je’s text, see the section starting from f. 152a (B19, S05461).  For holy Maitreya’s work, see S21, TD03786.  For Master Haribhadra’s, see S39, TD03793.
That is, as opposed to misperceptions we are born with.
In the Tibetan, referring to the particle te at the end of the first line of f. 125a of Master Haribhadra’s work (S39, TD03793).
This is a convention, in formal logic, for beginning a syllogism which expresses a universal truth.

The full title of the text we’re using is A Lamp that Illuminates, Totally, the Meaning of the Great Mother; Consisting of Interlinear Annotations for the Overview of the Perfection of Wisdom (B31, S00982).  The selection is from Volume 3.

For the Summary, see again S2, TD04048.  For Master Chandrakirti’s Verses on the Five Heaps, S12, TD03866.  The Lines of Commentary in Praise is another name for An Explication of the Levels of Deep Practice written by Master Jinamitra; see S13, TD04043.
These will be covered in the fifth reasoning, beginning at section E36.

This line is very often repeated in the Tibetan literature, but we have not been able to find it attributed to anything more than “sutra”—and so far we cannot find it or any variant in the sutras themselves.  Je Tsongkapa, in his Illumination of the True Intent, also uses it—unattributed—and then immediately links the word “separate flows” (rgyud re-re-ba) to “totally consistent type” (rigs mthun-pa nyid), meaning that each separate being has a flow of consciousness which continues on in its own unique flow.  The two concepts thus match each other, and Je Tsongkapa then uses Master Dharmakirti’s Commentary on Accurate Perception as his scriptural corroboration.  For the reference in Je Rinpoche, see ff. 157a–157b (B50, SA05408).  For the reference in Master Dharmakirti, see f. 137b (S16, TD04210).
This is a technical term (Skt: pṛthagjana, Tib: so-so skye-bo) which refers to a person who has not yet seen ultimate reality directly.

These three are mentioned by Je Rinpoche in his autocommentary: this karmic ripening (1) should be a karmically neutral entity, of the type that does not act as a spiritual obstacle; (2) it should continue on in an unbroken stream, for the length of our life; and (3) it should be a result projected into being by some previous good or bad action.  See f. 12a of the work (B54, ST05414B).

These lines, again, appear with fair frequency in the Tibetan literature; we see them variously attributed to “sutra”; to “the literature on higher knowledge (abhidharma)”; and to “the sutra on accurate perception”—which is another name for The Compendium on Accurate Perception, written by Master Dignaga (c. 440ad) (S15, TD04203).  They appear to be a later versed version of a section in the famed sutra, What I Really Meant, also a central source for the Mind Only School (see f. 19b, S35, KL00106). A variant cited by Kedrup Je in the chapter of his Ocean of Reasoning commenting upon the chapter on direct perception from Master Dharmakirti’s Commentary on Accurate Perception (see f. 5b, B16, S05505-3) seems to derive from a very similar passage in the commentary to A Journey to Langka written by Master Jnanavajra (see f. 65a, S14, TD04019).  We haven’t found any lines in the Journey itself that are very similar to those here.
Again, a versed version of a section found in Master Mokshakara Gupta’s work at ff. 342a–342b (S24, TD04264).

lemma: Collection of Works on the Levels
text: Refers to the five masterworks by Master Asanga on the variety of spiritual levels.  It’s sometimes difficult to divide these out correctly.  The following listing from the native catalog to the Derge edition of the Tengyur is very helpful: (1a) The Many Levels: The Main Presentation within the “Levels of Deep Practice” (S9, TD04035); (1b) The Levels of Listeners, from the “Levels of Deep Practice” (S8, TD04036); (1c) The Levels of Bodhisattvas, from the “Levels of Deep Practice” (S4, TD04037); (2) A Summary Presentation of the Levels of Deep Practice (S10, TD04038); (3a) A Summary of the Collection of Sutras, from the Summary of the Foundations, within the “Levels of Deep Practice” (S6, TD04039); (3b) A Summary of Vowed Morality, from the Summary of the Foundations, within the “Levels of Deep Practice” (S5, TD04040); (4) The Brief Explication, from the “Levels of Deep Practice” (S7, TD04042); and (5) A Summary of the Versions, from the “Levels of Deep Practice” (S3, TD04041).  See f. 445a of the catalog (B87, TD04569).
This variant for BSGO GZHI is so common in this excerpt that we have not corrected it further, as it seems acceptable to the author.

The idea that we could ever commit a good or bad act and then see that energy simply fade away before coming back to us as a pleasant or painful experience is a classic contradiction of the four fundamental laws of karma.  See for example Pabongka Rinpoche’s magnificent Gift of Liberation, Thrust into Our Hands, f. 226b (B67, S00004).
See f. 40b of the text, one of the Five Books of Maitreya (S22, TD04021).

The deep meditation where “there is no capacity of discrimination” refers to “no gross capacity of discrimination,” since—as we have seen in the main text—this mental function accompanies all states of mind.  It’s just that, at this point, we engage only in extremely subtle discrimination between objects.  A “cessation meditation” means, again, that mind and mental functions are very nearly shut down. A person who will “no longer return” is at the third of a set of four classic, high attainments which include (1) seeing emptiness directly, and thus “entering the stream” where relatively imminent freedom is inevitable; (2) having to return to a desire-realm rebirth only once more, since the corresponding negative emotions are being defeated; (3) going further to where we have no such emotions, and need not return to the desire realm at all; and (4) nirvana.  See for example f. 3b of A Dialectic Analysis of the Twenty Practitioners (B58, S00013), by Kedrup Tenpa Dargye (1493–1568), the great textbook writer from Sera Mey Monastery.
That is, a mental state in which we are permanently free of the stain of negative emotions—which would be nirvana.
The Buddha is saying that even actions like enjoying a war movie plant negative karmic seeds which shorten our lives.

lemma: How good it would be to strike
text: Needless to say, this would apply to military or any other kind of violence, performed for example with weapons.

Those referred to with the Sanskrit word arya, which connotes a person who is “realized” in the sense of having already undergone the experience of seeing emptiness (the fact that nothing in the universe comes from its own side) directly.
A technical term—bodhichitta—which refers to the wish to become fully enlightened, so that we have the power to help every living being in the universe.
We haven’t found a source for the other three benefits indicated.  As we have seen earlier, sutras quoted within this sutra may no longer be extant.

lemma: 35 different problems with the use of intoxicants
text: See ff. 411b–412b of the sutra (S10, KL00334).  Because this topic is so relevant in our modern times, we have included the entire list of the problems in Appendix A below.  A list of 36 problems appears below in the sutra itself.

These viewpoints need a bit of explanation.  The view that things cannot change is a necessary consequence of believing that they exist from their own side, and not as projections coming out of the karmic seeds in our minds.  Understanding that things are projections prevents us from beliefs that would necessitate their having come to a stop.  The view that things don’t exist at all is an over-reaction to hearing that they are devoid of any self-existence.  See the fine explanation of these points by Choney Lama Drakpa Shedrup (1675–1748) in his commentary upon the Heart Sutra (beginning at f. 17a, B4, S00220).

Five extremely serious bad deeds that are called “immediate” called because—if we commit one of these five in the current life—then “immediately” (meaning, without any other, intervening type of rebirth) we pass, with certainty, to the realms of hell.  See for example the excellent description of the group’s name by Panchen Lodru Leksang in his fine commentary on vowed morality (f. 138a of the first volume, B12, SL00059).  The five deeds are (1) killing one’s father; (2) killing one’s mother; (3) killing an enemy destroyer (someone who has reached nirvana); (4) causing a split in a spiritual community; and (5) causing a Buddha to bleed, out of harmful intent (meaning, this would not apply to a nurse drawing the Buddha’s blood during a medical examination).  The classic source for these is the fourth chapter of Master Vasubandhu’s Treasure House of Higher Knowledge (see ff. 14b–15a, S3, TD04089).
The former was a half-brother of Lord Buddha famed for his jealousy of the Buddha; the latter was an evil prince who schemed with Devadatta to kill the Buddha.

Tradition says that the tree itself is named from the sound that is made when fruits fall from the tree into bodies of water on whose shores they stand: sort of like “kerplop” in English.  See for example f. 3b of the praise of the 35 Buddhas by Lama Quicksilver (1772–1851) (B9, S06341).  Buddhist cosmology describes our world as a central mountain surrounded by four continents; this is the one to the south, where we live.

The verse may be found in the famed Collection of Tailored Teachings; see f. 322a (S7, KL00326).  Here it says though, perhaps more correctly, “For children, who know nothing of the holy path of goodness.”  The word “children” in such context is a common technical term for someone who is not a realized being, or arya; that is, someone who has yet to see ultimate reality directly.

lemma: A particularly powerful kind of karma
text: We haven’t been able to locate this quotation, or the text it is said to come from.  There is a single line in the Sutra of the Revelation which could be a reference to the mentioned work; see f. 2b (S6, KL00301).

In its most fundamental form, the belief that things are coming from their own side, rather from the seeds we’ve planted in our own minds.  This tenth misdeed is of course the worst, as it supplies the foundation for all nine of the other misdeeds.

Buddhist cosmology divides the suffering portion of the universe into three sectors: the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.  We ourselves live in the desire realm, so named because our main motivation is desire, in forms such as a desire for food or sex.  The form realm could be referred to as the “realm of beauty,” since the suffering beings who live there possess—temporarily—bodies of incredible beauty and power.  In the formless realm, beings possess practically no physical body and are nearly all mental; but still suffer immensely as they die.  See for example the commentary to the Treasure House by Gyalwa Gendun Drup (1391–1474), ff. 74a–74b (B5, SE05525).

Devadatta was the half-brother of Lord Buddha and—driven by his jealousy of the Buddha—tried many times to harm him; in addition to causing a schism in the spiritual community, an extremely serious misdeed.  The story of his attempt to murder the Buddha is found in the fourth part of the Foundation of Vowed Morality, beginning from f. 317a (S12, KL00001-4).  Kokalika was one of Devadatta’s followers; a well-known account of his retribution for their misdeeds may be found on ff. 423a–423b of the same volume.

The story of his sins is found, for example, in the same reference given above for those of Devadatta.  While still in the womb, it was foretold that when grown he would kill his own father, Bimbisara; thus his unusual name.  An “immediate” misdeed is one that takes us directly to the lowest of the realms of hell, with no chance of an intervening birth.

lemma: Sutra of the Fruits of Practicing Goodness
text: We have not found a sutra by this name, but Ajatashatru’s beautiful confession may be found for example on f. 359a of An Exalted Sutra of the Greater Way entitled “Clearing Away the Guilt of Ajatashatru” (S5, KL00216).
We have not found an original presentation of the verse outside of the two versions of All the Kinds of Karma.

lemma: The story of the rebirth of Renuka
text: The Sanskrit version of the Tibetan name here, dKar-sham, is not definite.  This would appear to be a story that we find in the Divisions of Vowed Morality, where the name is mentioned, and one of the characters is murdered near a certain house.  He prays to be reborn in the house so that the scene of the crime may be marked; but the prayer is mistakenly fulfilled by his being born as a snake under the porch of the place.  See ff. 172b–173a of the first volume of the work (S13, KL00003).

The following account of the karma of disrespecting one’s parents is quite famous, and has obviously inspired the title and some of the contents of the renowned Crown of Knives: Instructions for Developing the Good Heart in the Greater Way, composed by Master Dharma Rakshita (c. 950ad)—the teacher of the great Lord Atisha. The full texts of this extended poem—and the commentary by Trichen Tenpa Rabgye (1759–1815), with lecture notes by Gyalwang Lobsang Trinley Namgyel (fl. 1800)—are translated in the present Diamond Cutter Classics Series. We see another version of the story in a well-known compilation found in the Kangyur: The Hundred Stories of Saints (S11, KL00343; see ff. 151a–160a).  This version is important to us since the carvings at Borobudur monument used for our illustrations more closely follow it. The panels for this particular part of our text are not included among the rest from the monument, found in the buried lowest level.  They are drawn, rather, from the accounts of bodhisattvas (avadana literature) located on the first level aboveground.  See panels 106–112. Here are some notes on the differences between the two versions, as it may be confusing as we compare the text to the illustrations.  First of all, in the Hundred Accounts, our hero is not named Maitra Yajna, but rather Maitra Kanyaka.  Whereas the former name can be translated as “Gift of Love” (reflected in the ancient Tibetan translation of Byams-pa mchod-sbyin), the latter is rendered as “The Friendly One’s Daughter” (Tibetan mDza’-bo’i bu-mo), as his father’s name is said to have been “Friendly One.” Within the second version itself, this second name is explained in two different ways.  Maitra’s mother had given birth to several stillborn sons, and his parents were advised by a sage to give the next boy born the name of a girl, so as to mislead evil spirits trying to prevent a son who would keep the traditional Indian patrilineal line.  Later on in the same text, we see a comment that he was moreover a pretty child, to the point of appearing feminine. The name of the young man in our present version also has great meaning, when we consider his act of sacrifice in the final lines. In the present sutra, Maitra experiences prolonged happiness in the company of lovely goddesses on four different occasions, which is explained as the karmic result of his listening to his mother a number of times (there is some confusion about the number) before leaving on his journey.  These meetings with the goddesses in the Hundred Accounts though are presented as the result of Maitra’s offering his mother gold coins on four occasions; and in fact the number of coins gifted and the number of goddesses encountered match perfectly.  This version also seems to fit the Borobudur panels more closely. The reason Maitra has the coins to offer in the first place is that he wants to emulate his deceased father’s occupation, and different people give him different stories about what his father used to do; this is encouraged by his mother, who doesn’t want him to go to sea and possibly drown—as did his ship-captain father, when Maitra was only a toddler. Thus we see the young man working as a goldsmith in the Borobudur drawings, whereas in the sutra he seems to have always known what his father really did.  In the Hundred Accounts, in fact, he is so successful at goldsmithing that envious gold-business rivals make sure he learns Dad’s real work, and switches to the sea. Finally, the nature of the wheel that cuts the head in each story is somewhat different; in the Accounts, the fact that this wheel blazes in flame is emphasized; whereas in the sutra, it is clearly the crown of knives which so prominently figures in later literature, such as the famous poem on galactic love by Master Dharma Rakshita.  The version we see in the Borobudur carving is also more easily pictured as being very similar to the blade of a modern circular saw.
Our Sanskrit edition says “for his mother and father”; see the lines in the Sanskrit original in Appendix C, under the same section number.
Often a reference to those belonging to the family of bodhisattvas: any person dedicated to reaching enlightenment for the good of all living beings.
This same verse, in a different translation, may be found at ff. 187a–187b of the Foundation of Vowed Morality, Part 2 (S12, KL00001-2).

This refers to a person who has reached, not yet actually full Buddhahood, but rather nirvana—the permanent cessation of negative emotions; and who has done so without having to rely, in this life, upon countless spiritual teachers.  It is invariably noted, however, that they have relied upon such mentors in numerous previous lives.  See for example f. 194a of the famed commentary by Gyaltsab Je (1364–1432) to Master Asanga’s Compendium of Higher Knowledge (B8, S05435).

These are four famous levels of spiritual advancement.  A “stream enterer” is someone who has had a direct experience of ultimate reality, and because of this experience they can later reach a level where they only have to return once to the desire realm—the lowest of three divisions of the suffering universe.  Still later they advance to a place where they need never return to this realm at all, and then finally they reach a stage where they have permanently defeated the enemy of their negative emotions.

Diamonds were known in ancient India, found in the beds of ancient rivers once connected to the diamond pipes of Africa, before the continents split apart.  The art of cutting the diamonds was not yet understood, but it was known that the stones could draw a scratch against any other physical substance, and must therefore possess immeasurable power.  By tradition they were associated with lightning; it was thought that a diamond on the tip of the bolt must be how great trees could be split in half by a strike.

Buddhist cosmology says that every planet is composed of four principal continents, separated by a great ocean.

These six groups, beginning with the Class of the Four Great Kings, are all different types of pleasure beings who live in the desire realm—the same realm of overwhelming physical desires that we ourselves inhabit.  These are tremendously powerful creatures living very long lives of pleasure, burning karma at a tremendous rate and therefore normally headed for a hell realm afterwards. The unusual names of these and the following are explained for example in the literature on Higher Knowledge (Abhidharma); we have used here primarily two sources.  The first is Illumination of the Path to Freedom, by Gyalwa Gendrun Drup (1391–1474), starting from f. 97a.  The second is Sun of the True Thought (B2, S00027), written by Choney Drakpa Shedrup (1675–1748), beginning from folio 62b. The first group are so called because they live on the upper level of Mt Meru, the great central mountain of Buddhist cosmology, led by four great kings. The second group consists of 32 powerful pleasure beings under the leadership of the most powerful being here, Shakra—“Destroyer of a Thousand Cities.”  The third group no longer has to fight with the half-pleasure beings, a common and deadly distraction of this life form.  The fourth group is involved with especially many previous good deeds—thus the “bliss.” The fifth group possesses the power to emanate objects of plesaure that they themselves enjoy the use of; whereas the sixth group can share each other’s emanated distractions.

The seventeen groups listed here, beginning with Class of the Pure One, are levels of pleasure beings within the form realm, whose inhabitants possess exquisite physical forms.  Their names are explained as follows. Those of the Class of the Pure have been free of the impurity of harmful deeds, and constitute a family of such beings.  Those who “recite before the Pure One” sit before a powerful being named “Pure One” (Brahma) and recite the holy books—the Vedas—of ancient India.  The Great Pure One is like a leader of this area who is born before the other inhabitants, and dies after them, and is physically larger than them. Beings of “Lesser Light” have a halo of light around them which is lesser in its extent than that of beings who live in levels which are higher up than theirs.  Those of “Limitless Light” possess halos of nearly infinite light.  Light from the bodies of those at “Clear Light” is so powerful that it spreads even to other levels. Pleasure beings of “Lesser Virtue” get their name from the fact that they experience relatively less mental pleasure than those who inhabit the levels above them.  The ones of “Limitless Virtue” experience unlimited mental pleasure; whereas those of “Vast Virtue” experience a degree of mental pleasure which cannot be surpassed in these levels. The level called “Cloudless,” no longer possesses the cloud-like strata structure found at the levels below it.  The next level is “Born of Merit” in that it is created by the kind of good karma which will never be redirected to a lower realm.  “Great Result” is so named because there is no greater karmic result which can be achieved by a person who has yet to see, directly, the fact that things are not themselves.

The quartet mentioned here are levels of the formless realm, where pleasure beings are born as only mental beings, with no gross physical bodies.  The names are derived from those of the four types of deep meditation required to plant the seeds for this kind of rebirth; they feel as if their minds are shutting down completely.  Once the power of these seeds is exhausted, they inevitably drop to the realms of hell—thus these particular meditations are considered an alluring but deadly trap.

lemma: The way in which things are projected
text: See f. 23a (%S6, TD03860) of Master Chandrakirti’s other classic treatment of Arya Nagarjuna’s verses, where he says, “This too I have presented in great detail in Entering the Middle Way, so please go and find it there.”  The brief title of this second work in Sanskrit, by the way, is Prasanna Pada.  Prasanna means clarified, and pada can mean either words or verses.  The former, in Tibetan, is translated as tsig; and the latter as tsigs-su bcad-pa, which is sometimes abbreviated to tsigs.  The Tibetan translation of the title of the work in our reference edition of the Tengyur (the Derge) uses the latter spelling (f. 1b) {Jiki check carving}, and in the opening section we see Master Chandrakirti promising to clarify (gsal) the verses (here tsig-le’ur byas-pa), and not the words (ff. 1b-2a).  As such, the correct English translation of the title would seem to be A Clarification of the Verses, although subsequently the Tibetan abbreviation Tsig-gsal (A Clarification of the Words) basically became universal, and we see this spelling even at the end of the Tengyur version.  Later Tibetan commentators will also make statements such as: “Master Chandrakirti’s Clarification of the Words covers the wording of the Foundational Verses called ‘Wisdom,’ whereas Entering the Middle Way covers its intent” (Kyabje Pabongka Rinpoche, 1878-1941, in The "Key that Opens the Door to the Excellent Path," being Notes of an Explanation Granted when the Holder of the Diamond, the Good and Glorious Pabongka, Granted Profound Teachings upon "The Three Principal Paths" (f. 30b, %B4, S00034).

lemma: Level where a bodhisattva is acting out of aspiration
text: This is a difficult technical term whose meaning is often disputed in the literature, but it can be definitively described as relating to the first two of the five paths for a bodhisattva; that is, the path of accumulation and the path of preparation.  One of the best references appears in the famed Great Book on the Steps of the Teaching (bsTan-rim chen-mo) of Geshe Drolungpa Lodru Jungne (c. 1100ad), whose work provided the basis and title for Je Tsongkapa’s own masterwork, the Great Book on the Steps of the Path (Lam-rim chen-mo): “Everything from here [he is in a discussion of the path of accumulation] on down is referred to as a ‘level where one is acting out of aspiration,’ because the way in which one perceives suchness is limited to nothing more than focusing upon it in aspiration [rather than through a direct perception]” (f. 4256, %B22, SE00070-2). The great Kedrup Tenpa Dargye (1493-1568) of Sera Mey Tibetan Monastery, in his Overview of the Perfection of Wisdom, concurs with Geshe Drolungpa: “And so in general, both the path of accumulation and the path of preparation for a bodhisattva are given the name of ‘a level where the bodhisattva is acting out of aspiration” (f. 133b, %B23, SE00009-1). There is, by the way, a moving description and painted scene of how Je Tsongkapa “re-discovered” Geshe Drolungpa’s work, in the traditional rendering of his life known as the “Tsongkapa Eighty” (see the definitive biography by the great Jamyang Shepay Dorje [1648-1721], both the original Tibetan and the English translation, in The King of the Dharma: The Illustrated Life of Je Tsongkapa, Teacher of the First Dalai Lama, pp. 262-3 and p. 351, %E3).

Much of Ngawang Tashi’s text is written in the form of a debate between a proponent of his own school’s position, and an opponent.  Some of the opponent’s replies are by tradition assumed, and not written in the original Tibetan.  We have supplied them in the translation together with the opponent’s other statements, all in italics—so our reader can keep track of who’s talking at any given point.  We have also numbered each paragraph in the Tibetan text, to assist scholars in locating a specific section for comment or study.  In addition, we have given a name and number to each separate debate, for the reader’s convenience; and inserted as well the folio numbers of the original Tibetan manuscript.

The reader should note that the word “form” (Sanskrit: rūpa; Tibetan: gzugs) used in the following sections can refer to three different things: (1) the first of the five “heaps” or components of a person (Skt: skandha; Tib: phung-po), in which case it refers to the entire physical component of the person and their world; (2) the first of the twelve doors of sense (Skt: āyatana; Tib: skye-mched), in which case it refers to the object of the awareness of the eye (that is, colors and shapes); and (3) the first of the 18 categories (Skt: dhātu; Tib, khams), in which case it again refers to the object of the sense power of the eye, and the awareness based upon it.  The various arguments here depend on the potentially confusing overlap of the term for these three.

That is, not directly covered by our awareness; a classical example is the tip of a hair which is still attached to our head (we do not sense it if someone pinches it); as opposed to the root of the same hair (which we do sense, if someone pulls that hair out).  See for example Light on the Path to Freedom, the commentary to Master Vasubandhu’s Treasure House of Higher Knowledge (Abhidharma Kosha) by His Holiness Gyalwa Gendun Drup (1391-1474), the First Dalai Lama (ACIP digital text catalog #S05525, %B2, f. 32b).
